(Except for "And those who have been given knowledge see" [Saba' 6], and it is four verses.) "Four" here, is that what you have? "Four" is the correct wording. "And it is fifty-four or fifty-five verses," the correct wording is "four."

His statement, "Makkan except...". The Makkan surah, according to the well-known view, is what was revealed before the Hijrah, and the Madinan is what was revealed after the Hijrah. The majority of scholars judge Makkan and Madinan by time, not by place. What came after the Hijrah is Madinan, and what came before it is Makkan.

His statement, "except '[And those who have been given knowledge see]'". We have already explained that no exception may be made from the Makkan or Madinan surahs except with evidence. That is, if a surah is Makkan, all its verses are Makkan unless there is evidence otherwise, and if it is Madinan, all its verses are Madinan unless there is evidence otherwise. The author's exception of this verse, we will examine, God willing, when we reach it. If there is evidence that it was revealed in Madinah, we accept it; otherwise we do not.

He said: "Al-hamdu lillah" (All praise is due to Allah).

Before it: "Bismillahi-r-Rahmani-r-Rahim" (In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful). It has already been established that the basmalah (the phrase "In the name of Allah...") is an independent verse of the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, which is recited to separate surahs or to begin a surah, except in Bara'ah (Surat at-Tawbah), which has no basmalah, because it was not revealed with a basmalah between it and al-Anfal, so it was left out.

We have already explained that the prepositional phrase (al-jar wa al-majrur) is dependent on an omitted element, because every prepositional phrase must depend on something. The prepositional phrase is a ma'mul (a governed element), and every ma'mul needs an 'amil (a governing element). Therefore every prepositional phrase must have a mutaʿalliq (that to which it is attached), i.e., something it depends on. The same applies to the adverbial phrase.

The mutaʿalliq is either a verb or something that has the meaning of a verb. Here we estimate it as a verb, because the verb is the basic element of government. This is why nothing other than a verb governs like a verb except under conditions, and whatever's operation depends on conditions, that is because its basic state is non-operation. Pay attention now: every prepositional phrase must have...

* A student: "Dependent on an omitted element."

* The Shaykh: Give the reason. Because the prepositional phrase is a ma'mul, and every ma'mul must have an 'amil.

The mutaʿalliq is either a verb or what has the meaning of a verb. Here we estimate it as a verb. Why? Because it is the basic form; the basic form of government is verbs. Therefore non-verbs, such as nouns, verbal nouns and similar words, do not govern like verbs except under conditions, whereas the verb governs without conditions. We estimate it (the verb) as coming after the prepositional phrase, for two benefits:

The first benefit: to honour the beginning by mentioning the name of Allah.

The second benefit: to indicate restriction (hasr).

So we estimate the governing element as coming later, in view of these two benefits, and we estimate it as a specific verb. For example, at the beginning of recitation we say, "In the name of Allah I recite." At ablution: "In the name of Allah I perform ablution." At eating: "In the name of Allah I eat," and so on. We estimate it specifically because it is more indicative of the intended meaning. It is also correct to estimate it generally, saying, "In the name of Allah I begin," or "In the name of Allah I start," but the specific is better.

So now we have three matters: there must be a mutaʿalliq; it comes later; and it is specific. We have also learned the reasons.

Here, "Bismillah" is a singular noun in the construct state, so it is general in meaning, and the meaning is: "With every name of Allah I begin." Mentioning "Ar-Rahman" and "Ar-Rahim" rather than other names is fitting, because the basmalah is recited for seeking help, and the most fitting attribute for seeking help is mercy. Therefore the word of majesty (Allah) is followed by these two noble names.

"Allah" originally is al-Ilah (the God). This is the most correct view about it. The hamzah was dropped because of frequent use, just as the hamzah was dropped in "an-nas" (the people), whose original form is "unas," and the hamzah was dropped in "sharr" and "khayr" (evil and good), whose original forms are "ashar" and "akhyar."

As for "Ar-Rahman," it is one of the names of Allah indicating the vastness of His mercy, may He be exalted, because the pattern fa'lan indicates vastness and fullness. Look at words like ghadban (angry), nadman (regretful), sakran (drunk), atshan (thirsty), and rayyan (sated), and similar words, and you will find that this pattern indicates what? Vastness and fullness. This is why some of the early scholars said: "Ar-Rahman is a general mercy for all creation."

As for "Ar-Rahim," it indicates the act, that is, that He, may He be exalted, shows mercy through His vast mercy. So ar-Rahim indicates the act, which is bestowing mercy upon the one who is shown mercy, and ar-Rahman indicates the attribute, which is Allah's being characterised by this vast mercy.

Then he said: "Al-hamdu lillah" (All praise is due to Allah): He, exalted, praised Himself with this, and what is meant by it is praise by its content, which is the affirmation of praise. It is the description of Allah, exalted, with what is beautiful.

His statement: "Al-hamdu lillahi alladhi lahu ma fi as-samawat" (All praise is due to Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens...) [Saba' 1].

"Al-hamdu lillah": The scholars say that the definite article "al" here is for comprehensiveness (istighraq), meaning every praise. The "al" of comprehensiveness is one that can be replaced by "kull" (every). Like: "Indeed, mankind is in loss" [al-'Asr 2], meaning every human being is in loss. "And mankind was created weak" [an-Nisa' 28], meaning every human being. So what is the "al" in "al-hamdu lillah"?

* A student: Comprehensiveness.

* The Shaykh: Comprehensiveness. So its meaning is that every praise belongs to Allah. The lam here is for entitlement (istihqaq) and exclusivity (ikhtisas): for entitlement, because no one deserves to be praised for his own essence except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; and for exclusivity, because praise that encompasses all praiseworthy qualities belongs only to Allah.

The author says: "He, exalted, praised Himself with that," meaning Allah, exalted, praised Himself with this attribute, which is praise. "And what is meant by it is praise by its content, which is the affirmation of praise," meaning this is not a renewal of praising Allah, but a commendation of Allah through the content of praise. "And it is the description of Allah, exalted, with what is beautiful." If the author had said "with perfection," it would have been more general, since praise is describing the praised one with perfection. If one repeats describing Him with perfection, it becomes commendation. Allah, exalted, says: "All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds" [al-Fatihah 2], and Allah responds: "My servant has praised Me." "The Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful" [al-Fatihah 3], Allah responds: "My servant has extolled Me" [recorded by Muslim (395/38) from Abu Hurayrah]. Allah, exalted, is praised for His intrinsic perfection and for His perfection that extends to others, that is, for His perfection in His essence, and for His perfection in His actions and His beneficence, exalted is He. So He is praised for both. As for others, they are praised only for their actions, if their actions are praiseworthy. But praise for the essence itself is not for anyone except Allah.

For example, if we praise Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for His attributes of perfection, such as hearing, sight, knowledge, power, greatness and similar, this is praise for intrinsic perfection. If Allah, exalted, is praised for His favours and bounties, this is praise for perfection that extends to others. If we praise Him, exalted, for sending rain, sending down books, sending messengers, and removing harm, this is praise for extended perfection.

"Al-hamdu lillahi alladhi lahu ma fi as-samawati wa ma fi al-ard" (All praise is due to Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth) [Saba' 1]: (in sovereignty and creation).

"Alladhi lahu ma fi as-samawat" serves as a kind of reason for the praise, because this description indicates causation, that is, Allah praises Himself because He owns what is in the heavens and what is on the earth.

His statement: "Lahu ma fi as-samawati wa ma fi al-ard" includes rational and non-rational beings, and for this reason He used "ma" so that it includes both. He gave precedence to non-rational beings because they are greater in number by type. As for number, there is doubt about this, because the angels, peace be upon them, are without doubt rational, and no one can count them except Allah. There is not a space of four fingers in the sky except that there is an angel in it [recorded by Ibn Majah (4190) and at-Tirmidhi (2312) from Abu Dharr, who narrated it as a marfu' hadith: "The sky creaked and it has a right to creak, there is not a space of four fingers in it except that an angel is placing his forehead in prostration to Allah."]

His statement: "As-samawati wa ma fi al-ard." "As-samawat" is plural, and it is pluralised because there are many. How many? Seven heavens, each above the other, and it is derived from sumuww, which means height and elevation.

"Wa ma fi al-ard" is singular in form, but what is meant is the category, so it includes the seven earths. The earths are seven by explicit Sunnah and seven by the apparent meaning of the Qur'an. They are seven by explicit Sunnah, due to the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever takes unjustly a span of land, it will be hung around his neck on the Day of Resurrection from seven earths" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3198) and Muslim (1610/137), the wording being Muslim's, from Sa'id ibn Zayd].

And by the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, due to the saying of Allah, exalted: "Allah is the One who created seven heavens and of the earth, the like thereof" [at-Talaq 12]. The likeness here is certainly not in attribute, so it must be in number.

The author's statement: "Malikan wa khalqan" (in sovereignty and creation) means that He is the One who created them, exalted, and He is their Owner and Regulator. If the author had said "and management," it would have been clearer, although the word "malikan" (sovereignty) implies management. Allah, exalted, has whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth in creation: none created them except Allah; and in sovereignty: none owns them except Allah; and in management: no one has management over them in absolute terms except Allah, exalted.

His statement: "Wa lahu al-hamdu fi al-akhirah" (And to Him belongs praise in the Hereafter), "as in this world, His allies praise Him when they enter Paradise."

His statement: "Wa lahu al-hamdu fi al-akhirah." Here He specified praise in the Hereafter, although He is praised in this world and the Hereafter, as Allah, exalted, says in another verse: "To Him is praise in the first and the last, and to Him is the judgement" [al-Qasas 70]. But He mentioned it because the manifestation of His praise in the Hereafter is clearer and more evident, since in this world there are those who deny the praise of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and disbelieve in Him. And [...] except that this world is a nature that interacts by itself, and has no regulator. Whoever holds this belief, can he praise Allah? Never, it is impossible, even if he sees good and the repelling of evil, he does not praise Allah, because he does not acknowledge Him. But in the Hereafter, no one can help but praise Allah, so praise in the Hereafter is for Allah.

Just as in the Hereafter, no one is praised except rarely. Allah said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praised station" [al-Isra' 79]. As for the rest of the people whom Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has not praised, they have no praise in the Hereafter. You praise in this world the one who does good to you, but in the Hereafter you do not praise your friend or companion, unless that happens after entering Paradise, perhaps.

He says: "Wa lahu al-hamdu fi al-akhirah" (as in this world), meaning as He has praise in this world. It seems that the author, may Allah have mercy on him, with this statement, means that he omitted the other part because the context indicates it, as in the saying of Allah, exalted: "And He made for you garments that protect you from the heat" [an-Nahl 81], meaning and the cold.

His statement: "[His allies praise Him when they enter Paradise]." Allah, exalted, says: "And they will say, 'Praise be to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us and has caused us to inherit the land'" [az-Zumar 74].

But the correct view is that He is praised even for His requital of the disbelievers. At the end of Surat az-Zumar, when Allah mentioned the driving of the people of the Fire to the Fire and the driving of the people of Paradise to Paradise, He said: "And it will be judged between them in truth, and it will be said, 'All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds'" [az-Zumar 75]. Allah, exalted, is praised for His complete justice and His complete grace, and for His recompense of the people of the Fire, on what basis? On the basis of justice, so He is praised for it.

He said: "[His allies praise Him when they enter Paradise], 'And He is the Wise' [in His actions], 'the All-Aware' [of His creation]."

"Al-Hakim": The author says "in His action," and this is deficient, because He is wise in His legislation and also in His action, which is the decree (al-qadar). Wisdom is not specific to action; even in legislation, which is through His speech, legislation is revelation, and it is the speech of Allah, not His action. Rather, it is speech. Likewise His action is wise.

Wisdom (al-hikmah) is derived from ihkam, which is perfection of work. This is why it is said in its definition that it is placing a thing in its proper place, and this is perfection.

But we have already learned that al-Hakim has two meanings: the Judge (al-Hakim) and the One who perfects (al-Muhkim), since it derives from judgement (al-hukm) and perfection (al-ihkam). How many kinds is the judgement of Allah?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes.

* The student: Legislative and cosmic.

* The Shaykh: Correct, the judgement is legislative and cosmic. And wisdom also has two kinds?

* A student: Judgement is from perfection.

* The Shaykh: From where is the judgement?

* The student: Wisdom...

* The Shaykh: Yes, two kinds.

* The student: Wisdom is from perfection.

* The Shaykh: It is all from perfection, no, it has no connection with judgement.

* A student: Formal and final.

* The Shaykh: Formal and final. The formal means that this thing being in this specific form is in accordance with wisdom, and the final means that the purpose of this thing is a wisdom for which Allah is praised.

For example: the prayer being in this manner, fasting in this manner, and ablution in this manner, these are in legislative matters.

Likewise, in cosmic matters, the creation of man in this manner, the sun and the moon, and similar things, these are formal wisdom, meaning that the thing being in this particular form is without doubt in accordance with wisdom. Then the purpose of that thing is another wisdom.

This formal and final wisdom exists in legislation, then what? And in decree. If you multiply two by two, it is four. There is final wisdom in legislation, formal wisdom in legislation, final wisdom in decree, formal wisdom in decree, and all of this is established for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. When a person believes in this, he is at peace with the judgements of Allah, cosmic and legislative, and no objection arises in his mind, because he knows that this proceeds from wisdom. When he knows it proceeds from wisdom, no doubt remains in his heart that this is the exact correct thing, which wisdom requires. By this a person becomes at peace with the law of Allah, and at peace also with the decree of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and knows that this is the correct thing, and nothing else is permissible.

His statement: "[The All-Aware]." The author says: "of His creation." Al-Khabir means the one who possesses khibrah, which is knowledge of the hidden aspects of matters. From this, the farmer is called khabir, because he conceals the seed by ploughing. So al-Khabir is the one who possesses khibrah, which is knowledge of the hidden aspects of matters.

Does that contradict knowledge of the outward aspects of matters? No, rather it confirms it, because whoever knows the hidden aspects of matters certainly knows the outward aspects.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, always pairs wisdom with might and knowledge. Here it is paired with what? With the knowledge contained in khibrah. Allah pairs it with that to make clear that His wisdom, exalted is He, is based on His knowledge, and that if it appears to you that something is not wise, that is due to deficiency in your knowledge. Otherwise, if you had knowledge and understanding, you would know that wisdom lies in what Allah legislated and what He decreed.

Then He explained or detailed some of His knowledge, saying: "[He knows what enters the earth] [Saba' 2], like water and other things; [and what emerges from it], like plants and other things; [and what descends from the sky], like provision and other things; [and what ascends into it], it rises, from deeds and other things." This is by way of detail.

"Ya'lamu ma yalig fi al-ard" (He knows what enters the earth). "Ma" is a relative pronoun that conveys generality, and "yaliju" means "enters." Everything that enters the earth, Allah, exalted, knows it.

The author says: "like water." Does water enter the earth or come out of it? It enters and comes out. When Allah sends down water from the sky, He makes it enter the earth as springs, and when Allah, exalted, wants it to come out, it comes out by a means or without a means.

His statement: "and other things." What is other than water that enters the earth?

* A student: The dead.

* The Shaykh: The dead, and what else?

* A student: Animals, like snakes.

* The Shaykh: Yes, and things that have burrows in the earth. Right? Do we not say plants as well? Plants too, all their seeds enter the earth.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 34, verse 1–2 (part 2 of 2):

The point is that what enters the earth cannot be counted in its kinds, let alone its individual members, and it is extremely vast. Allah, glorified and exalted, knows it all; even the ant that enters its hole, Allah knows it.

﴿وَمَا يَخْرُجُ مِنْهَا﴾ (and what comes out of it). The author says: (like plants and other things). Plants are clear. "Other things" are like water, minerals and the animals that spread over the earth. Do we say: and among that is man?

﴿مِنْهَا خَلَقْنَاكُمْ﴾ [Ta-Ha 55] (From it We created you). This is the origin, yes indeed. ﴿مِنْهَا خَلَقْنَاكُمْ وَفِيهَا نُعِيدُكُمْ﴾ (From it We created you, and into it We will return you): it is bringing out and putting back in. ﴿وَاللَّهُ أَنْبَتَكُمْ مِنَ الْأَرْضِ نَبَاتًا (١٧) ثُمَّ يُعِيدُكُمْ فِيهَا وَيُخْرِجُكُمْ إِخْرَاجًا﴾ [Nuh 17-18] (And Allah has caused you to grow from the earth like plants. Then He will return you into it and bring you out with a (final) bringing forth).

He says: ﴿وَمَا يَنْزِلُ مِنَ السَّمَاءِ﴾ [Saba 2] (and what descends from the sky) (of provision and other things). How does provision descend from the sky? Do you stay at home every day and dates descend on you from the sky, or clothes? No, but provision comes by rain. For example, Allah sends down rain, so the earth grows and water and pasture come out of it: ﴿مَتَاعًا لَكُمْ وَلِأَنْعَامِكُمْ﴾ [An-Nazi'at 33] (as a provision for you and your livestock). Is it clear?

Besides this, what else descends? The command of Allah, Mighty and Majestic descends: ﴿يُدَبِّرُ الْأَمْرَ مِنَ السَّمَاءِ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ﴾ [As-Sajdah 5] (He arranges the affair from the heaven to the earth). Angels also descend, and shooting stars are thrown at the devils, and many other things of this kind. And Allah knows it.

﴿وَمَا يَعْرُجُ﴾ (and what ascends). He says: (ascends ﴿فِيهَا﴾ of deeds and other things).

Here ﴿يَعْرُجُ﴾ means "ascends", yes? And ya'ruju is transitive with (ila) as Allah said: ﴿تَعْرُجُ الْمَلَائِكَةُ وَالرُّوحُ إِلَيْهِ﴾ [Al-Ma'arij 4] (The angels and the Spirit ascend to Him), and He said: ﴿يُدَبِّرُ الْأَمْرَ مِنَ السَّمَاءِ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ ثُمَّ يَعْرُجُ إِلَيْهِ﴾ [As-Sajdah 5] (then it ascends to Him). And here He said: ﴿يَعْرُجُ فِيهَا﴾ (ascends into it). The grammarians differed regarding such cases. Some of them said: a preposition is used with the meaning of another preposition that suits the verb; that is, the preposition is taken to mean another preposition that suits the verb. For example, they say (fi) means (ila).

Others say: rather, the preposition remains on its original meaning, and the verb is made to include (takmin) a meaning that suits that preposition. This is the view of the Basrans. So they say: ﴿يَعْرُجُ﴾ includes, along with its apparent meaning, which is ascending, the meaning of entering. That is, it ascends and enters into it. The intention is not only ascending, nor only entering; it ascends and enters into it.

Earlier in our study of the introduction to tafsir by Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah (takmin), we noted that this view is the correct and verified view: that the verb is made to include a meaning that suits the preposition. This is because such inclusion gives the verb two meanings:
First: the apparent meaning of the wording.
Second: the meaning it includes to suit the preposition attached to it.
This becomes clear to you in His saying: ﴿عَيْنًا يَشْرَبُ بِهَا عِبَادُ اللَّهِ﴾ [Al-Insan 6] (a spring from which the servants of Allah drink). It is known that we do not drink with a spring; it is not a tool, not a vessel, not an instrument of drinking. You say: I drink with the cup, correct. But does one drink with it while it is a spring? It cannot be a vessel for him.

Some scholars hold that we take the ba' (bi) to mean (min), i.e., "drink from it."
Others hold that we make ﴿يَشْرَبُ﴾ include the meaning of ﴿يَرْوَى﴾ (to quench). When we make (yashrabu) include the meaning of (yarwa), we gain two benefits: drinking, and what else? Quenching. But if we say that the ba' means (min), we do not gain this benefit.

So the point is that the correct view is that we make a verb include a meaning that suits the preposition, and we do not make the preposition mean another preposition.

He says: (﴿وَهُوَ الرَّحِيمُ﴾ to His friends ﴿الْغَفُورُ﴾ [Saba 2] to them). This too is specification without evidence.

The word ﴿الرَّحِيمُ﴾ has no mentioned object, and the author, may Allah have mercy on him, says: (to His friends). Accordingly, His enemies would have no mercy. This is the author's statement. And ﴿الْغَفُورُ﴾ is also for His friends, so His enemies have no forgiveness.

But the correct view is generality, because these two names are unrestricted, so they remain on their unrestricted sense. He is merciful even to His enemies: Allah has given the disbelieiver health and provision of clothing, food, drink, dwelling, spouse and family, and all this is mercy, but it is a general mercy, meaning it is not special like the mercy of the believers.

Forgiveness is also deserved by one who repents from his enmity toward Allah, and when he repents he becomes one of the friends of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. But a person may have both enmity and friendship, or not? ﴿خَلَطُوا عَمَلًا صَالِحًا وَآخَرَ سَيِّئًا﴾ [At-Tawbah 102] (They mixed a righteous deed with another evil one), and they deserve the forgiveness of Allah, glorified and exalted. And Allah knows best.

* Student: (...) specific to the believers.
* Shaykh: No, general, as we said a moment ago: al-Rahim, its meaning is specific to the act, meaning conveying mercy to the one shown mercy. After it, tawhid, I think?
* Student: The indication of the seven.
* Shaykh: Yes indeed.
* Student: Is there not a possibility that these seven are an added punishment upon them?
* Shaykh: No, there is no such possibility.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes indeed, we left it, because some scholars declared it weak (...).

﴿الْحَكِيمُ﴾ [Saba 1] means "ruling" (hakim, a judge), so it is an intensive form (fa'il). And if hakim is from ahkama, then it means muhkim (one who perfects).
And fa'il comes with the meaning of mufil. We have recited to you a verse earlier:
"Is it from Rayhana, the calling, the hearing, that keeps me awake..."
(...).

* Student: The benefits.
* Shaykh: The benefits.
* Among the benefits of the preceding verses: the establishment of complete praise for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in His saying: ﴿الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ﴾ and so on to the end.
Second: that this praise which is established for Him is what He deserves; from His saying: ﴿لِلَّهِ﴾, because the lam, as we said, is for entitlement and specificity.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, praising Himself for the benefit of the servants; because we cannot praise Allah or count His praises. So when Allah praises Himself, this is for our benefit, because He, Mighty and Majestic, teaches us how to praise Him and how to extol Him. He is worthy of praising Himself, glorified and exalted, and extolling Himself for the benefit of His servants. Otherwise He is free of needing to show us the attributes of perfection that He shows, free of needing us to know that; but this is for our benefit.

This benefit may be built upon a hypothetical question: How does Allah praise Himself? And is a person praising himself considered a virtue or not?

The answer: it is said that Allah praises Himself not because He needs us to praise Him or to know His perfection, since He is perfect; but for what? For our benefit, since we cannot count His praise, and we do not know what to praise Him with except through His revelation.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the generality of Allah's dominion, from His saying: ﴿الَّذِي لَهُ مَا فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَمَا فِي الْأَرْضِ﴾ [Saba 1] (to Whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth). Here He praised Himself for the generality of His dominion. He may praise Himself for His act, such as: ﴿الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الَّذِي لَهُ مَا فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَمَا فِي الْأَرْضِ﴾ [Saba 1], and He may praise Himself for His legislation, such as: ﴿الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الَّذِي خَلَقَ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضَ وَجَعَلَ الظُّلُمَاتِ وَالنُّورَ﴾ [Al-An'am 1], ﴿الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الَّذِي أَنْزَلَ عَلَى عَبْدِهِ الْكِتَابَ وَلَمْ يَجْعَلْ لَهُ عِوَجًا﴾ [Al-Kahf 1].
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the heavens are plural, meaning more than one, from His saying: ﴿السَّمَاوَاتِ﴾; and other evidence establishes that they are seven, and likewise the earth.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the manifestation of Allah's perfection on the Day of Resurrection is clearer than in this world, from His saying: ﴿وَلَهُ الْحَمْدُ فِي الْآخِرَةِ﴾ (And to Him belongs praise in the Hereafter). So dominion is general, and the clear, evident manifestation of praise occurs in the Hereafter.
* Among them: the establishment of resurrection, from His saying: ﴿الْآخِرَةِ﴾.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the establishment of Allah's cosmic and legislative decree and His wisdom related to the cosmos and related to the law.
* Following from this principle: the obligation to submit to His cosmic and legislative decree, such that we want no objection to it, even if it comes in what appears to contradict wisdom; we must suspect our minds, because when it is established that He, glorified and exalted, is wise in both the cosmic and the legislative judgment, it follows that we must submit to the cosmic and legislative decree, since it proceeds from wisdom; but that wisdom may be hidden from us.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the generality of Allah's knowledge, derived from His saying: ﴿الْخَبِيرُ﴾ and the detail that follows it, because the Khabir is the one who knows the inner realities, and one who knows the inner realities knows the outer ones.
* Among its benefits: the establishment of these two noble names of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: al-Hakim (the Wise) and al-Khabir (the All-Aware).
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that among the rhetorical methods is generalization followed by detail, from His saying: ﴿الْخَبِيرُ (١) يَعْلَمُ﴾ to the end [Saba 1-2].
The benefit of this rhetorical method is that when a matter comes in general terms, souls become eager for its details; so when the details arrive upon souls that are yearning for them, they fall more strongly upon the soul and take firmer root in the heart. Is that not so?

If I tell you: Something great happened last night, and you did not know; at one in the night last night a great event happened, which you did not know. What would it be? You long for it, you strain to know what this great thing is. But if I tell you: Last night, for example, a star was thrown and gave off a great light, in any case you accept this report, but it is not like the first, because you will say: What is this great thing? (...) a great thing, what is this thing? (...) what is this thing? Until it reaches your heart, and you have been yearning for it greatly.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the completeness of Allah's disposal of His creatures: this one enters, this one exits, this one descends, this one ascends: ﴿يَعْلَمُ مَا يَلِجُ فِي الْأَرْضِ وَمَا يَخْرُجُ مِنْهَا وَمَا يَنْزِلُ مِنَ السَّمَاءِ وَمَا يَعْرُجُ فِيهَا﴾ [Saba 2].
* Among its benefits, which is a rhetorical benefit: beginning with what is closest to man, even if something else is more noble; because you speak of what enters the earth and what comes out of it before you speak of what descends from the sky and what ascends into it.
Here this benefit is based on the premise that the sky is nobler than the earth. Is this agreed upon? Do not hurry: is it agreed that the sky is nobler than the earth, or the earth nobler than the sky?
This is a matter of disagreement among the scholars, with much debate. Some hold that the sky is nobler, and say: the sky, even if it contained only the angels brought near, is a high direction, and in the sky also is Allah, Mighty and Majestic, above it.
Others hold that the earth is nobler, saying: because the best of creation, the prophets and messengers, were created from it. So it is nobler. This dispute, though it may be said to be one of the superfluous matters of knowledge, nevertheless at first glance a person sees the sky as nobler than the earth; but the earth is mentioned here because it touches us more and we know more about it.
* Also among the benefits of the noble verse: the establishment of mercy and forgiveness for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in His saying: ﴿وَهُوَ الرَّحِيمُ الْغَفُورُ﴾. Here He placed al-Rahim before al-Ghafur, although in the Qur'an it is more common to place al-Ghafur before al-Rahim; this is because of the benefits and interests that exist in the heavens and the earth, and benefits and interests come from the effects of what? Mercy. And averting calamities comes from the effects of forgiveness, because forgiveness is the erasing of the sin in which disliked things revolve, while mercy is the attainment of good.
Mercy, according to the People of the Sunnah and the Community, is one of the attributes of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, a real attribute established for Him. The Ash'arites say that mercy is benevolence, or the will to benevolence, so they explain it as the thing done by Allah, meaning blessings, or the will to blessings. Why? Because they affirm the attribute of what? The attribute of will; so they explain mercy as the will to bestow and benevolence, or as the bestowing and benevolence itself.
But we have already noted that the correct and definitively established view is that the texts of the Book and the Sunnah concerning the names and attributes of Allah are to be taken according to their apparent meaning.
Is there a need to say "fitting for Allah"? No; we say "fitting for Allah" only for clarification, because we know with certain knowledge that their apparent meaning is fitting for Allah, and their apparent meaning is not, as the people of negation (ta'til) claim, resemblance (tashbih); for if the apparent meaning of the texts of the Book and the Sunnah in the names and attributes of Allah were resemblance or likeness, then the apparent meaning of the Qur'an and Sunnah in this matter would be disbelief; because whoever likens Allah to His creation has disbelieved, having denied His saying: ﴿لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِ شَيْءٌ﴾ [Ash-Shura 11] (There is nothing like unto Him). And it is impossible that the apparent meaning of the truth should be falsehood and disbelief. Therefore, when we say that the texts of the Book and Sunnah concerning the names and attributes of Allah are to be taken according to their apparent meaning, which is fitting for Allah, this is for the sake of what? For the sake of clarification. Otherwise we know with certain knowledge, more certain than the sun, that its apparent meaning is what is fitting for Allah, so there is no need to restrict it with that; but we may restrict it only for clarification.
Is mercy an attribute of perfection in itself, regardless of the one it is attributed to, or an attribute of deficiency? It is in reality an attribute of perfection, even mercy in (...).
....................... ∗∗∗ ...like placing the sword in the place of generosity
The verse is well known, is it not?
He says: placing generosity... Generosity: giving and spending.
Placing generosity in the place of the sword is harmful to nobility: ... like placing the sword in the place of generosity.
The wisdom of this: he says that placing generosity in the place of the sword is harmful to nobility and to good character. Why? Because the one who deserves the sword, it is best not to put the sword to him. A criminal corrupting the earth whom we have seized and overpowered: we say, "O boy, look, this villa is yours, this car is yours, and this warehouse full of treasures of gold and silver is yours, because you are a criminal." Is that wisdom or not? It is not wisdom.
Like placing the sword in the place of generosity: a person of goodness and kindness, deserving of honor, is brought and placed on the executioner's mat, and we say, "We will kill you now, because you are a benefactor." Is this wisdom or not? It is not wisdom. So this verse is among the greatest verses of wisdom, and al-Mutanabbi is known as the wisest of poets.
* Student: Abu al-'Ala.
* Shaykh: No, al-Mutanabbi.

So we say: mercy is an attribute of perfection in itself, and when it is ascribed to Allah it becomes more and more perfect.

(Except for "And those who have been given knowledge see" [Saba' 6], and it is four verses.) "Four" here, is that what you have? "Four" is the correct wording. "And it is fifty-four or fifty-five verses," the correct wording is "four."

His statement, "Makkan except...". The Makkan surah, according to the well-known view, is what was revealed before the Hijrah, and the Madinan is what was revealed after the Hijrah. The majority of scholars judge Makkan and Madinan by time, not by place. What came after the Hijrah is Madinan, and what came before it is Makkan.

His statement, "except '[And those who have been given knowledge see]'". We have already explained that no exception may be made from the Makkan or Madinan surahs except with evidence. That is, if a surah is Makkan, all its verses are Makkan unless there is evidence otherwise, and if it is Madinan, all its verses are Madinan unless there is evidence otherwise. The author's exception of this verse, we will examine, God willing, when we reach it. If there is evidence that it was revealed in Madinah, we accept it; otherwise we do not.

He said: "Al-hamdu lillah" (All praise is due to Allah).

Before it: "Bismillahi-r-Rahmani-r-Rahim" (In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful). It has already been established that the basmalah (the phrase "In the name of Allah...") is an independent verse of the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, which is recited to separate surahs or to begin a surah, except in Bara'ah (Surat at-Tawbah), which has no basmalah, because it was not revealed with a basmalah between it and al-Anfal, so it was left out.

We have already explained that the prepositional phrase (al-jar wa al-majrur) is dependent on an omitted element, because every prepositional phrase must depend on something. The prepositional phrase is a ma'mul (a governed element), and every ma'mul needs an 'amil (a governing element). Therefore every prepositional phrase must have a mutaʿalliq (that to which it is attached), i.e., something it depends on. The same applies to the adverbial phrase.

The mutaʿalliq is either a verb or something that has the meaning of a verb. Here we estimate it as a verb, because the verb is the basic element of government. This is why nothing other than a verb governs like a verb except under conditions, and whatever's operation depends on conditions, that is because its basic state is non-operation. Pay attention now: every prepositional phrase must have...

* A student: "Dependent on an omitted element."

* The Shaykh: Give the reason. Because the prepositional phrase is a ma'mul, and every ma'mul must have an 'amil.

The mutaʿalliq is either a verb or what has the meaning of a verb. Here we estimate it as a verb. Why? Because it is the basic form; the basic form of government is verbs. Therefore non-verbs, such as nouns, verbal nouns and similar words, do not govern like verbs except under conditions, whereas the verb governs without conditions. We estimate it (the verb) as coming after the prepositional phrase, for two benefits:

The first benefit: to honour the beginning by mentioning the name of Allah.

The second benefit: to indicate restriction (hasr).

So we estimate the governing element as coming later, in view of these two benefits, and we estimate it as a specific verb. For example, at the beginning of recitation we say, "In the name of Allah I recite." At ablution: "In the name of Allah I perform ablution." At eating: "In the name of Allah I eat," and so on. We estimate it specifically because it is more indicative of the intended meaning. It is also correct to estimate it generally, saying, "In the name of Allah I begin," or "In the name of Allah I start," but the specific is better.

So now we have three matters: there must be a mutaʿalliq; it comes later; and it is specific. We have also learned the reasons.

Here, "Bismillah" is a singular noun in the construct state, so it is general in meaning, and the meaning is: "With every name of Allah I begin." Mentioning "Ar-Rahman" and "Ar-Rahim" rather than other names is fitting, because the basmalah is recited for seeking help, and the most fitting attribute for seeking help is mercy. Therefore the word of majesty (Allah) is followed by these two noble names.

"Allah" originally is al-Ilah (the God). This is the most correct view about it. The hamzah was dropped because of frequent use, just as the hamzah was dropped in "an-nas" (the people), whose original form is "unas," and the hamzah was dropped in "sharr" and "khayr" (evil and good), whose original forms are "ashar" and "akhyar."

As for "Ar-Rahman," it is one of the names of Allah indicating the vastness of His mercy, may He be exalted, because the pattern fa'lan indicates vastness and fullness. Look at words like ghadban (angry), nadman (regretful), sakran (drunk), atshan (thirsty), and rayyan (sated), and similar words, and you will find that this pattern indicates what? Vastness and fullness. This is why some of the early scholars said: "Ar-Rahman is a general mercy for all creation."

As for "Ar-Rahim," it indicates the act, that is, that He, may He be exalted, shows mercy through His vast mercy. So ar-Rahim indicates the act, which is bestowing mercy upon the one who is shown mercy, and ar-Rahman indicates the attribute, which is Allah's being characterised by this vast mercy.

Then he said: "Al-hamdu lillah" (All praise is due to Allah): He, exalted, praised Himself with this, and what is meant by it is praise by its content, which is the affirmation of praise. It is the description of Allah, exalted, with what is beautiful.

His statement: "Al-hamdu lillahi alladhi lahu ma fi as-samawat" (All praise is due to Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens...) [Saba' 1].

"Al-hamdu lillah": The scholars say that the definite article "al" here is for comprehensiveness (istighraq), meaning every praise. The "al" of comprehensiveness is one that can be replaced by "kull" (every). Like: "Indeed, mankind is in loss" [al-'Asr 2], meaning every human being is in loss. "And mankind was created weak" [an-Nisa' 28], meaning every human being. So what is the "al" in "al-hamdu lillah"?

* A student: Comprehensiveness.

* The Shaykh: Comprehensiveness. So its meaning is that every praise belongs to Allah. The lam here is for entitlement (istihqaq) and exclusivity (ikhtisas): for entitlement, because no one deserves to be praised for his own essence except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; and for exclusivity, because praise that encompasses all praiseworthy qualities belongs only to Allah.

The author says: "He, exalted, praised Himself with that," meaning Allah, exalted, praised Himself with this attribute, which is praise. "And what is meant by it is praise by its content, which is the affirmation of praise," meaning this is not a renewal of praising Allah, but a commendation of Allah through the content of praise. "And it is the description of Allah, exalted, with what is beautiful." If the author had said "with perfection," it would have been more general, since praise is describing the praised one with perfection. If one repeats describing Him with perfection, it becomes commendation. Allah, exalted, says: "All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds" [al-Fatihah 2], and Allah responds: "My servant has praised Me." "The Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful" [al-Fatihah 3], Allah responds: "My servant has extolled Me" [recorded by Muslim (395/38) from Abu Hurayrah]. Allah, exalted, is praised for His intrinsic perfection and for His perfection that extends to others, that is, for His perfection in His essence, and for His perfection in His actions and His beneficence, exalted is He. So He is praised for both. As for others, they are praised only for their actions, if their actions are praiseworthy. But praise for the essence itself is not for anyone except Allah.

For example, if we praise Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for His attributes of perfection, such as hearing, sight, knowledge, power, greatness and similar, this is praise for intrinsic perfection. If Allah, exalted, is praised for His favours and bounties, this is praise for perfection that extends to others. If we praise Him, exalted, for sending rain, sending down books, sending messengers, and removing harm, this is praise for extended perfection.

"Al-hamdu lillahi alladhi lahu ma fi as-samawati wa ma fi al-ard" (All praise is due to Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth) [Saba' 1]: (in sovereignty and creation).

"Alladhi lahu ma fi as-samawat" serves as a kind of reason for the praise, because this description indicates causation, that is, Allah praises Himself because He owns what is in the heavens and what is on the earth.

His statement: "Lahu ma fi as-samawati wa ma fi al-ard" includes rational and non-rational beings, and for this reason He used "ma" so that it includes both. He gave precedence to non-rational beings because they are greater in number by type. As for number, there is doubt about this, because the angels, peace be upon them, are without doubt rational, and no one can count them except Allah. There is not a space of four fingers in the sky except that there is an angel in it [recorded by Ibn Majah (4190) and at-Tirmidhi (2312) from Abu Dharr, who narrated it as a marfu' hadith: "The sky creaked and it has a right to creak, there is not a space of four fingers in it except that an angel is placing his forehead in prostration to Allah."]

His statement: "As-samawati wa ma fi al-ard." "As-samawat" is plural, and it is pluralised because there are many. How many? Seven heavens, each above the other, and it is derived from sumuww, which means height and elevation.

"Wa ma fi al-ard" is singular in form, but what is meant is the category, so it includes the seven earths. The earths are seven by explicit Sunnah and seven by the apparent meaning of the Qur'an. They are seven by explicit Sunnah, due to the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever takes unjustly a span of land, it will be hung around his neck on the Day of Resurrection from seven earths" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3198) and Muslim (1610/137), the wording being Muslim's, from Sa'id ibn Zayd].

And by the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, due to the saying of Allah, exalted: "Allah is the One who created seven heavens and of the earth, the like thereof" [at-Talaq 12]. The likeness here is certainly not in attribute, so it must be in number.

The author's statement: "Malikan wa khalqan" (in sovereignty and creation) means that He is the One who created them, exalted, and He is their Owner and Regulator. If the author had said "and management," it would have been clearer, although the word "malikan" (sovereignty) implies management. Allah, exalted, has whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth in creation: none created them except Allah; and in sovereignty: none owns them except Allah; and in management: no one has management over them in absolute terms except Allah, exalted.

His statement: "Wa lahu al-hamdu fi al-akhirah" (And to Him belongs praise in the Hereafter), "as in this world, His allies praise Him when they enter Paradise."

His statement: "Wa lahu al-hamdu fi al-akhirah." Here He specified praise in the Hereafter, although He is praised in this world and the Hereafter, as Allah, exalted, says in another verse: "To Him is praise in the first and the last, and to Him is the judgement" [al-Qasas 70]. But He mentioned it because the manifestation of His praise in the Hereafter is clearer and more evident, since in this world there are those who deny the praise of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and disbelieve in Him. And [...] except that this world is a nature that interacts by itself, and has no regulator. Whoever holds this belief, can he praise Allah? Never, it is impossible, even if he sees good and the repelling of evil, he does not praise Allah, because he does not acknowledge Him. But in the Hereafter, no one can help but praise Allah, so praise in the Hereafter is for Allah.

Just as in the Hereafter, no one is praised except rarely. Allah said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praised station" [al-Isra' 79]. As for the rest of the people whom Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has not praised, they have no praise in the Hereafter. You praise in this world the one who does good to you, but in the Hereafter you do not praise your friend or companion, unless that happens after entering Paradise, perhaps.

He says: "Wa lahu al-hamdu fi al-akhirah" (as in this world), meaning as He has praise in this world. It seems that the author, may Allah have mercy on him, with this statement, means that he omitted the other part because the context indicates it, as in the saying of Allah, exalted: "And He made for you garments that protect you from the heat" [an-Nahl 81], meaning and the cold.

His statement: "[His allies praise Him when they enter Paradise]." Allah, exalted, says: "And they will say, 'Praise be to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us and has caused us to inherit the land'" [az-Zumar 74].

But the correct view is that He is praised even for His requital of the disbelievers. At the end of Surat az-Zumar, when Allah mentioned the driving of the people of the Fire to the Fire and the driving of the people of Paradise to Paradise, He said: "And it will be judged between them in truth, and it will be said, 'All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds'" [az-Zumar 75]. Allah, exalted, is praised for His complete justice and His complete grace, and for His recompense of the people of the Fire, on what basis? On the basis of justice, so He is praised for it.

He said: "[His allies praise Him when they enter Paradise], 'And He is the Wise' [in His actions], 'the All-Aware' [of His creation]."

"Al-Hakim": The author says "in His action," and this is deficient, because He is wise in His legislation and also in His action, which is the decree (al-qadar). Wisdom is not specific to action; even in legislation, which is through His speech, legislation is revelation, and it is the speech of Allah, not His action. Rather, it is speech. Likewise His action is wise.

Wisdom (al-hikmah) is derived from ihkam, which is perfection of work. This is why it is said in its definition that it is placing a thing in its proper place, and this is perfection.

But we have already learned that al-Hakim has two meanings: the Judge (al-Hakim) and the One who perfects (al-Muhkim), since it derives from judgement (al-hukm) and perfection (al-ihkam). How many kinds is the judgement of Allah?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes.

* The student: Legislative and cosmic.

* The Shaykh: Correct, the judgement is legislative and cosmic. And wisdom also has two kinds?

* A student: Judgement is from perfection.

* The Shaykh: From where is the judgement?

* The student: Wisdom...

* The Shaykh: Yes, two kinds.

* The student: Wisdom is from perfection.

* The Shaykh: It is all from perfection, no, it has no connection with judgement.

* A student: Formal and final.

* The Shaykh: Formal and final. The formal means that this thing being in this specific form is in accordance with wisdom, and the final means that the purpose of this thing is a wisdom for which Allah is praised.

For example: the prayer being in this manner, fasting in this manner, and ablution in this manner, these are in legislative matters.

Likewise, in cosmic matters, the creation of man in this manner, the sun and the moon, and similar things, these are formal wisdom, meaning that the thing being in this particular form is without doubt in accordance with wisdom. Then the purpose of that thing is another wisdom.

This formal and final wisdom exists in legislation, then what? And in decree. If you multiply two by two, it is four. There is final wisdom in legislation, formal wisdom in legislation, final wisdom in decree, formal wisdom in decree, and all of this is established for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. When a person believes in this, he is at peace with the judgements of Allah, cosmic and legislative, and no objection arises in his mind, because he knows that this proceeds from wisdom. When he knows it proceeds from wisdom, no doubt remains in his heart that this is the exact correct thing, which wisdom requires. By this a person becomes at peace with the law of Allah, and at peace also with the decree of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and knows that this is the correct thing, and nothing else is permissible.

His statement: "[The All-Aware]." The author says: "of His creation." Al-Khabir means the one who possesses khibrah, which is knowledge of the hidden aspects of matters. From this, the farmer is called khabir, because he conceals the seed by ploughing. So al-Khabir is the one who possesses khibrah, which is knowledge of the hidden aspects of matters.

Does that contradict knowledge of the outward aspects of matters? No, rather it confirms it, because whoever knows the hidden aspects of matters certainly knows the outward aspects.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, always pairs wisdom with might and knowledge. Here it is paired with what? With the knowledge contained in khibrah. Allah pairs it with that to make clear that His wisdom, exalted is He, is based on His knowledge, and that if it appears to you that something is not wise, that is due to deficiency in your knowledge. Otherwise, if you had knowledge and understanding, you would know that wisdom lies in what Allah legislated and what He decreed.

Then He explained or detailed some of His knowledge, saying: "[He knows what enters the earth] [Saba' 2], like water and other things; [and what emerges from it], like plants and other things; [and what descends from the sky], like provision and other things; [and what ascends into it], it rises, from deeds and other things." This is by way of detail.

"Ya'lamu ma yalig fi al-ard" (He knows what enters the earth). "Ma" is a relative pronoun that conveys generality, and "yaliju" means "enters." Everything that enters the earth, Allah, exalted, knows it.

The author says: "like water." Does water enter the earth or come out of it? It enters and comes out. When Allah sends down water from the sky, He makes it enter the earth as springs, and when Allah, exalted, wants it to come out, it comes out by a means or without a means.

His statement: "and other things." What is other than water that enters the earth?

* A student: The dead.

* The Shaykh: The dead, and what else?

* A student: Animals, like snakes.

* The Shaykh: Yes, and things that have burrows in the earth. Right? Do we not say plants as well? Plants too, all their seeds enter the earth.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 34, verse 1–2 (part 2 of 2):

The point is that what enters the earth cannot be counted in its kinds, let alone its individual members, and it is extremely vast. Allah, glorified and exalted, knows it all; even the ant that enters its hole, Allah knows it.

﴿وَمَا يَخْرُجُ مِنْهَا﴾ (and what comes out of it). The author says: (like plants and other things). Plants are clear. "Other things" are like water, minerals and the animals that spread over the earth. Do we say: and among that is man?

﴿مِنْهَا خَلَقْنَاكُمْ﴾ [Ta-Ha 55] (From it We created you). This is the origin, yes indeed. ﴿مِنْهَا خَلَقْنَاكُمْ وَفِيهَا نُعِيدُكُمْ﴾ (From it We created you, and into it We will return you): it is bringing out and putting back in. ﴿وَاللَّهُ أَنْبَتَكُمْ مِنَ الْأَرْضِ نَبَاتًا (١٧) ثُمَّ يُعِيدُكُمْ فِيهَا وَيُخْرِجُكُمْ إِخْرَاجًا﴾ [Nuh 17-18] (And Allah has caused you to grow from the earth like plants. Then He will return you into it and bring you out with a (final) bringing forth).

He says: ﴿وَمَا يَنْزِلُ مِنَ السَّمَاءِ﴾ [Saba 2] (and what descends from the sky) (of provision and other things). How does provision descend from the sky? Do you stay at home every day and dates descend on you from the sky, or clothes? No, but provision comes by rain. For example, Allah sends down rain, so the earth grows and water and pasture come out of it: ﴿مَتَاعًا لَكُمْ وَلِأَنْعَامِكُمْ﴾ [An-Nazi'at 33] (as a provision for you and your livestock). Is it clear?

Besides this, what else descends? The command of Allah, Mighty and Majestic descends: ﴿يُدَبِّرُ الْأَمْرَ مِنَ السَّمَاءِ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ﴾ [As-Sajdah 5] (He arranges the affair from the heaven to the earth). Angels also descend, and shooting stars are thrown at the devils, and many other things of this kind. And Allah knows it.

﴿وَمَا يَعْرُجُ﴾ (and what ascends). He says: (ascends ﴿فِيهَا﴾ of deeds and other things).

Here ﴿يَعْرُجُ﴾ means "ascends", yes? And ya'ruju is transitive with (ila) as Allah said: ﴿تَعْرُجُ الْمَلَائِكَةُ وَالرُّوحُ إِلَيْهِ﴾ [Al-Ma'arij 4] (The angels and the Spirit ascend to Him), and He said: ﴿يُدَبِّرُ الْأَمْرَ مِنَ السَّمَاءِ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ ثُمَّ يَعْرُجُ إِلَيْهِ﴾ [As-Sajdah 5] (then it ascends to Him). And here He said: ﴿يَعْرُجُ فِيهَا﴾ (ascends into it). The grammarians differed regarding such cases. Some of them said: a preposition is used with the meaning of another preposition that suits the verb; that is, the preposition is taken to mean another preposition that suits the verb. For example, they say (fi) means (ila).

Others say: rather, the preposition remains on its original meaning, and the verb is made to include (takmin) a meaning that suits that preposition. This is the view of the Basrans. So they say: ﴿يَعْرُجُ﴾ includes, along with its apparent meaning, which is ascending, the meaning of entering. That is, it ascends and enters into it. The intention is not only ascending, nor only entering; it ascends and enters into it.

Earlier in our study of the introduction to tafsir by Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah (takmin), we noted that this view is the correct and verified view: that the verb is made to include a meaning that suits the preposition. This is because such inclusion gives the verb two meanings:
First: the apparent meaning of the wording.
Second: the meaning it includes to suit the preposition attached to it.
This becomes clear to you in His saying: ﴿عَيْنًا يَشْرَبُ بِهَا عِبَادُ اللَّهِ﴾ [Al-Insan 6] (a spring from which the servants of Allah drink). It is known that we do not drink with a spring; it is not a tool, not a vessel, not an instrument of drinking. You say: I drink with the cup, correct. But does one drink with it while it is a spring? It cannot be a vessel for him.

Some scholars hold that we take the ba' (bi) to mean (min), i.e., "drink from it."
Others hold that we make ﴿يَشْرَبُ﴾ include the meaning of ﴿يَرْوَى﴾ (to quench). When we make (yashrabu) include the meaning of (yarwa), we gain two benefits: drinking, and what else? Quenching. But if we say that the ba' means (min), we do not gain this benefit.

So the point is that the correct view is that we make a verb include a meaning that suits the preposition, and we do not make the preposition mean another preposition.

He says: (﴿وَهُوَ الرَّحِيمُ﴾ to His friends ﴿الْغَفُورُ﴾ [Saba 2] to them). This too is specification without evidence.

The word ﴿الرَّحِيمُ﴾ has no mentioned object, and the author, may Allah have mercy on him, says: (to His friends). Accordingly, His enemies would have no mercy. This is the author's statement. And ﴿الْغَفُورُ﴾ is also for His friends, so His enemies have no forgiveness.

But the correct view is generality, because these two names are unrestricted, so they remain on their unrestricted sense. He is merciful even to His enemies: Allah has given the disbelieiver health and provision of clothing, food, drink, dwelling, spouse and family, and all this is mercy, but it is a general mercy, meaning it is not special like the mercy of the believers.

Forgiveness is also deserved by one who repents from his enmity toward Allah, and when he repents he becomes one of the friends of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. But a person may have both enmity and friendship, or not? ﴿خَلَطُوا عَمَلًا صَالِحًا وَآخَرَ سَيِّئًا﴾ [At-Tawbah 102] (They mixed a righteous deed with another evil one), and they deserve the forgiveness of Allah, glorified and exalted. And Allah knows best.

* Student: (...) specific to the believers.
* Shaykh: No, general, as we said a moment ago: al-Rahim, its meaning is specific to the act, meaning conveying mercy to the one shown mercy. After it, tawhid, I think?
* Student: The indication of the seven.
* Shaykh: Yes indeed.
* Student: Is there not a possibility that these seven are an added punishment upon them?
* Shaykh: No, there is no such possibility.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes indeed, we left it, because some scholars declared it weak (...).

﴿الْحَكِيمُ﴾ [Saba 1] means "ruling" (hakim, a judge), so it is an intensive form (fa'il). And if hakim is from ahkama, then it means muhkim (one who perfects).
And fa'il comes with the meaning of mufil. We have recited to you a verse earlier:
"Is it from Rayhana, the calling, the hearing, that keeps me awake..."
(...).

* Student: The benefits.
* Shaykh: The benefits.
* Among the benefits of the preceding verses: the establishment of complete praise for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in His saying: ﴿الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ﴾ and so on to the end.
Second: that this praise which is established for Him is what He deserves; from His saying: ﴿لِلَّهِ﴾, because the lam, as we said, is for entitlement and specificity.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, praising Himself for the benefit of the servants; because we cannot praise Allah or count His praises. So when Allah praises Himself, this is for our benefit, because He, Mighty and Majestic, teaches us how to praise Him and how to extol Him. He is worthy of praising Himself, glorified and exalted, and extolling Himself for the benefit of His servants. Otherwise He is free of needing to show us the attributes of perfection that He shows, free of needing us to know that; but this is for our benefit.

This benefit may be built upon a hypothetical question: How does Allah praise Himself? And is a person praising himself considered a virtue or not?

The answer: it is said that Allah praises Himself not because He needs us to praise Him or to know His perfection, since He is perfect; but for what? For our benefit, since we cannot count His praise, and we do not know what to praise Him with except through His revelation.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the generality of Allah's dominion, from His saying: ﴿الَّذِي لَهُ مَا فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَمَا فِي الْأَرْضِ﴾ [Saba 1] (to Whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth). Here He praised Himself for the generality of His dominion. He may praise Himself for His act, such as: ﴿الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الَّذِي لَهُ مَا فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَمَا فِي الْأَرْضِ﴾ [Saba 1], and He may praise Himself for His legislation, such as: ﴿الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الَّذِي خَلَقَ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضَ وَجَعَلَ الظُّلُمَاتِ وَالنُّورَ﴾ [Al-An'am 1], ﴿الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الَّذِي أَنْزَلَ عَلَى عَبْدِهِ الْكِتَابَ وَلَمْ يَجْعَلْ لَهُ عِوَجًا﴾ [Al-Kahf 1].
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the heavens are plural, meaning more than one, from His saying: ﴿السَّمَاوَاتِ﴾; and other evidence establishes that they are seven, and likewise the earth.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the manifestation of Allah's perfection on the Day of Resurrection is clearer than in this world, from His saying: ﴿وَلَهُ الْحَمْدُ فِي الْآخِرَةِ﴾ (And to Him belongs praise in the Hereafter). So dominion is general, and the clear, evident manifestation of praise occurs in the Hereafter.
* Among them: the establishment of resurrection, from His saying: ﴿الْآخِرَةِ﴾.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the establishment of Allah's cosmic and legislative decree and His wisdom related to the cosmos and related to the law.
* Following from this principle: the obligation to submit to His cosmic and legislative decree, such that we want no objection to it, even if it comes in what appears to contradict wisdom; we must suspect our minds, because when it is established that He, glorified and exalted, is wise in both the cosmic and the legislative judgment, it follows that we must submit to the cosmic and legislative decree, since it proceeds from wisdom; but that wisdom may be hidden from us.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the generality of Allah's knowledge, derived from His saying: ﴿الْخَبِيرُ﴾ and the detail that follows it, because the Khabir is the one who knows the inner realities, and one who knows the inner realities knows the outer ones.
* Among its benefits: the establishment of these two noble names of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: al-Hakim (the Wise) and al-Khabir (the All-Aware).
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that among the rhetorical methods is generalization followed by detail, from His saying: ﴿الْخَبِيرُ (١) يَعْلَمُ﴾ to the end [Saba 1-2].
The benefit of this rhetorical method is that when a matter comes in general terms, souls become eager for its details; so when the details arrive upon souls that are yearning for them, they fall more strongly upon the soul and take firmer root in the heart. Is that not so?

If I tell you: Something great happened last night, and you did not know; at one in the night last night a great event happened, which you did not know. What would it be? You long for it, you strain to know what this great thing is. But if I tell you: Last night, for example, a star was thrown and gave off a great light, in any case you accept this report, but it is not like the first, because you will say: What is this great thing? (...) a great thing, what is this thing? (...) what is this thing? Until it reaches your heart, and you have been yearning for it greatly.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the completeness of Allah's disposal of His creatures: this one enters, this one exits, this one descends, this one ascends: ﴿يَعْلَمُ مَا يَلِجُ فِي الْأَرْضِ وَمَا يَخْرُجُ مِنْهَا وَمَا يَنْزِلُ مِنَ السَّمَاءِ وَمَا يَعْرُجُ فِيهَا﴾ [Saba 2].
* Among its benefits, which is a rhetorical benefit: beginning with what is closest to man, even if something else is more noble; because you speak of what enters the earth and what comes out of it before you speak of what descends from the sky and what ascends into it.
Here this benefit is based on the premise that the sky is nobler than the earth. Is this agreed upon? Do not hurry: is it agreed that the sky is nobler than the earth, or the earth nobler than the sky?
This is a matter of disagreement among the scholars, with much debate. Some hold that the sky is nobler, and say: the sky, even if it contained only the angels brought near, is a high direction, and in the sky also is Allah, Mighty and Majestic, above it.
Others hold that the earth is nobler, saying: because the best of creation, the prophets and messengers, were created from it. So it is nobler. This dispute, though it may be said to be one of the superfluous matters of knowledge, nevertheless at first glance a person sees the sky as nobler than the earth; but the earth is mentioned here because it touches us more and we know more about it.
* Also among the benefits of the noble verse: the establishment of mercy and forgiveness for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in His saying: ﴿وَهُوَ الرَّحِيمُ الْغَفُورُ﴾. Here He placed al-Rahim before al-Ghafur, although in the Qur'an it is more common to place al-Ghafur before al-Rahim; this is because of the benefits and interests that exist in the heavens and the earth, and benefits and interests come from the effects of what? Mercy. And averting calamities comes from the effects of forgiveness, because forgiveness is the erasing of the sin in which disliked things revolve, while mercy is the attainment of good.
Mercy, according to the People of the Sunnah and the Community, is one of the attributes of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, a real attribute established for Him. The Ash'arites say that mercy is benevolence, or the will to benevolence, so they explain it as the thing done by Allah, meaning blessings, or the will to blessings. Why? Because they affirm the attribute of what? The attribute of will; so they explain mercy as the will to bestow and benevolence, or as the bestowing and benevolence itself.
But we have already noted that the correct and definitively established view is that the texts of the Book and the Sunnah concerning the names and attributes of Allah are to be taken according to their apparent meaning.
Is there a need to say "fitting for Allah"? No; we say "fitting for Allah" only for clarification, because we know with certain knowledge that their apparent meaning is fitting for Allah, and their apparent meaning is not, as the people of negation (ta'til) claim, resemblance (tashbih); for if the apparent meaning of the texts of the Book and the Sunnah in the names and attributes of Allah were resemblance or likeness, then the apparent meaning of the Qur'an and Sunnah in this matter would be disbelief; because whoever likens Allah to His creation has disbelieved, having denied His saying: ﴿لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِ شَيْءٌ﴾ [Ash-Shura 11] (There is nothing like unto Him). And it is impossible that the apparent meaning of the truth should be falsehood and disbelief. Therefore, when we say that the texts of the Book and Sunnah concerning the names and attributes of Allah are to be taken according to their apparent meaning, which is fitting for Allah, this is for the sake of what? For the sake of clarification. Otherwise we know with certain knowledge, more certain than the sun, that its apparent meaning is what is fitting for Allah, so there is no need to restrict it with that; but we may restrict it only for clarification.
Is mercy an attribute of perfection in itself, regardless of the one it is attributed to, or an attribute of deficiency? It is in reality an attribute of perfection, even mercy in (...).
....................... ∗∗∗ ...like placing the sword in the place of generosity
The verse is well known, is it not?
He says: placing generosity... Generosity: giving and spending.
Placing generosity in the place of the sword is harmful to nobility: ... like placing the sword in the place of generosity.
The wisdom of this: he says that placing generosity in the place of the sword is harmful to nobility and to good character. Why? Because the one who deserves the sword, it is best not to put the sword to him. A criminal corrupting the earth whom we have seized and overpowered: we say, "O boy, look, this villa is yours, this car is yours, and this warehouse full of treasures of gold and silver is yours, because you are a criminal." Is that wisdom or not? It is not wisdom.
Like placing the sword in the place of generosity: a person of goodness and kindness, deserving of honor, is brought and placed on the executioner's mat, and we say, "We will kill you now, because you are a benefactor." Is this wisdom or not? It is not wisdom. So this verse is among the greatest verses of wisdom, and al-Mutanabbi is known as the wisest of poets.
* Student: Abu al-'Ala.
* Shaykh: No, al-Mutanabbi.

So we say: mercy is an attribute of perfection in itself, and when it is ascribed to Allah it becomes more and more perfect.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 34, verse 3 (part 1 of 2):

Then He, may He be exalted, says: "And those who disbelieve say, 'The Hour will not come upon us.'" [Saba' 3] Those who disbelieved in Allah, may He be mighty and majestic, and in His power and His wisdom, said, "The Hour will not come upon us." Did they utter this wording, or did they utter the meaning of this wording?

The answer: They uttered this wording, because the original is what is transmitted from others; it is transmitted in its exact words and its distinct expression. So they said, "The Hour will not come upon us."

In another place they said: "Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?" [Ya-Sin 78]. Their expressions in denying the Resurrection varied. They said, "The Hour will not come upon us," meaning: it is impossible for the Hour to come upon us. Yet Allah says: "And that the Hour is coming, there is no doubt about it, and that Allah will raise those who are in the graves." [al-Hajj 7]. So they denied the saying of Allah, relying on the improbability their minds assigned to these decayed bones returning to become living human beings. They did not know that He who originated creation is able to restore it: "And it is He who originates creation and then repeats it, and that is easier for Him." [al-Rum 27].

So their doubt in this denial is what? Merely improbability. This is the first point.

Second: They say, "If you are truthful that we will be resurrected, bring our fathers, raise them for us." This is a challenge out of its proper place, because the Messengers did not tell them, "You will be resurrected now." When will they be resurrected? When creation perishes, when all creatures come to an end and everyone dies, then they will be resurrected. So this challenge is out of place. Had the Messengers said that the first of people would be resurrected now while the last of them still existed, it would have been correct to say, "Bring our fathers if you are truthful." But since they said that they will be resurrected after all of creation that is to be resurrected has perished, this challenge does not apply.

In sum, their doubt is improbability, and a challenge out of its proper place, when they said, "Bring our fathers."

Allah, may He be mighty and majestic, says: "Say, 'Yes, by my Lord, it will surely come upon you.'" [Saba' 3]. "Yes" (bala) is used to nullify a negation. "Say, 'Yes, by my Lord, it will surely come upon you.'" Allah commanded His Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, to declare the opposite of what they said, emphasizing it with an oath, a lam, and a nun: "by my Lord, it will surely come upon you."

I say: "Bala" is a response that nullifies a negation; "wa-Rabbi" is an oath; the lam is for emphasis, and the nun is also for emphasis. So the sentence is emphasized with three emphatics.

"Liya'tiyannakum" means: the Hour. This is one of the three places in which Allah commanded His Prophet to swear.

The second place: His saying, "And they ask you, 'Is it true?' Say, 'Yes, by my Lord, it is indeed true.'" [Yunus 53].

The third place: His saying, "Those who disbelieved claim that they will never be resurrected. Say, 'Yes, by my Lord, you will surely be resurrected; then you will be informed of what you did, and that is easy for Allah.'" [al-Taghabun 7].

Allah, may He be exalted, only commanded His Prophet Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, to swear on this because of its importance and greatness, and because it is the requirement of eloquence. The requirement of eloquence is that the one who denies is addressed with speech emphasized by one emphatic, or two, or three, according to what the statement requires.

Because of the importance of this subject, Allah commanded His Prophet Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, to swear upon it.

If you say: What is the benefit of an oath in front of one who denies? For whoever denies you without an oath will deny you with an oath, so what is the benefit?

The answer has two aspects.

The first aspect: This is the requirement of the Arabic language, that reports are emphasized with various kinds of emphatics.

The second: Emphasis indicates that the speaker is certain of what he swears upon, just as he is certain of what he swears by. Just as we are certain of Allah, may He be mighty and majestic, in His existence and perfection, we are also certain of what He swore upon, which is the coming of the Hour.

He says: "Say, 'Yes, by my Lord, it will surely come upon you, the Knower of the Unseen'" ("'alimi al-ghayb"). "'Alimi al-ghayb" is in the genitive (bi-l-jarr). According to me, it is said: (in the genitive as an adjective, and in the nominative as the predicate of a subject). And "'allami" is in the genitive. So there are three readings in it.

* A student: "'Alim."

* The Shaykh: No, "'allami" is correct, and "'allami" is genitive. So the readings are three: "'alimi" in the nominative and genitive, and "'allami" only in the genitive.

His saying "'alimi al-ghayb": the relevance of mentioning this attribute to establishing the Resurrection is clear, because the establishment of the Hour is part of the knowledge of the Unseen, and the One who informed of it is the All-Knowing of the Unseen. When this report comes from the Knower of the Unseen, it is obligatory for us to accept it. As for a report about the future coming from one who is ignorant and does not know, we reject it; and if it comes from one who knows, we accept it. The knowledge of Allah of the Unseen is something known even among the disbelievers, for Allah, glorified and exalted, informs of things which then happen and they witness them, and this is something they do not doubt. Therefore, after affirming the coming of the Hour, Allah described Himself with this attribute, because it is known to them. So when this report comes from the Knower of the Unseen, whose knowledge of the Unseen they acknowledge, the report becomes emphatic and certain.

His saying "'alimi al-ghayb" in the genitive is an adjective of "Rabb", because "Rabb" is genitive.

So we say in its parsing: the waw is a particle of oath and genitive; "Rabbi" is the thing sworn by, in the genitive by the apparent kasra; "Rabb" is in construct, and the yaa' is a pronoun in the genitive position, built on sukun. Is this parsing correct?

* A student: Not apparent.

* The Shaykh: The ba' of "Rabbi".

* A student: There is no yaa'.

* The Shaykh: There is one; in my copy "Rabbi" has a yaa'.

* Students: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes. Then it is inflected in the genitive by a presumed kasra on the letter before the yaa' of the speaker, its appearance prevented by the occupation of the place with the harmonizing vowel. So this kasra is not the kasra of inflection. Do you understand? We say this because a case like "Rabbi Allah" might arise: how is it genitive? This is not genitive; this kasra is for harmony. So the kasra was already present before the particle of genitive entered, and therefore the inflectional kasra is presumed on the letter before the yaa' of the speaker.

So it is genitive, and "'alimi al-ghayb" is an adjective of "Rabb", and an adjective of a genitive is genitive.

As for the nominative, one says: (predicate of a subject), meaning: He is the Knower of the Unseen, and the whole sentence is either a circumstantial clause from "Rabb", or a resumptive clause explaining His being characterized by this knowledge.

The unseen is what is hidden from a person, and it is a relative matter, but absolute unseen belongs only to Allah, may He be mighty and majestic.

I say: The unseen is a relative matter, because something may be hidden from you that is not hidden from others. The shopkeeper by the mosque, whose dealings now are unseen to us, is not unseen to someone who has witnessed them. So the unseen is relative.

Therefore, is the report about a thing that has occurred considered part of the unseen that belongs to Allah? No; because whoever it occurred to and happened in front of knows it. But the unseen in the future is what belongs to the specific knowledge of Allah, may He be mighty and majestic. For this reason, whoever claims knowledge of the future unseen contradicts the saying of Allah: "Say, 'None in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah.'" [al-Naml 65]. And whoever claims knowledge of an unseen that has already occurred, that is not absolute unseen but a relative unseen known to one who witnessed it and unknown to one who did not.

Does the unseen in His saying "'alimi al-ghayb" include both, or only the future? It includes both, because whatever has occurred, even in very distant times, Allah knows it, and whatever will occur, Allah knows it. So the absolute unseen covers both what has occurred and what has not, and the awaited future is among the specific attributes of Allah's knowledge, while the unseen restricted to what has occurred is not among the specific attributes of Allah's knowledge; rather, it is attained by everyone who witnessed it.

His saying "La ya'zubu 'anhu" (nothing escapes Him).
