The second is the legislative decree, which is when it relates to what Allah has commanded, such as His words: ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾ [al-Isra' 23]. The decree here is legislative, for if it were destinal, it would have occurred, and all people would have worshipped Allah without associating partners. Here the decree is destinal.

﴿So when We decreed upon him﴾, i.e., We determined it for him, and he died. He said: (He remained standing on his staff for a year, dead, while the jinn continued the heavy labours as usual, not realising his death until the termite ate his staff and he fell dead.) Yes, all that the author mentioned is clear from the verse: when Allah decreed death upon him, he remained for a period while the jinn did not know he had died; they were working, wearied, because he had assigned them that. He died while remaining reclining on his staff. First: the author, may Allah have mercy on him, says: (he remained a year). Restricting this remaining to a year has no evidence; but there is no doubt he remained for a period while they worked before him and did not know he was dead. As for restricting it to a year, or less, or more, that requires evidence.

Our statement that he was leaning on his staff has evidence from the verse, for He said: ﴿when he fell﴾, and this is impossible unless he was leaning.

He says: (﴿It did not show them his death except the creature of the earth﴾, from the verb "uriḍat al-khashabah" in the passive, i.e., the termite ate it). The word "al-ard" (earth): is the intended meaning the genus, i.e., the creature that is in the earth, or the verbal noun? The author holds that what is intended is a verbal noun derived from "uriḍat al-khashabah", i.e., the termite ate it; that is, it did not show them his death except the creature that (...) the wood (...). On this basis, the word "ard" is a verbal noun of: "arada, ya'rudu, ardan", like "daraba, yadribu, darban". This is the explanation of the author's words, may Allah have mercy on him. What he established is far from the meaning of the verse; for when you understand "except the creature of the earth", you do not at all understand what the author established; rather what comes to the mind is that the intended "earth" is the genus, i.e., the creature that emerges from the earth.

﴿It was eating his staff﴾: there is a difficulty here, this is an addition: "min" is a preposition, and here ﴿minsa'atahu﴾ is in the accusative. How can this be?
* A student: a noun that is not declined (ism la yanṣarif).
* The Shaykh: a noun that is not declined; a noun that is not declined becomes declined when it is annexed, and here ﴿minsa'atahu﴾ is annexed to the pronoun.
* Student: a noun (...).
* The Shaykh: How is it a noun? Where is "noun" from?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: This is one word, yes. Did you write "min" alone? You have it in the Mushaf.
* Student: No.
* The Shaykh: Good.
* Student: Is the depiction (of images) said to be not forbidden...?
* The Shaykh: It does not follow that because they depicted their statues and worshipped them, they are forbidden.
* Student: (...) he depicted their statues (...).
* The Shaykh: Correct, but it may be permissible, yet they reached through it something forbidden; it is among the causes of shirk, undoubtedly. In any case, we say in the author's words the word "tamathil", since its meaning of timthal is everything you shape after something else, it does not necessarily mean images of animals; it may be images of trees, palaces and the like.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: According to the author's words? As an answer to a presumed question: how do they depict an animal, or a human, for example? He answered that images in his time were not forbidden.
* Student: The mihrab (...)?
* The Shaykh: The mihrab of the mosque is called ṭāq (niche).
* Student: When Dawud died, was (...) and he was leaning on his staff?
* The Shaykh: Or you mean Sulayman.
* Student: Yes, Sulayman (...).
* The Shaykh: No, not at all; he was leaning on his staff like this and died and remained like this.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: (...) only after a period.
* Student: Do the earth not consume the prophets?
* The Shaykh: Yes, correct.
* Student: (...) the righteous?
* The Shaykh: No, for the righteous we do not affirm that the earth does not consume them; but some of them may be found whom the earth has not consumed, whereas the certainty is only for the prophets.
* Benefits of the verses that have passed us:
Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They made for him whatever he willed of sanctuaries﴾. In this verse there are benefits, among them: that Allah the Exalted subjected the jinn to Sulayman, who worked for him whatever he willed; this is not possible for any human. Yes, jinn may perhaps work for some humans in some things, but not in what one wills.
* Among its benefits: the permissibility of lofty construction, from His words: ﴿of sanctuaries﴾.
* Among its benefits: the permissibility of statues. Does this include statues of animals, trees, seas and rivers?
Yes, according to the author's words it includes them, since he said: (this was before the prohibition of images). On the second possibility it does not include them, since timthal is applied to everything that is a likeness of something else, and it need not be in the form of an animal. So in the author's view the ruling is abrogated for the law of the Prophet ﷺ; hence a benefit is derived from it: the permissibility of abrogation in legal rulings. On the second possibility, it is not evidence for the permissibility of animal statues.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the demonstration of the abundance of Sulayman's soldiers and his generosity, since the basins are like reservoirs and the cooking pots are fixed.
* Among its benefits: the obligation of performing thanks to Allah the Mighty and Majestic, from His words: ﴿Work, family of Dawud, thankfully﴾, and the imperative in origin denotes obligation.
* Among its benefits: that the thankful for blessings are few, from His words: ﴿And few of My servants are thankful﴾, and the purpose of this clause is to urge thankfulness.
* Among its benefits: the affirmation of general servitude, encompassing all, from His words: ﴿of My servants﴾, for what is meant is general servitude encompassing all.
* Among its benefits: that David, peace be upon him, is the father of a complete branch of the Children of Israel, from His words: ﴿family of Dawud﴾, as one says: Banu Tamim, Banu Zuhrah, and the like.
Then He said: ﴿So when We decreed upon him death﴾. I think we did not complete it; God willing, we will cover it in the future.
Allah the Exalted said: ﴿It was eating his staff﴾, read with the hamzah and without it, with an alif; that is, there are two readings of ﴿minsa'atahu﴾. The second reading makes the hamzah an alif: ﴿minsatahu﴾. For this reason he said: (with hamzah and without it), but if we omit it, it is (with an alif; because yunsa'u means: is driven away and rebuked by it).
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, we have: (rebuked).
Yes, indeed. It seems the author, may Allah have mercy on him, wishes to explain the derivation of this word, that it is from nasa', meaning driving away and rebuking; a person rebukes with his staff by striking whoever is addressed, and drives away by striking. This shows that the word is Arabic. However, some exegetes say the word is non-Arabic, from words that were Arabicised; and if a word is from Arabicised vocabulary, it is not derived from Arabic. Every word that has a derivation from Arabic is Arabic. In any case (...) this is easy; the important point is that the minsa'ah is the staff by which a thing is driven away and rebuked.

(﴿So when he fell﴾ dead ﴿the jinn saw clearly﴾) The clause, as you see, is a conditional clause, and its conditional particle is ﴿lamma﴾. It has passed us that "lamma" comes in several meanings: it may be conditional, it may be negative, it may mean "except", and fourth, it may be temporal, meaning "when".
Here it is used conditionally, as evidenced by the fact that a condition and an answer follow it: ﴿So when he fell, the jinn saw clearly﴾.
Negative, as in His words: ﴿Nay, they have not yet tasted My punishment﴾ [Sad 8], i.e., they have not tasted.
It comes in the sense of "except", as in His words: ﴿There is no soul but that over it is a guardian﴾ [al-Tariq 4], i.e., except that over it is a guardian.
It comes in the sense of "when", temporal, as when you say: "You honoured me when (lamma) I visited you", i.e., when I visited you. Good; thus it comes in four ways.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 34, verses 13–17 (part 2 of 4):**

﴿تَبَيَّنَتِ الْجِنُّ﴾ "Then the jinn saw clearly." ﴿تَبَيَّنَتِ﴾ means: they knew, and it became clear to them. The author explained it with his words: (it was revealed to them ﴿أَنْ﴾ [that] – a lightened form, meaning that they ﴿لَوْ كَانُوا يَعْلَمُونَ الْغَيْبَ﴾ [if they had known the unseen]).

﴿أَنْ﴾ is a lightened form. Of what? Of the heavy form (*an-nāṣibah*, the heavy "inna"-type particle). When the heavy form is lightened, its subject must be omitted, and its predicate is a full clause. Here the predicate is ﴿لَوْ كَانُوا يَعْلَمُونَ الْغَيْبَ مَا لَبِثُوا فِي الْعَذَابِ الْمُهِينِ﴾ [If they had known the unseen, they would not have remained in the humiliating punishment].

Its i'rab (grammatical analysis, a technical term) is that you say: ﴿أَنْ﴾ is a lightened form of the heavy particle; its subject is a hidden pronoun of the matter (*ḍamīr al-sha'n*); and the clause ﴿لَوْ كَانُوا يَعْلَمُونَ الْغَيْبَ﴾ is in the place of a nominative (raf') as its predicate (...).

In the author's words "(that they)" there is a reference to what preceded: we said that the pronoun of the matter should suit the context. It may be singular, it may be plural, it may be for the third person, and it may be for the second person. This differs from what most grammarians hold, since they make it singular third person and say "(that he)," meaning "the situation."

﴿لَوْ كَانُوا يَعْلَمُونَ الْغَيْبَ مَا لَبِثُوا﴾ ﴿لَوْ﴾ is conditional, and its response is ﴿مَا لَبِثُوا﴾. ﴿لَوْ﴾ comes as conditional, as a verbal-noun particle (*maṣdariyyah*), and as meaning "wished that." It is conditional as in this verse, and as in your saying: "If you visited me, I would honour you." It is maṣdariyyah when it comes after "wadda" (wished), as in the verse: ﴿وَدُّوا لَوْ تُدْهِنُ فَيُدْهِنُونَ﴾ [They wish you would compromise, so they would compromise] (al-Qalam 9), meaning: that you compromise. These are only two meanings.

Right, here it is conditional. What is its condition-verb?
* Student: ﴿مَا لَبِثُوا﴾.
* Shaykh: No. The condition-verb is ﴿كَانُوا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾, and its response is ﴿مَا لَبِثُوا فِي الْعَذَابِ الْمُهِينِ﴾.

(﴿لَوْ كَانُوا يَعْلَمُونَ الْغَيْبَ﴾ and among it what was hidden from them, the death of Solomon – ﴿مَا لَبِثُوا فِي الْعَذَابِ الْمُهِينِ﴾ the hard labour for them, because they thought he was alive, which is the opposite of their thinking that they knew the unseen.) This is clear, because if they had known the unseen, they would have known that he had died before he fell down, through the eating of his staff by the termite. Perhaps they used to think or claim that they knew the unseen, so God Most High wished to show their condition to them and to others, and that they do not know the unseen. Yet the unseen that occurred here is not absolute unseen, but relative unseen, since whoever was very close to Solomon might have known that he had died.

The author says: (and among it what was hidden from them, the death of Solomon – ﴿مَا لَبِثُوا﴾, that is, they did not remain ﴿فِي الْعَذَابِ الْمُهِينِ﴾ which brought them humiliation and disgrace). And the author said: (the hard work, by their thinking him alive, which is contrary to their thinking that they knew the unseen). That is: they used to think they knew the unseen, so when he fell dead it became clear to them that they did not know the unseen.

He said: (And it was known that it was a year by calculating what the termite ate of the staff after his death, one day and night for example). This is an answer to what was said: that he remained a year while dead and it was not known. As if a speaker said: what informed you that it was a year? He said: we knew that by calculation, because we calculated what was eaten in a day and night from the staff, and measured what had passed by it. For example, if it eats one centimetre in a day and night, we know it eats three hundred and sixty centimetres in a year, and we know this from the length of the staff. But in reality this is not fixed, since it may eat more one day than the day before, or the reverse. And also, who said that it ate this amount in a day and night, so that what had passed could be known by it? This needs evidence. Therefore the correct view is what we said before: that we have no need to determine the period Solomon remained, and that such matters are not relied upon and are not adopted unless they come from the Lawgiver, from the Prophet (ﷺ), or come in the Book of God. As for what comes from the Children of Israel in such matters, we say: we withhold judgement; we neither confirm nor deny.

Then God Most High said: ﴿لَقَدْ كَانَ لِسَبَإٍ فِي مَسْكَنِهِمْ﴾ [There was certainly for Sheba in their dwelling-place a sign] (Saba' 15), and so on to the end.

This sentence, as you know, is emphasised by three emphatics?
* Student: *qad*.
* Shaykh: This is *qad*.
* Student: *wa-kāna*.
* Shaykh: No, *kāna* is not one of the emphasis particles. It is emphasised by three emphatics.
* Student: The *lām*, and *qad*.
* Student: And the implied oath.
* Shaykh: And the implied oath, yes, correct. Because this is on the presumption of an oath, meaning: "By God, there was certainly for Sheba…". And *kāna* here indicates mere occurrence, meaning that it is stripped of indication of time, since this verse remains until now; everyone who reads its report (...).

(﴿لَقَدْ كَانَ لِسَبَإٍ﴾ with or without diptote declension: a tribe named after one of their ancestors among the Arabs.) Saba' is the name of a man called Saba', who was from Qahtan. Genealogists among historians differed on whether Qahtan was of the *al-'Arab al-'āribah* (the original Arabs) or the *al-'Arab al-musta'ribah* (the Arabized Arabs). The well-known view is that they are of the original Arabs who came before Ibrahim. But al-Bukhari narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) passed by two tribes of the Ansar who were shooting arrows at each other, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said to them: "Shoot, O sons of Isma'il, for your father was an archer."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (2899) from the hadith of Salama ibn al-Akwa' (may Allah be pleased with him).]] This indicates that they are Arabized Arabs, because the Ansar, namely the Aws and the Khazraj, are well known to be all from the tribes of Yemen, from Qahtan. They dispersed in the lands after the flood and settled in Madinah. On this basis, the apparent meaning of al-Bukhari's hadith is that all of Qahtan were from the sons of Isma'il.

The summary is that scholars of genealogy divide the Arabs into two categories: whoever was before Ibrahim are the original Arabs, and whoever was after him, from his descendants, are the Arabized Arabs.

The point is that Saba' is the name of a man who had many children; it is reported in a hadith that they were ten. Six of them remained in Yemen and four in Syria, and they spread through the land and multiplied.

There are two readings concerning it. The author says: (with or without diptote declension). ﴿لِسَبَإٍ﴾ is the declined form, and without declension ﴿لِسَبَأَ﴾.

He says: (﴿فِي مَسَاكِنِهِمْ﴾ in Yemen ﴿آيَةٌ﴾ [a sign]). The author says ﴿فِي مَسَاكِنِهِمْ﴾, giving the reading of the plural. I have not seen him mention the singular reading. There are two canonical readings (*sab'iyyah*, the seven readings): the singular reading ﴿فِي مَسْكَنِهِمْ﴾ and the plural reading ﴿فِي مَسَاكِنِهِمْ﴾. There is no difference between them in meaning, because *maskan* is singular, and the singular construct noun is general, covering everything that falls under that meaning. Have you not seen His saying: ﴿وَإِنْ تَعُدُّوا نِعْمَةَ اللَّهِ لَا تُحْصُوهَا﴾ [If you count the blessings of Allah, you cannot number them] (Ibrahim 34)? Here "blessing" is singular, and He says of it: "you cannot number them," so they are many. Thus *maskan* in meaning is equivalent to *masākin*, since it is a singular construct noun, and the singular construct is general.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, mine has: ﴿مَسَاكِنِهِمْ﴾ in your Mus-haf.
* Students: (...).
* Shaykh: No, the one I have is the one with the author's handwriting: ﴿مَسْكَنِهِمْ﴾.

In any case, ﴿مَسَاكِنِهِمْ﴾ is a canonical reading, and ﴿مَسْكَنِهِمْ﴾ is also a canonical reading. *Maskan* is what a person dwells in and is settled in, such as houses, gardens, orchards, and the like.

﴿آيَةٌ﴾ [a sign] means an indicator. God Most High says: ﴿وَآيَةٌ لَهُمْ أَنَّا حَمَلْنَا ذُرِّيَّتَهُمْ فِي الْفُلْكِ الْمَشْحُونِ﴾ [And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring in the laden ship] (Ya-Sin 41), and ﴿أَوَلَمْ يَكُنْ لَهُمْ آيَةً أَنْ يَعْلَمَهُ عُلَمَاءُ بَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ﴾ [Is it not a sign for them that the scholars of the Children of Israel know it?] (al-Shu'ara' 197). So *āyah* means the indicator that points to a thing. What does this sign point to? It points to the power of God, the Mighty and Majestic, and to His blessing, and ultimately to His wisdom.

Grammatically, ﴿آيَةٌ﴾ is the delayed subject of *kāna*, and ﴿لِسَبَإٍ﴾ is its fronted predicate.

The author said: (a sign indicating the power of God), and I add: and His beneficence and bounty, and ultimately His wisdom, because these dwellings – as will come – were destroyed on account of their turning away.

He said: (﴿جَنَّتَانِ﴾ is an apposition [*badal*]). From what? From ﴿آيَةٌ﴾. It may also be an explanatory apposition (*'atf bayān*), because it clarified and explained the sign. A *jannah* is an orchard with many trees; it is so named because it covers those in it, that is, it conceals them. We have already learned that this root, *j-n-n*, revolves around the meaning of concealment and hiddenness.

﴿جَنَّتَانِ عَنْ يَمِينٍ وَشِمَالٍ﴾ [Two gardens, on the right and on the left]. He says: (on the right and left of their valley). This valley was between mountains, and at the edges of this valley were these great gardens of varied trees with abundant fruit, and they were in the best state of comfort, plenty and security.

He says: ﴿عَنْ يَمِينٍ وَشِمَالٍ﴾, meaning that when they were on the right and left of the valley, it gained a wonderful, awe-inspiring and attractive view. God Most High says: (﴿كُلُوا مِنْ رِزْقِ رَبِّكُمْ وَاشْكُرُوا لَهُ﴾ [Eat from the provision of your Lord and be grateful to Him] for what He provided you of blessing in the land of Sheba), and so on to the end. That is, God, Glorified and Exalted, placed in these two gardens much good, and made their enjoyment easy. Therefore He said: ﴿كُلُوا مِنْ رِزْقِ رَبِّكُمْ﴾. What does this indicate: difficulty or ease? Ease, as when I set food before you and say: "Eat." So these gardens yield their fruits without hardship, rather with ease and facility.

His saying ﴿مِنْ رِزْقِ رَبِّكُمْ﴾ [from the provision of your Lord]: *rizq* means giving, as in His saying: ﴿وَإِذَا حَضَرَ الْقِسْمَةَ أُولُو الْقُرْبَى وَالْيَتَامَى وَالْمَسَاكِينُ فَارْزُقُوهُمْ مِنْهُ﴾ [And when the division is attended by relatives, orphans and the needy, provide for them from it] (al-Nisa' 8).

And His saying ﴿مِنْ رِزْقِ رَبِّكُمْ﴾: *al-Rabb* (the Lord) has already been explained to us as meaning the Creator, the Owner, the Governor. Lordship here is a particular lordship, because of God's special care for them through what He gave them in these gardens.

﴿وَاشْكُرُوا لَهُ﴾ [and be grateful to Him]: this is what they are required to do, as a recompense or as a display of the blessing of God, Glorified and Exalted, upon them. Gratitude, as already explained, relates to the heart, the tongue and the limbs. That is: acknowledge that this blessing is from whom? From God; praise God for it; and act with your limbs in obedience to Him, so that you render thanks in the manner required of you.

(﴿وَاشْكُرُوا لَهُ﴾ for what He provided you of blessing in the land of Sheba.) ﴿اشْكُرُوا لَهُ﴾: sometimes the verb *shakara* is transitive by itself, so one says *shakartu Allāh* (I thanked God), and one also says *shakartu lahu* (I thanked him). It is among the verbs that occur in Arabic both intransitive and transitive. When is it intransitive? With ﴿لَهُ﴾: when the preposition *lām* comes, it is intransitive; when the preposition does not come, it is transitive. So if you say *shakartu Allāh*, it is transitive; if you say *shakartu li-llāh*, it is intransitive.

He says: ﴿بَلْدَةٌ طَيِّبَةٌ وَرَبٌّ غَفُورٌ﴾ [A good land and a forgiving Lord]. What is the i'rab of ﴿بَلْدَةٌ طَيِّبَةٌ﴾?
* Student: It is the predicate of an omitted subject.
* Shaykh: What is the estimate (taqdir)?
* Student: "This is a land."
* Shaykh: Or "it is a land," yes.

(﴿بَلْدَةٌ طَيِّبَةٌ﴾ in which there are no salt-marshes, no mosquito, no fly, no flea, no scorpion, and no snake; a stranger passes through it, and in his clothes there are lice, and the lice die because of the goodness of its air.) This (...)! We only say: it is a good land. As for a stranger who comes from the desert with lice in his clothes, and the lice die because of the goodness of the air, God knows best. But we say: there is no doubt that God's description of it as good means that it is among the best lands in its air, in its cold and in its heat. In it there is no severe heat nor biting cold, nor is there foulness of air and water and the like. So take from it whatever you wish of the goodness of dwelling in everything that is called good.

﴿بَلْدَةٌ طَيِّبَةٌ وَرَبٌّ غَفُورٌ﴾: he means: and God is a forgiving Lord. Forgiving for what? Forgiving of sins. So God bestowed upon them two blessings: the blessing of dwelling and its goodness, and the blessing of forgiveness. The blessing of forgiveness includes safety from sins and their punishments in the Hereafter, and in the good land is safety from calamities in this world.

*Al-Ghafur* is an intensive form (*sigha mubalaghah*); its active participle is *ghafir*. It is derived from *ghafr*, meaning covering together with protection. From it comes the saying: *al-mighfar*, the helmet that a person wears to protect himself from arrows in battle. There is covering and concealment in it, and also protection. Likewise the forgiveness of sins: its meaning is that God conceals your sin and protects you from its punishment.

(﴿وَرَبٌّ غَفُورٌ﴾ ﴿فَأَعْرَضُوا﴾ [But they turned away] from His thanks and disbelieved ﴿فَأَرْسَلْنَا عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ [so We sent upon them]), and so on to the end.

The *fa'* here is coordinating, meaning that despite these blessings – great gardens, a good land, forgiveness of sins if they obey God – He said: ﴿فَأَعْرَضُوا﴾ [but they turned away]. Turned away from what? He says: they turned away from thanking God and disbelieved; they turned away from gratitude and met this blessing with disbelief. So what was their outcome? He said: ﴿فَأَرْسَلْنَا عَلَيْهِمْ سَيْلَ الْعَرِمِ﴾ [So We sent upon them the flood of al-'Arim]. The *fa'* here is coordinating and also indicates causation: that is, because of their turning away We sent upon them the flood of al-'Arim. This is God's custom among His creatures, as He said: ﴿وَضَرَبَ اللَّهُ مَثَلًا قَرْيَةً كَانَتْ آمِنَةً مُطْمَئِنَّةً يَأْتِيهَا رِزْقُهَا رَغَدًا مِنْ كُلِّ مَكَانٍ فَكَفَرَتْ بِأَنْعُمِ اللَّهِ فَأَذَاقَهَا اللَّهُ لِبَاسَ الْجُوعِ وَالْخَوْفِ بِمَا كَانُوا يَصْنَعُونَ﴾ [And Allah presents an example: a town secure and at ease, its provision coming to it abundantly from every place, but it denied the favours of Allah, so Allah made it taste the garment of hunger and fear for what they used to do] (al-Nahl 112). These people turned away, so God destroyed their dwellings.

(﴿أَرْسَلْنَا عَلَيْهِمْ سَيْلَ الْعَرِمِ﴾: *al-'Arim* is the plural of *'aramah*, which is what holds back water, whether a dam or other construction, until the time they need it; that is, the flood of their valley that was held back by what was mentioned, so it flooded their two gardens and their wealth.)

﴿سَيْلَ الْعَرِمِ﴾: *al-'Arim* means the dam. That is, this flood is attributed to the dam; or it means "the flood of al-'Arim" by way of attributing a thing to its quality, that is, the raging, sweeping flood that destroys everything that passes over it. The meaning is that God, Glorified and Exalted, sent upon them a great flood, through the collapse of the dam that they had built between these mountains. This solid dam was where the floods gathered, and the earth absorbed them and they emerged as springs. When this dam cracked, the waters flowed without measure, by the power of God, Glorified and Exalted. So He said: ﴿أَرْسَلْنَا عَلَيْهِمْ سَيْلَ الْعَرِمِ﴾. He says: ﴿وَبَدَّلْنَاهُمْ بِجَنَّتَيْهِمْ جَنَّتَيْنِ﴾ [And We exchanged their two gardens for two gardens]: the former gardens, or the two former gardens, all of them had good fruit that is eaten and benefited from, through sale and purchase and otherwise. As for the exchange, he says: (﴿وَبَدَّلْنَاهُمْ بِجَنَّتَيْهِمْ جَنَّتَيْنِ ذَوَاتَيْ﴾ the dual of *dhawāt*, the singular being *dhāt*). Is that how it is in your text? Singular is more correct. Do you have the dual *dhawātay* or *dhāt*?
* Students: *dhawāt*.
* Shaykh: Right. Originally it is *dhāt* in the singular, and *dhawāt* is the plural. The plural was made dual, and it became ﴿ذَوَاتَيْ أُكُلٍ﴾. It is possible to say, contrary to the author's statement, that the original is *dhāt*, but when it became dual the *waw* returned, so it became *dhawātay*, meaning "two possessors," because *dhāt* means "possessor" (*ṣāḥibah*). God Most High says: ﴿وَالسَّمَاءِ ذَاتِ الْبُرُوجِ﴾ [By the sky containing constellations] (al-Buruj 1), that is, possessing the constellations.

﴿ذَوَاتَيْ أُكُلٍ خَمْطٍ﴾ [two gardens of bitter produce]. The author says: (bitter, ugly; with *ukul* read as "that which is eaten" with idafah (genitive construction), and without it), and it is conjoined with ﴿وَأَثْلٍ﴾ [and tamarisk]. That is, there are two readings: ﴿ذَوَاتَيْ أُكُلِ خَمْطٍ﴾ with the genitive construction, and without it ﴿ذَوَاتَيْ أُكُلٍ خَمْطٍ﴾. The genitive reading is clear: *ukul* means "that which is eaten," and *khamt* is that which is made bitter (*yukhmaṭu khamṭan*). It is the *arak* tree, as Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them) explained, and *arak* is the tree of these tooth-sticks (*masawik*); it has very simple leaves, and it is not especially delicious. That is why the author says: (bitter, ugly), instead of fruits, vegetables and crops and the like. He says *ukul* means "eaten," that is: two possessors of eaten things that are made bitter. ﴿وَأَثْلٍ﴾ [and tamarisk]: instead of the fruiting, delightful trees, tamarisk took their place. Some said that *athl* is the *tarfah* (tamarisk); but the correct view is that it is other than the *tarfah*, because the *tarfah* stays small and does not grow large, whereas *athl* is well known, as the author says.
* Student: Is *arak* the *ukul* or the *khamt*?
* Shaykh: No, the *khamt*.
* Student: And the *ukul*?
* Shaykh: No, *ukul* means that it is eaten, *khamṭan*, i.e., it is eaten as bitter.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 34, verses 13–17 (part 3 of 4):

He said: ﴿and some tamarisk trees, a few﴾. Here he said ﴿and some lote trees﴾, and there he said ﴿bitter foliage and tamarisk﴾, because the lote tree (sidr) is the best of these three kinds, and they were given only a small amount of it, ﴿some lote trees﴾, which is also little. Although the phrase ﴿some lote trees﴾ indicates paucity, this paucity was emphasized by his saying ﴿a few﴾.

The summary now: when these people turned away and did not give thanks to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, Allah sent the flood upon them, which drowned their wealth and destroyed their buildings, and replaced those two gardens with two gardens that are not equal to, and do not even approach, what came before. ﴿Two gardens bearing bitter fruit﴾ is not abundant. ﴿Bitter foliage﴾, and the author said: (it is bitter and repulsive). ﴿And tamarisk and some lote trees, a few﴾, instead of those great, beneficial and useful gardens.

﴿That We recompensed them for their disbelief﴾ (﴿That﴾ refers to the substitution, ﴿We recompensed them﴾). Had the author said "that substitution and the sending of the flood," it would have been more general and comprehensive, or had he said "that which has been mentioned," it would have been more comprehensive. (﴿We recompensed them for their disbelief﴾ with their disbelief.) The author said: (with their disbelief), which tells us that the ﴿mā﴾ is a verbal-noun (masdariyyah) particle, and the ﴿bi﴾ is causative; that is: We recompensed them with this recompense, by drowning their wealth, destroying their buildings, and replacing the two gardens with these two gardens.

﴿For what they disbelieved﴾, meaning: because of their disbelief. ﴿And do We recompense except the ungrateful?﴾ ﴿And is not recompensed except the ungrateful?﴾ (with the yā' and nūn, with the zāy vowelled with a kasrah and the kafūr in the accusative, meaning: no one is called to account except him.)

Regarding His saying ﴿hal nujāzī﴾, there are two readings: ﴿nujāzī﴾, and on this reading ﴿al-kafūr﴾ must be in the accusative as the direct object. The second reading is ﴿yujāzā﴾, and on it ﴿al-kafūr﴾ is in the nominative as the deputy subject. The interrogative here carries the sense of negation, since it is followed by ﴿illā﴾; so ﴿hal nujāzī illā al-kafūr﴾ means: We do not recompense except an ungrateful one. The word ﴿mujāzāh﴾ here means "calling to account" or "repaying an action in kind." ﴿Al-kafūr﴾ is an intensive form (ṣīghat mubālaghah), meaning one who possesses disbelief in Allah, glorified and exalted is He. And Allah knows best.

* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: It is a general statement that includes this and that. That is: We do not punish except those who disbelieve in Allah, whether it is ingratitude (kufr nicmah), in which case one is recompensed according to the measure of one's sin, or disbelief that takes one out of the religion. The meaning of "two gardens" is not two orchards, one on the right and one on the left. The meaning is gardens. But the scholars said: since these gardens were connected, they became like one garden. It is well known that if it were one orchard and another orchard, this would not be a sign (āyah), it would be simple. But these are gardens connected to one another, on the right side of the valley and the left side of the valley. Since they were connected to one another, they became as if they were one, as if it were one garden on the right and one garden on the left.

﴿When We decreed death for him﴾, and so on to the end.

* From the benefits of this verse: first, that death is the end of every living being, however great its kingdom. Solomon was among the greatest of kings in dominion, yet his kingdom did not save him from death.
* Among them: that all matters belong to Allah, as shown by His saying ﴿When We decreed death for him﴾.
* Among them: that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is described with greatness, majesty and perfection, because the ﴿Nā﴾ here does not denote plurality but magnificence (ta'ẓīm). The word (...) indicates either plurality or magnificence, and plurality is impossible here, so it must be for magnificence.
* Among them: that a contemptible thing may bring about something great and momentous. This is derived from His saying ﴿It was only the creature of the earth that showed them his death﴾. This is a matter in which Allah's custom has been established: a thing may be insignificant yet lead to a great result. We now do not know how to bury our dead except through the guidance of the crow, do we not? Likewise, all the magnificent and beautiful engineering structures were learned from the bee's handiwork. Also, all the machines that people now invent, you find them resembling the creatures of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, such as aircraft and others. From this we know that insignificant things may be of great benefit to a person, and dangerous matters may follow from them.
* Among them: that attributing a thing to its known cause is permissible. This is derived from His saying ﴿It was only the creature of the earth that showed them his death﴾, where the showing is attributed to the creature of the earth, even though the creature did not eat the staff so that the jinn would learn of Solomon's death. No, but it was a cause. So attributing a thing to a cause known by the Shari'ah or by the senses is permissible, even if the word "Allah" is not mentioned. For example, if you say: "Had it not been for so-and-so, I would have perished," and it is true that so-and-so is the one who rescued you, this is permissible provided you do not believe that this cause is the sole agent. What is forbidden is attributing a thing to a cause alongside Allah joined by the conjunction "and," or attributing a thing to a cause whose causality is known neither from the Shari'ah nor from the senses, because this would be of the category of illusions and fancies.
* Among the benefits of the verse: caution, or warning, against the creature of the earth. Yes indeed. As long as it eats wood and such things, beware of it. How many a person has had his valuable library, worth a great deal, ruined by the creature of the earth? Therefore, be attentive: do not let termites eat your books.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: attributing an action, or attributing a thing, to one who did not perform it by his own choice. This is derived from His saying ﴿So when he fell down, the jinn saw clearly﴾. Falling (kharr) may be attributed to an agent acting by choice, and it may be attributed to an agent acting without choice. You say: "The water fell (kharra al-mā')," and you say: "He fell dead (kharra mayyitan)." Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿They fell down in prostration﴾ [as-Sajdah 15], and ﴿and they fall upon their faces weeping﴾ [al-Isrā' 109]. This one is by choice.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the jinn do not know the unseen, and the proof of this is clear: ﴿Had they known the unseen, they would not have remained in the humiliating punishment.﴾
* Among them: that sensory events that occur are demonstrative proofs (adillah burhāniyyah). This benefit means reasoning from sensory matters. Because Allah proved that they do not know the unseen by the fact that they remained in punishment through the hard labour they were doing, you may infer intelligible matters from perceptible matters, and this is well known.
* Among the benefits of the verse: that the jinn possess intellects, as shown by His saying ﴿the jinn saw clearly﴾, and this is so, because Allah gave them intellects by which they are guided to the interests of their religion and their worldly life.
* Among them: naming hard labour a punishment, as shown by His saying ﴿they remained in the punishment﴾, even though Solomon, peace be upon him, did not have them work for him as a punishment for them, but as an obligation. From this we know that the word "punishment" may be applied to what is not a punishment, as in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): «Travel is a piece of punishment»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1804) and Muslim (1927/179), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]].

And His saying, ﴿There was certainly for Sheba in their dwelling place﴾, and so on to the end, contains evidence for the use of emphasis (ta'kīd) in important matters, even if the addressee is neither a denier nor hesitant. This is derived from the emphasis on this story in His saying ﴿There was certainly for Sheba﴾, because emphasis, as we know, is required when addressing a denier, is appropriate when addressing one who hesitates, and is contrary to eloquence (balāghah) otherwise. This is the known position of the scholars of rhetoric. But by reflecting on what has come in the noble Qur'an, we find that important matters, even when addressed to someone who does not deny them or hesitate about them, are emphasized by Allah, as in this story and others.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: this great sign, which indicates the power and wisdom of Allah. It is the story of them in general terms: they were enjoying blessings in their homes, gardens, palaces and other things. When they turned away, the situation was reversed. So there is a lesson in it, a sign in many respects: a sign indicating the power of Allah, a lesson for those who disobey Allah, a lesson for those who obey Allah, and a sign indicating the wisdom of Allah. By reflecting on this verse you will find in it various kinds and types of signs. Now, having explained these verses, we said: a sign indicating the power of Allah, since He created for them these great gardens and then replaced them with others that are not comparable to them in anything. It indicates what? His wisdom, the Mighty and Majestic, since He gave them that good when they were turned toward Allah, and deprived them of it when they turned away and became arrogant toward His obedience. A sign for those who take heed among the people of sins, for in it there is a warning to them that Allah's blessing upon them may be removed because of their sins. A sign for the obedient, who take heed from it that as long as they remain in obedience to Allah, Allah's blessing revolves around them. These are four aspects of it being a sign.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that these gardens yield their fruit abundantly, as shown by His saying ﴿Eat from the provision of your Lord﴾.
* Among its benefits: the obligation of giving thanks to Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, as shown by His saying ﴿and be grateful to Him﴾. Gratitude is obligatory by reason as well as by the Shari'ah. As for its obligation by the Shari'ah, the verses commanding it are numerous. As for its obligation by reason, it is because sound reason requires that whoever does good to you, you thank him for it. Whoever does not thank people does not thank Allah. That is, everyone sees that it is wrong for a person to bestow upon you some good, and then you deny him and do not thank him. Everyone knows that this is wrong, and that it is obligatory to give thanks.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the lands of Allah are divided into good and bad, as shown by His saying ﴿a good land﴾. What is the nature of the goodness in this land? Is it the goodness of the soil, the goodness of the climate, or the goodness of its fruits? The answer: it encompasses all of that. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And the good land, its vegetation comes forth by the permission of its Lord, and that which is bad, its vegetation comes forth only sparingly. Thus do We vary the signs for a people who give thanks﴾ [al-A'rāf 58].
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of the lordship of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and of His forgiveness, in His saying ﴿and a Lord who is Forgiving﴾.

Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿But they turned away, so We sent upon them the flood of the dam﴾ [Saba' 16], and so on to the end.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the explanation of the condition of these people, that they exchanged the blessing of Allah for disbelief. It was incumbent upon them, since Allah had bestowed these blessings upon them, that they should give thanks to Him and perform obedience to Allah, but they turned away.
* Among its benefits: the punishment of those who turn away, in accordance with what the wisdom of Allah requires. Allah said in another verse: ﴿So each of them We seized for his sin﴾ [al-'Ankabūt 40]. Punishments are always of the same kind as the deed. These people, when they became arrogant toward Allah's blessing and disbelieved in Him because of these gardens, were replaced with gardens that were bad compared with what they had been given before.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse also: the establishment of causes. From where is this taken? ﴿But they turned away, so We sent﴾. Allah made their turning away the cause of the sending.
* Among its benefits: that sins are a cause for the removal of blessings, as shown by His saying ﴿But they turned away, so We sent﴾. While they were enjoying blessings, when they turned away, Allah sent upon them this destructive flood. There are many witnesses to this in the Qur'an, among them His saying: ﴿And Allah presents an example: a town that was secure and tranquil, its provision coming to it abundantly from every place, but it denied the blessings of Allah, so Allah made it taste the garment of hunger and fear for what they used to do﴾ [an-Naḥl 112]. Among them His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And if the people of the towns had believed and been mindful of Allah, We would have opened for them blessings from the heaven and the earth, but they denied, so We seized them for what they used to earn. Then are the people of the towns secure from Our punishment coming to them at night while they are sleeping? Or are the people of the towns secure from Our punishment coming to them in the morning while they are at play? Do they feel secure from the plan of Allah? None feels secure from the plan of Allah except the losing people﴾ [al-A'rāf 96–99].

* Among its benefits: rain, which is a blessing and a mercy, can become a punishment and a torment. This is shown by His words here, ﴿sayl al-'arim﴾ (the torrent of the dam-breach). The flood in its origin, which is the gathering of rain until it rushes forth, is originally good, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Do they not see that We drive the water to the barren land and bring forth thereby crops from which eat their livestock and themselves?﴾ [al-Sajdah 27]. Is this good or not? It is good, but at times it becomes a punishment.

* Among its benefits: a clarification of the misguidance of those people who, when calamities such as these floods and the like befall them, are not affected by them and say: "This is the requirement of nature." Yet these destructive floods are only a punishment from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, a punishment by which He tests those who are tormented and deters those who are of their kind.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a demonstration of the power of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in sending these sweeping torrents that drowned their fruits and crops, and after these fruits and crops there grew ﴿khamt, and tamarisk, and a few lote-trees﴾. What is a lote-tree? "A few lote-trees" means a small amount. Thus, in place of those great gardens, this took their place.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the wisdom in Allah, Mighty and Majestic, making in place of the two gardens two other gardens. Obedience is light, righteousness and success, so it is fitting that its recompense be bestowal. Disobedience is darkness and corruption, so it is fitting that in it there be this evil substitute in comparison with what came before.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿That We requited them for their disbelief. And do We requite [anyone] except the ungrateful?﴾ [Saba' 17].

﴿That We requited them for their disbelief﴾: In this is evidence that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, does not requite anyone with a punishment except for his deed, by His words: ﴿for their disbelief﴾.

* Also in it: the affirmation of causes, because the particle "bi" (ba') here denotes causation.

* Also in it: the difference between (yajzi) and (yujazi). Here He said: ﴿do We requite [yujazi] except the ungrateful﴾. But (yajzi) is used for reward, and (yujazi) for punishment. So some scholars have said: you say to the disbeliever, "jazaka Allah" (جازاك الله), and you say to the Muslim, "jazaka Allah" (جزاك الله). For good, we say jazā (جزى), and for evil we say jāzā (جازى). The reason for this is that good is pure bestowal, whereas punishment is requital and retribution. For this reason we say jāzāhu, the verb is formed in the pattern of mufā'alah (the third verbal form, which implies reciprocity), and mufā'alah originally occurs between two parties.

He, the Exalted, says: (﴿And We placed between them and the towns that We had blessed﴾ with water and trees) and so on to the end. ﴿And We placed between them﴾: all the additions, all the attribution of the verb now to "nā" (We), which indicates majesty.

﴿We placed between them﴾: the pronoun refers to Saba'. ﴿And between the towns that We had blessed﴾: "qurā" is the plural of "qaryah," which is a town, whether large or small. It was called a qaryah because it gathers (yajmaʿu) people. What is well known among people, that a qaryah is a small city, is a conventional usage (iṣṭilāḥ ʿurfī). Otherwise, God says about Umm al-Qurā (the Mother of Towns): ﴿And how many a town, mightier in strength than your town which has expelled you﴾ [Muhammad 13]. So "qaryah" is the name of a settlement, whether it is large or small, and it was named so because it gathers people.

As for His saying ﴿the towns that We had blessed﴾, which towns did God bless? It has been said: they are the towns of Yemen, such as Sanaa and similar places. It has also been said: they are the towns of Syria (al-Shām). Each of the two opinions has a basis, because God, glorified and exalted, blessed Syria and He blessed Yemen. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O God, bless for us our Syria and our Yemen" [narrated by al-Bukhari (1037), and Ahmad (5641), whose wording this is, from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, may God be pleased with them both]. For this reason the exegetes differed: is the intended meaning of "the towns that God had blessed" the towns of Syria, or the towns of Yemen? Which of the two is the greater favour: that the intended meaning be the towns of Syria or the towns of Yemen? The towns of Syria, because they are far away. They go to Syria and return from it. Thus He says: ﴿And We placed between them and the towns that We had blessed visible towns﴾.

The author (al-Baghawi) said: (﴿We had blessed in them﴾ with water and trees), meaning and fruits, (and they are the towns of Syria to which they travel for trade. ﴿Visible towns﴾ continuous from Yemen to Syria). ﴿Visible﴾ means clear, so that some of them can be seen from others. For if a town is far from the next, it does not become visible. When you leave one town for another that is far from it, would the second town be visible to you? You would not find anyone to guide you. But when they are continuous and close together, what becomes [the state]? Visible, apparent to the eye. These are towns connected to one another from Yemen to Syria. Those who said that the intended meaning is the towns of Yemen said: it is not known that there were towns connected from Yemen to Syria. They said that the reality indicates otherwise, and that the intended meaning of the towns is the towns of Yemen. In any case, each of the two opinions has a basis.

He said: (﴿Visible towns﴾ continuous from Yemen to Syria). ﴿And We determined the travel therein﴾ means: We made it measured in stages, so that they halt from one town to another, stage by stage. He says: (﴿We determined the travel therein﴾ such that they rest midday in one and spend the night in another until the end of their journey, and they have no need to carry provisions or water). This is the meaning of "determining the travel": that it is measured in stages according to these towns. They rest at midday in one and spend the night in another, then rest at midday in the next and spend the night in another, and so on. There is no doubt that determining the travel in this way is one of God's blessings upon people. The routes that have no towns are usually dangerous and frightening roads. But when they are continuous, they become easier for the traveller and more reassuring, and even closer to the journey. For when you walk from one town to another, you feel that you have completed a stage. Like the Noble Qur'an now, since it was divided into verses, surahs and parts, it became easier for the reader. A book divided into chapters and sections is easier. Likewise the physical road: if towns follow one another along it, it is easier than a long road that wearies a person and in which he does not feel that he has covered any stage. For this reason God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We determined the travel therein﴾.

﴿Travel therein by night and day, secure﴾. The author said: (We said: travel). On this basis, this sentence is in the accusative position as a quoted speech of an omitted verb: "We said: travel."

Is this statement legislative or decreed? It is decreed (qadarī), meaning that God said to them: travel on these roads.

﴿Therein by night﴾ means in these towns. (﴿By night and day, secure﴾ fearing neither by night nor by day). This is among God's blessings: that they travel by night and day, secure, fearing no one, fearing neither loss nor a shortage of water nor a lack of food. But what happened? They were not patient with this blessing, God forbid. ﴿They said: Our Lord, make the distances between our journeys far﴾. They did not give thanks for the blessing, and it was incumbent upon them to thank God for this blessing and to hold fast to it, but they were not patient with it, so they asked God to make the distances between their journeys far, so that the journeys would be long with no towns in them. This is similar to the words of the companions of Moses to him: ﴿We will not be patient with one kind of food, so call upon your Lord to bring forth for us of what the earth grows: of its herbs, its cucumbers, its garlic, its lentils and its onions﴾ [al-Baqarah 61]. Although at first they used to eat with ease the manna and quails, without hardship and with good food, they were not patient with it. These people were not patient with this either. The people of Saba' were not patient with this blessing, which is among the finest blessings in journeys.

They said: (﴿Our Lord, make the distances between our journeys far﴾. In a reading that is one of the seven recognised readings (qirāʾah sabʿiyyah): ﴿Make far the distances between our journeys﴾ to Syria; make them deserts (mafāwiz)). Mafāwiz is the plural of mafāzah, which means lands in which one fears destruction. It was called mafāzah by way of optimism (tafāʾul), though in reality it is not a mafāzah; it is destruction and a place of ruin. But the Arabs apply a thing to its opposite out of optimism, as they called the broken one "jabīr" (one who is set right). This is similar. The author, in explaining ﴿Make far the distances between our journeys﴾, says: (make them deserts). Why? He said: (so that they might look down upon the poor by riding mounts and carrying provisions and water, and so they became insolent toward the blessing). When the towns were visible and close together, and there was no need to carry provisions or water-skins, the rich and the poor were equal in these routes, each enjoying the blessing on these roads. But when the distances increased, to whose share did this fall? The rich. So they asked God to make the distances between their journeys far, so that they might boast over their poor. These rich people would ride camels and carry whatever provisions they wished, while the poor could not do so. This is the reason they called upon God to make the distances between their journeys far.

He says: ﴿And they wronged themselves﴾. In what way? Either by disbelief, or by calling upon God, glorified and exalted, to make the distances between their journeys far. Thus they did not accept His blessing of this ease.

(﴿So We made them tales﴾ for those after them, ﴿and We scattered them completely﴾ we dispersed them throughout the lands utterly, ﴿Indeed in that﴾ mentioned, ﴿are signs﴾ lessons ﴿for every steadfast one﴾ against sins ﴿and grateful one﴾ for blessings). ﴿We made them tales﴾: "aḥādīth" is the plural of "ḥadīth," which is what people speak about. That is to say, after they had existed, they became a report among the reports.

(...) Their stories became tales that people talk about. You say: such-and-such happened, and so-and-so. This is among the well-known proverbs: "They were scattered like the scattering of Saba'" (tafarraqū ayādī Saba'), meaning that they were dispersed as Saba' was dispersed.

God, the Exalted, said: ﴿We made them tales﴾: after they had been real, established things, they became tales. This is like the words of the poet:

While a man is seen in it as one who gives news, until he is seen as a news item among the reports.

﴿We scattered them completely﴾ means: We dispersed them throughout the lands, every dispersal, and they were driven out and scattered, because they were ungrateful for the blessing and wronged themselves.
﴿Indeed in that are signs for every steadfast one, grateful one.﴾ ﴿Indeed in that﴾: the demonstrative refers to everything mentioned earlier: these visible towns and the ease of travel, then their request that God make the distances between their journeys far, then their being scattered throughout the lands completely.

﴿Are signs﴾: lessons. How does He say "signs" when it is one story? He says: because it is one story, but it comprises parts, and each part deserves to be a sign.

As for His saying ﴿for every steadfast one﴾: "ṣabbār" is an intensive form, meaning one who has much patience in trials. Patience (ṣabr) linguistically means restraint, and in the Sharia it means restraining oneself from what is forbidden at the time of calamities.

People, in calamities, have four levels: the level of discontent (suKHṭ), the level of patience (ṣabr), the level of contentment (riḍā), and the level of gratitude (shukr), which is the highest of them. Discontent is forbidden, patience is obligatory, contentment is recommended according to the preponderant opinion, and gratitude likewise is recommended. For this reason He says here: ﴿for every steadfast one﴾ patient in what? The author clarified it: (against sins). Indeed, and also in the decrees of God, and also in the commands of God, because patience has three kinds: patience in obeying God, patience in refraining from His disobedience, and patience in the decrees of God.

﴿Grateful﴾ means one who stands in thanks to God, with his heart, tongue and limbs, giving thanks to God, glorified and exalted, for His blessings. As for it being a sign for the patient, that is clear. How is it a sign for the grateful? Because when a person looks at their condition, that when they were grateful to God, God had bestowed these blessings upon them, he takes it as evidence that the gratitude to God is what makes the blessing of God remain upon the servant.

God, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿And We placed between them and the towns that We had blessed visible towns﴾ [Saba' 18]. In this verse is the explanation of God's blessing upon Saba', in that He made the towns extend from Yemen to Syria, close to one another.

* Also in it: that roads between neighbouring towns are safer and closer to security, by His saying: ﴿Travel therein by night and day, secure﴾.

* Among its benefits: that travel in them is measured stage by stage between these towns. The measuring of the journey, as we said, has a benefit, and what follows from this benefit is: measuring the journey is more invigorating to the traveller and easier for him, because if there is a great distance between towns, the traveller tires and becomes bored. But if he travels, covering them stage by stage, that is more invigorating for him and easier on him. We have mentioned that from this is the division of the Qur'an and of the subjects of knowledge in written books, so that a person covers them stage by stage, which makes it easier for him.

Perhaps we can take from it a benefit for one who wishes to memorise the Qur'an: that he should memorise it little by little, because some people recite to him a full page and then he goes back to memorise it, and it is difficult for him. But if he memorises it verse by verse, this is generally easier.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: security in one's homeland is among the greatest blessings, by His saying: ﴿nights and days, secure﴾, and no one is unaware that security is among the greatest blessings.

Then He said: ﴿So they said: Our Lord, make the distances between our journeys far﴾ [Saba' 19]. In this is evidence that these people were not patient with these blessings, but sought their removal and change. And was this statement by the tongue or by action? In other words, did they actually say ﴿Our Lord, make the distances between our journeys far﴾, or, when they wronged themselves and disbelieved, did that become the cause of the distance between these towns, since they were ruined, corrupted and destroyed? The first is the apparent meaning of the wording: that they actually said it, and God made the distance between them.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that these people, when they were insolent toward the blessing and unable to be patient with it, added to that the wronging of themselves through disbelief, from His saying: ﴿And they wronged themselves﴾.

* Among its benefits: that these people became tales for people after them. This is a kind of disgrace and shame, God forbid, that a person's affair becomes widely known so that he becomes a story for those who come after him. For this reason He said: ﴿So We made them tales﴾.

* Also among its benefits: that these people, whom God had blessed by gathering them in their towns and tribes, were completely torn apart, dispersed throughout the lands, by His saying: ﴿And We scattered them completely﴾.

* Among its benefits: that what God, the Mighty and Majestic, does to the disobedient and the wrongdoers is a sign for those who take heed, whether it is harm, so that they are patient, or ease, so that they give thanks, by His saying: ﴿Indeed in that are signs for every steadfast one, grateful one﴾.

* Among its benefits: the virtue of patience and gratitude: patience in hardship and gratitude in ease. A person is always afflicted by one of these two calamities: either hardship or ease. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We test you with evil and good as a trial﴾ [al-Anbiya' 35]. The one granted success is the one who gives each state what it deserves. In hardship, it is obligatory upon him to be patient and to await relief. He should know that when God, the Mighty and Majestic, decrees hardship upon him so that he may be patient, that is a blessing from God upon him. How so? Because patience, as we know, is a high rank, and the station of the patient is among the highest of ranks and stations. If there is nothing by which the servant is tested, he will not attain this rank, station or degree. There must be harm and calamities through which a person is patient, so that he may attain the rank of the patient. Likewise gratitude is a high rank that is attained only by one who is granted success. For when God makes a person taste prosperity after adversity, he is generally inclined to boast, rejoice and be insolent. But when gratitude in ease and patience in affliction are combined in him, he attains the rank of the patient and grateful. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "And know that victory comes with patience, relief comes with distress, and with hardship there is ease" [narrated by Ahmad (2803), from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with him]. Awaiting relief is an aid to patience, for when a person despairs and does not await relief, the world becomes narrow for him and his calamity is multiplied. But when he awaits relief, believing in it, the matter becomes easy for him.

He, the Exalted, says: (﴿And We placed between them and the towns that We had blessed﴾ with water and trees) and so on to the end. ﴿And We placed between them﴾: all the additions, all the attribution of the verb now to "nā" (We), which indicates majesty.

﴿We placed between them﴾: the pronoun refers to Saba'. ﴿And between the towns that We had blessed﴾: "qurā" is the plural of "qaryah," which is a town, whether large or small. It was called a qaryah because it gathers (yajmaʿu) people. What is well known among people, that a qaryah is a small city, is a conventional usage (iṣṭilāḥ ʿurfī). Otherwise, God says about Umm al-Qurā (the Mother of Towns): ﴿And how many a town, mightier in strength than your town which has expelled you﴾ [Muhammad 13]. So "qaryah" is the name of a settlement, whether it is large or small, and it was named so because it gathers people.

As for His saying ﴿the towns that We had blessed﴾, which towns did God bless? It has been said: they are the towns of Yemen, such as Sanaa and similar places. It has also been said: they are the towns of Syria (al-Shām). Each of the two opinions has a basis, because God, glorified and exalted, blessed Syria and He blessed Yemen. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O God, bless for us our Syria and our Yemen" [narrated by al-Bukhari (1037), and Ahmad (5641), whose wording this is, from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, may God be pleased with them both]. For this reason the exegetes differed: is the intended meaning of "the towns that God had blessed" the towns of Syria, or the towns of Yemen? Which of the two is the greater favour: that the intended meaning be the towns of Syria or the towns of Yemen? The towns of Syria, because they are far away. They go to Syria and return from it. Thus He says: ﴿And We placed between them and the towns that We had blessed visible towns﴾.

The author (al-Baghawi) said: (﴿We had blessed in them﴾ with water and trees), meaning and fruits, (and they are the towns of Syria to which they travel for trade. ﴿Visible towns﴾ continuous from Yemen to Syria). ﴿Visible﴾ means clear, so that some of them can be seen from others. For if a town is far from the next, it does not become visible. When you leave one town for another that is far from it, would the second town be visible to you? You would not find anyone to guide you. But when they are continuous and close together, what becomes [the state]? Visible, apparent to the eye. These are towns connected to one another from Yemen to Syria. Those who said that the intended meaning is the towns of Yemen said: it is not known that there were towns connected from Yemen to Syria. They said that the reality indicates otherwise, and that the intended meaning of the towns is the towns of Yemen. In any case, each of the two opinions has a basis.

He said: (﴿Visible towns﴾ continuous from Yemen to Syria). ﴿And We determined the travel therein﴾ means: We made it measured in stages, so that they halt from one town to another, stage by stage. He says: (﴿We determined the travel therein﴾ such that they rest midday in one and spend the night in another until the end of their journey, and they have no need to carry provisions or water). This is the meaning of "determining the travel": that it is measured in stages according to these towns. They rest at midday in one and spend the night in another, then rest at midday in the next and spend the night in another, and so on. There is no doubt that determining the travel in this way is one of God's blessings upon people. The routes that have no towns are usually dangerous and frightening roads. But when they are continuous, they become easier for the traveller and more reassuring, and even closer to the journey. For when you walk from one town to another, you feel that you have completed a stage. Like the Noble Qur'an now, since it was divided into verses, surahs and parts, it became easier for the reader. A book divided into chapters and sections is easier. Likewise the physical road: if towns follow one another along it, it is easier than a long road that wearies a person and in which he does not feel that he has covered any stage. For this reason God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We determined the travel therein﴾.

﴿Travel therein by night and day, secure﴾. The author said: (We said: travel). On this basis, this sentence is in the accusative position as a quoted speech of an omitted verb: "We said: travel."

Is this statement legislative or decreed? It is decreed (qadarī), meaning that God said to them: travel on these roads.

﴿Therein by night﴾ means in these towns. (﴿By night and day, secure﴾ fearing neither by night nor by day). This is among God's blessings: that they travel by night and day, secure, fearing no one, fearing neither loss nor a shortage of water nor a lack of food. But what happened? They were not patient with this blessing, God forbid. ﴿They said: Our Lord, make the distances between our journeys far﴾. They did not give thanks for the blessing, and it was incumbent upon them to thank God for this blessing and to hold fast to it, but they were not patient with it, so they asked God to make the distances between their journeys far, so that the journeys would be long with no towns in them. This is similar to the words of the companions of Moses to him: ﴿We will not be patient with one kind of food, so call upon your Lord to bring forth for us of what the earth grows: of its herbs, its cucumbers, its garlic, its lentils and its onions﴾ [al-Baqarah 61]. Although at first they used to eat with ease the manna and quails, without hardship and with good food, they were not patient with it. These people were not patient with this either. The people of Saba' were not patient with this blessing, which is among the finest blessings in journeys.

They said: (﴿Our Lord, make the distances between our journeys far﴾. In a reading that is one of the seven recognised readings (qirāʾah sabʿiyyah): ﴿Make far the distances between our journeys﴾ to Syria; make them deserts (mafāwiz)). Mafāwiz is the plural of mafāzah, which means lands in which one fears destruction. It was called mafāzah by way of optimism (tafāʾul), though in reality it is not a mafāzah; it is destruction and a place of ruin. But the Arabs apply a thing to its opposite out of optimism, as they called the broken one "jabīr" (one who is set right). This is similar. The author, in explaining ﴿Make far the distances between our journeys﴾, says: (make them deserts). Why? He said: (so that they might look down upon the poor by riding mounts and carrying provisions and water, and so they became insolent toward the blessing). When the towns were visible and close together, and there was no need to carry provisions or water-skins, the rich and the poor were equal in these routes, each enjoying the blessing on these roads. But when the distances increased, to whose share did this fall? The rich. So they asked God to make the distances between their journeys far, so that they might boast over their poor. These rich people would ride camels and carry whatever provisions they wished, while the poor could not do so. This is the reason they called upon God to make the distances between their journeys far.

He says: ﴿And they wronged themselves﴾. In what way? Either by disbelief, or by calling upon God, glorified and exalted, to make the distances between their journeys far. Thus they did not accept His blessing of this ease.

(﴿So We made them tales﴾ for those after them, ﴿and We scattered them completely﴾ we dispersed them throughout the lands utterly, ﴿Indeed in that﴾ mentioned, ﴿are signs﴾ lessons ﴿for every steadfast one﴾ against sins ﴿and grateful one﴾ for blessings). ﴿We made them tales﴾: "aḥādīth" is the plural of "ḥadīth," which is what people speak about. That is to say, after they had existed, they became a report among the reports.

(...) Their stories became tales that people talk about. You say: such-and-such happened, and so-and-so. This is among the well-known proverbs: "They were scattered like the scattering of Saba'" (tafarraqū ayādī Saba'), meaning that they were dispersed as Saba' was dispersed.

God, the Exalted, said: ﴿We made them tales﴾: after they had been real, established things, they became tales. This is like the words of the poet:

While a man is seen in it as one who gives news, until he is seen as a news item among the reports.

﴿We scattered them completely﴾ means: We dispersed them throughout the lands, every dispersal, and they were driven out and scattered, because they were ungrateful for the blessing and wronged themselves.
