* Among its benefits: that the lordship (rububiyyah) of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is divided into general and specific, and the specific into more specific and specific; based on His saying: ﴿And your Lord is Guardian over all things﴾, which is a lordship more specific than the specific. His lordship over His special servants, such as the prophets, is more specific than His lordship over believers in general, and His lordship over believers is more specific than His lordship over people in general. Look at ﴿I have only been commanded to worship the Lord of this city, which He has made sacred﴾ [an-Naml 91]: is it specific or general?
* A student: General.
* The Shaykh: O brothers, the Lord of this city is specific; how is it general? ﴿The Lord of this city which He has made sacred﴾: since specific lordship here may give the impression that His lordship is restricted to this city, after this He said: ﴿and to Him belongs everything﴾, which is general.

Then Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿Say, "Call upon those you claimed besides Allah"﴾ [Saba' 22]. In this is evidence that in debate it is proper to challenge the opponent regarding what is known not to be the case; based on His saying: ﴿Say, "Call upon those you claimed"﴾. So every caller to the truth must challenge these falsifiers by presenting, against their falsehood, some of the negation; and just as this applies to association with Allah, it also applies to what is less than it. The one calling to Allah the Mighty and Majestic should have knowledge of matters so that he can argue about them, for whoever lacks knowledge in them will be left bewildered and unable to confront the opponent.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that these idols invoked besides Allah own nothing for themselves, and therefore own nothing for others. They have no sovereignty, no share in sovereignty, no assistance in disposing of affairs, and no intercession. The matter here is clear: ﴿They do not possess an atom's weight in the heavens or in the earth, and they have no partnership in them, and He has no supporter among them﴾ [Saba' 22], meaning, no supporter for Allah from among them. ﴿And intercession will not benefit with Him except for one whom He permits﴾.
* Among its benefits: the affirmation of intercession by Allah's permission; based on His saying: ﴿And intercession will not benefit with Him except for one whom He permits﴾. Had intercession been of no benefit at all, the exception would not be valid; and had it benefited absolutely, the negation would not be valid. Note: if intercession absolutely benefited, whether or not Allah permitted it, the negation would not be valid; and if it absolutely benefited, the exception would not be valid. Therefore it benefits by Allah's permission.

* * *

﴿And intercession will not benefit with Him﴾, that is, with Allah, ﴿except for one whom He permits﴾. Here, ﴿intercession will not benefit with Him except for one whom He permits﴾ is due to the completeness of His dominion, so the negation here includes an affirmation, namely the completeness of sovereignty. For it is part of the completeness of sovereignty that no one speaks in the presence of the king to whom intercession is made except with his permission. For this reason, you find that when a person has awe among people and is in a gathering, people do not speak out of reverence for him; and when a ruler is awe-inspiring, no one dares to speak in his place of sitting, or even privately with his brother, because they stand in awe of him. So, because of the completeness of the sovereignty of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, no one can intercede except with His permission, even His most special servants, the prophets, and most special of them Muhammad ﷺ, cannot intercede except when Allah permits. Even in the station of mercy on the Day of Resurrection, when Allah makes one hundred mercies through which He shows mercy to creation, in the station of mercy and at the height of distress and grief which calls for Allah's mercy, the Messenger ﷺ cannot intercede at all except with Allah's permission. Why? Because of the completeness of the sovereignty of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. If intercession benefits only with Allah's permission, then can these idols, which are despised by Allah and lowly in rank before Him, intercede for their worshippers? Never. Even Jesus, peace be upon him, who was worshipped besides Allah, cannot intercede for his worshippers; for this reason he says on the Day of Resurrection: ﴿I said to them only what You commanded me: "Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord"﴾ [al-Ma'idah 117], and he cannot intercede for them.

﴿And intercession will not benefit with Him except for one whom He permits﴾. It was mentioned in the previous lesson that Allah does not permit except when both the intercessor and the one interceded for are among the people of intercession. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And how many an angel is there in the heavens whose intercession will not avail at all except after Allah gives permission to whom He wills and approves﴾ [an-Najm 26], and the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿And they do not intercede except for those whom He approves﴾ [al-Anbiya' 28]. For this reason the scholars said: the conditions of intercession are three: Allah's approval of the intercessor, His approval of the one interceded for, and the third, His permission for the intercession.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿until, when fear is removed from their hearts, they say, "What has your Lord said?"﴾. Here ﴿until﴾ is inceptive (ibtida'iyyah), not terminal (ghayatiyyah), because "until" (hatta) comes for limit, comes for beginning, and comes for causation, and it has several meanings. Whoever wishes to study them should refer to the book al-Mughni, meaning Mughni al-Labib by Ibn Hisham, may Allah have mercy on him, for it is beneficial for the student of knowledge.

He says: ﴿Until, when fear is removed﴾, in which there are two readings: ﴿fuzzi'a﴾ and ﴿fazza'a﴾, as the author said: (with the active and passive forms).
﴿From their hearts﴾, that is, the hearts of the creatures, or the hearts of the angels; there are two opinions among the scholars on this, and their explanation will come, Allah willing.
﴿Fuzzi'a 'an qulubihim﴾: he said: (the fear is uncovered from them by the permission concerning it). ﴿Fazza'a﴾ and ﴿fuzzi'a﴾ mean: removed the fear, and it is not ﴿fazza'a﴾ meaning to inflict fear, but rather meaning to remove it, and it is a verb used to express negation, because there are verbs used to express the removal of a meaning, that is, its opposite. They said: from this is their saying: qarrada al-ba'ir (he de-ticked the camel). What does qarrada mean? It removed the ticks from it. (...) Do you know the camel and the tick in it?
* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Known; the tick is known.
* A student: I don't know.
* The Shaykh: You know the camel. The tick is a thing that is in a camel's hide, a small insect that bites the camel and drinks its blood. What is its name?
* A student: Jarad.
* The Shaykh: Jarad? No, no.
* A student: Like lice, shaykh?
* The Shaykh: Like lice for humans; it is the lice of camels.
* The student: It grips (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. When it grips the skin, you can never release it, unless you grip it yourself and pull it off forcibly.
In any case, God willing, we may go out to the desert, see a camel with ticks, and show you them.
So the point is that qarrada al-ba'ir does not mean placing ticks on it; it means removing them from it. So ﴿fuzzi'a 'an qulubihim﴾ or ﴿fazza'a 'an qulubihim﴾ means: removed the fear.
﴿From their hearts﴾: the author said: (by the permission concerning it), that is, concerning the intercession. On this view, the pronoun here refers to the one interceded for; that is, when the one interceded for has been overtaken by distress, grief, and sorrow, as well as fear and dread, and then Allah permits the intercession, the fear is removed from the hearts, because relief is near.
He said: (﴿until, when fear is removed from their hearts﴾) by the permission concerning it, ﴿they say﴾, some of them to others, rejoicing, ﴿they say, "What has your Lord said?"﴾ concerning it, that is, concerning the intercession. ﴿They say﴾ the saying ﴿the truth﴾, that is, He has indeed permitted it, ﴿and He is the Most High﴾ above His creation by subjugation, ﴿the Great﴾, the Magnificent).
The author, may Allah have mercy on him, informed us that the pronoun in (from their hearts) refers to whom? To the one interceded for, for before intercession the one interceded for is overtaken by fear and dread because of his sins or other things; when permission for intercession is given, the fear is removed. And they say: "What did Allah say?" He describes that: one of them says to another: ﴿They say the truth﴾, that is, they say the true word, ﴿the truth﴾ meaning what is established and corresponds to its proper place.

Previously we established that truth in reports means truthfulness, and truth in rulings means justice, as God Most High says: ﴿The word of your Lord is fulfilled in truth and justice. None can alter His words, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ [al-An'am 115]. So this is the view the author (al-Sa'di) took: that the pronoun in "from their hearts" refers to those who were granted intercession, and that "tafzi'" means removing fear, which is fear of God's permission to intercede. Yes, the context does not reject this. However, it is established in a sound hadith from the Prophet ﷺ that the intended meaning is different, namely that it refers to the angels who are in the presence of God. When God speaks through revelation, they swoon. When they swoon, fear is removed from their hearts, meaning the fear is taken away, and then they ask one another, "What did your Lord say?" It is answered, "The Truth; and He is the Most High, the Great."

When the Sunnah explains the Quran, it takes precedence. We have also previously said that if the Quran indicates several meanings that do not contradict one another, it is understood to include all of them, because it is broader and greater than what human thought can reach. My thinking may reach one thing, another's thinking another, and a third's a third, and the verse as a whole allows all of these, so it is taken to include them. But if it allows only one meaning, then it must be understood in the sense supported by evidence.

Some scholars said: the fear is removed from their hearts at death, not on the Day of Resurrection when intercession is permitted. But this is weak. Although it is possible that fear is removed from the heart at death and a person acknowledges the truth, when Pharaoh was drowning, what did he say? ﴿Until, when drowning overtook him, he said: "I believe that there is no god except the One in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am among the Muslims"﴾ [Yunus 90]. And God the Glorified and Exalted says: ﴿So when they saw Our punishment, they said: "We believe in God alone, and we disbelieve in what we used to associate with Him"﴾ [Ghafir 84]. But this meaning is weak. The verse is therefore caught between what the author said and what the sound hadith establishes. The hadith definitively indicates what it reports, while what the author mentioned is possible and is not rejected by the verse.

God's words ﴿They say, "The truth"﴾: "the truth" (al-haqq). What is its i'rab (grammatical analysis)? What is it? It is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (masdar), meaning: they said the true statement. It cannot be an object of "qala" (said), because the verb "qala" (say) takes as its object only a sentence or something with the meaning of a sentence. "Qala" takes only a sentence or what is equivalent to one. A sentence, as in God's words: ﴿He said, "I am the servant of God"﴾ [Maryam 30]. Where is the object of "said"? ﴿I am the servant of God﴾ is a sentence. Or what has the meaning of a sentence, as when you say: "I said a poem," "I said a word." These have the meaning of a sentence, because a word, a poem, or a verse is only a sentence.

Now, if you say: What do you say about God's words: ﴿It is said to those who were mindful of God, "What has your Lord sent down?" They say, "Good"﴾ [al-Nahl 30]?

We say: this is not an object of "qala" but the object of an omitted verb. What is the estimated (implied) verb?

Student: "They said a good statement."

Shaykh: No.

Student: "He sent down good."

Shaykh: He sent down good: ﴿It is said to those who were mindful of God, "What has your Lord sent down?" They say, "Good."﴾

The author, may God have mercy on him, said: (﴿And He is the Most High﴾ above His creation by subjugation). This is either a deficiency or a shortcoming, because God's highness is not by subjugation alone. His highness has three types: the highness of subjugation, the highness of rank, and the highness of essence. But the author, may God pardon us and him, seems not to recognize the highness of essence. Those who deny the essential highness of God, the Glorified and Exalted, divide into two groups: the Hulūliyyah (those who hold that God is indwelling in creation), and the Mu'attilah (those who deny His attributes entirely).

The Hulūliyyah say: you must believe that God is in every place in His essence, and deny His highness above. Wherever you are, in the mosque, in the market, on land, or at sea, God the Glorified and Exalted is in that place in His essence. If you are in a latrine, He is in the latrine. The latrine is the place of relieving oneself, and God forbid, they did not exalt God above filth and defilement. We ask God for well-being. There is no doubt that this is pure disbelief, and no one doubts the disbelief of one who holds this belief.

The second group who deny the highness say: it is not permissible for us to say that God is above the world, nor beneath it, nor to the right or left, nor in front or behind, nor connected or separated. This is pure negation (ta'til). That is: if someone said to you, "Describe for us the nonexistent," you would find no description more comprehensive of the nonexistent than this description, which is neither above the world nor beneath it, neither to the right nor left, neither behind nor in front, neither connected nor separated. This is certainly not existent. As for the messengers and their followers, they believe that God the Mighty and Majestic is in His essence above everything. This is what reason, natural disposition (fitrah), consensus, the Book, and the Sunnah indicate. Let us review this matter. Although, praise be to God, the matter is clear, still the Book indicates that God in His essence is above His Throne in various ways: sometimes by mention of highness, as in ﴿He is the Most High, the Mighty﴾ [al-Baqarah 255]; sometimes by mention of aboveness, ﴿He is the Subduer over His servants﴾ [al-An'am 18]; sometimes by mention of things ascending to Him, ﴿To Him ascends good speech﴾ [Fatir 10]; and sometimes by mention of things descending from Him, ﴿He arranges the affair from the heaven to the earth﴾ [al-Sajdah 5]. The evidences in the Book of God for His highness, the Glorified and Exalted, are thus varied.

As for the Sunnah, it likewise indicates God's highness in His essence through the Prophet's ﷺ words, actions, and tacit approval. He ﷺ said: "Our Lord is God, who is in the heaven."[1] And he said: "Will you not trust me, when I am the trustworthy one of the One who is in the heaven?"[2]

As for his action: on the Day of 'Arafah, while delivering that great sermon, he said to the people: "Have I not conveyed?" They said: "Yes." He said: "O God, bear witness," raising his finger to the sky and pointing it toward the sky: "O God, bear witness." This is an action of the Sunnah, his gesture ﷺ when God was mentioned. As for tacit approval: he ﷺ was brought a slave girl, and he asked her: "Where is God?" She said: "In the heaven." He said: "Free her, for she is a believer."[3] He said this, and this is considered tacit approval. Thus the Sunnah varies in its indication of God's highness in His essence.

As for consensus: the early generations (salaf) from among the Companions, the Successors, and the leading scholars of the Ummah agreed that God the Most High is in the heaven in His essence. None of them said, not even a single letter, that God is not in the heaven, or that God is in every place in His essence, ever.

As for reason: ask your reason, is perfection in the highness of essence or in negating highness from it? The first, without doubt. Highness of essence indicates perfection; it is perfection itself. If highness is perfection, then it is known by reason that the Lord is characterized by perfection, and so highness is established for Him by reason. As for natural disposition: ask your nature when you ask God for something. Suppose you have not studied or attended mosques or anything. When you ask God the Mighty and Majestic for something, where does your heart turn? Upward. This is why Abu al-Ma'ali al-Juwayni used to argue, saying: "God existed and nothing was before Him, and His Throne was upon the water." He intended by this to deny God's istiwa' (settling) over the Throne, which necessarily entails affirming highness. Abu al-'Ala al-Hamadhani, may God have mercy on him, said to him: "Leave aside the mention of the Throne, and tell us about this innate necessity we find in ourselves. No knower has ever said 'O God' without finding in his heart a necessity to seek highness." That is correct. Al-Juwayni struck his head and cried out, saying: "Al-Hamadhani has bewildered me." Why? Because the natural evidence cannot be disputed. If a disputant contests it with you, you say: this man is insane.

Student: Is there in the hadith that was narrated (...)?

Shaykh: What?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: No, when he said: "His Throne was upon the water, and God existed and nothing was before Him." He did not mention "settled over the Throne." He did not mention His istiwa' over the Throne. He wanted to establish that God did not settle over the Throne, so His highness is negated.

Student: He omitted something from the hadith, then?

Shaykh: No, not at all. It is the same hadith, but he wanted to establish that God existed and nothing was before Him, and His Throne was upon the water. That is, there is no istiwa' or highness in it.

So now we say: the natural matter can never be denied by anyone. If someone denied that the hungry seek food, would he be believed? If he said the hungry do not seek food, would he be believed? No. This is why Abu al-Ma'ali al-Juwayni was bewildered and unable to answer, because this is a natural evidence that no one disputes.

Thus the evidences agree on God's highness in His essence. As for His highness in His attributes, whether attributes of decree or of subjugation, all who ascribe themselves to Islam acknowledge it, even the Jahmiyyah, the Ash'aris, and others acknowledge that God the Glorified and Exalted is high with a non-literal, metaphorical highness, which is the highness of attributes.

The author, may God have mercy on him, said: (﴿And He is the Most High﴾ above His creation by subjugation; ﴿the Great﴾, the Mighty). There is no doubt that this is not an exact tafsir. But it seems the author took it from pairing "the Mighty" with "the Most High" in the Verse of the Throne, where He said: ﴿and He is the Most High, the Mighty﴾ [al-Baqarah 255], and here He said: ﴿the Most High, the Great﴾. He explained ﴿the Great﴾ as what? As the Mighty. But the correct view is that ﴿al-Kabir﴾ does not mean the Mighty. Rather, it means the Possessor of Greatness (al-Kibriya'), and it means that nothing resembles God in His essence. The seven heavens and the seven earths in His hand, the Glorified and Exalted, are like a mustard seed in the hand of one of us. That is, the seven heavens with their greatness and the seven earths are like what would be if a person put a mustard seed in his hand. You know the mustard seed; the mustard seed is small. How big is it?

Student: Sesame.

Another student: Lentil seeds.

Shaykh: As big as sesame. This mustard seed, if you put it in your hand, is nothing. This too is an illustration for the sake of approximation. God is greater and more majestic, and all creatures are nothing compared to Him, the Glorified and Exalted. So we should say that ﴿al-Kabir﴾ does not mean the Mighty, but conveys another meaning: the One who possesses greatness, who is not likened to any of His creation. The seven heavens and the seven earths in His hand are like a mustard seed in the hand of one of us.

(...) In this verse is evidence for affirming intercession, because of His words: ﴿and intercession does not benefit with Him except for whom He permits﴾. If you say: what is the basis for establishing intercession, given that it is a negation? ﴿intercession will not benefit﴾. (...) He did not say: "and intercession will not be." ﴿and intercession will not benefit﴾ indicates its affirmation, but it does not benefit except with His permission.

Among the benefits of the noble verse: the greatness of God the Most High and the strength of His sovereignty. From where is this derived?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: What is the basis of that: it indicates God's greatness and the strength of His sovereignty. What is the basis of the indication?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: That is not in it... He did not say that God is strong, possessor of authority, or great, possessor of authority. But it indicates that by necessary implication. What is the basis of the indication?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: (...).

Student: (...).

Shaykh: Unlike created beings, however great their kingdom, where an intercessor enters upon the king or ruler and intercedes without permission. The greater the sovereign, the greater the awe, and no one speaks except by God's permission, as He said in Surat "Amma yatasa'alun": ﴿and the angels in ranks, none speak except one whom the Most Merciful permits, and he speaks rightly﴾ [al-Naba' 38].

Among the benefits of the noble verse: cutting off every means by which the polytheists hold on to their gods. What is its basis?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: Yes, cutting off all the means by which they argue that these gods benefit them, which are:

Student: (...).

Shaykh: Yes, and that intercession does not benefit. This is the last possible means, and yet God negated it.

Among the benefits of the noble verse: the demonstration of God the Mighty and Majestic's generosity toward both the intercessor and the one for whom intercession is made. From where do you derive God's generosity toward the intercessor and the one interceded for?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: Well done.

Among the benefits of the noble verse: that God the Glorified and Exalted speaks with audible speech. We now derive these benefits based on the preferred view regarding His words: ﴿until, when fear is removed from their hearts﴾.

Student: (...).

Shaykh: How?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: It is possible that ﴿except for whom He permits﴾, but I meant in the verse: ﴿when fear is removed from their hearts﴾.

Student: (...).

Shaykh: What is between them?

Student: (...) the angels swooned.

Shaykh: The angels swooned, and had they not heard His speech, they would not have swooned.

Among the other benefits of the noble verse: that the speech of God the Mighty and Majestic is not like the speech of created beings, but greater, because whoever hears it swoons unless God the Mighty and Majestic strengthens him, by His words: ﴿until, when fear is removed from their hearts﴾.

Among its benefits: that the word of God the Mighty and Majestic is entirely true, by His words: ﴿They say, "The truth"﴾.

Among its benefits: the affirmation of Lordship, by His words: ﴿What has your Lord said?﴾

Among its benefits: the affirmation of His highness, the Glorified and Exalted, by His words: ﴿And He is the Most High﴾. It is divided into the highness of essence and the highness of attributes, and both are established for God the Mighty and Majestic.

Among its benefits: the affirmation of greatness for God the Glorified and Exalted, by His words: ﴿the Most High, the Great﴾.

Among its benefits also: that the angels have intellects, understanding, perception, and hearts, by His words: ﴿until, when fear is removed from their hearts﴾. But are their hearts like the hearts of human beings? God knows best. We do not know their modality. The angels are a light-created people who do not eat or drink, and have no bodily cavities or intestines, because only one who eats and drinks needs a body cavity and intestines.

Student: (...)?

Shaykh: No. They speak. Did I say they do not speak? They speak. What I said is that they do not eat or drink.

Among the benefits of the verse: that the angels speak: ﴿They say, "What has your Lord said?" They say, "The truth, and He is the Most High, the Great."﴾

---

[1] Abu Dawud (3892) from Abu al-Darda', who said: I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say: "Whoever among you suffers a pain, or a brother of his suffers it, let him say: Our Lord is God, who is in the heaven..." the hadith.

[2] Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (4351) and Muslim (1064/144), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may God be pleased with him.

[3] Narrated by Muslim (537/33) from the hadith of Mu'awiyah ibn al-Hakam al-Sulami, may God be pleased with him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 34, verses 20–23 (part 1 of 3):

Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And Iblis had certainly confirmed his assumption about them﴾. He said: ﴿ṣadaqa﴾ is read with light and with heavy emphasis (takhfif and tashdid). ﴿ṣadaqa﴾ means what? It means he reported the truth. And ﴿ṣaddaqa﴾ means he who reports the truth. So the person is either one who reports or one who is reported to. The one who reports, we say ṣadaqa, and the one who is reported to, we say ṣaddaqa. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says ﴿ṣadaqa﴾ and ﴿ṣaddaqa﴾, and the two readings here carry the meaning of ṣidq (truthfulness) and taṣdīq (confirmation). The benefit of these two readings is that they indicate two meanings, which become clear when each is explained.

He said: (﴿ṣadaqa ʿalayhim﴾ or ﴿ṣaddaqa ʿalayhim﴾, that is, the unbelievers among them, Saba', ﴿Iblis had confirmed his assumption﴾ that by his misleading they would follow him, ﴿so they followed him﴾. So ṣadaqa with light emphasis means he was truthful in his assumption, or ṣaddaqa with heavy emphasis means he found his assumption to be true.)

Iblis had an assumption about the children of Adam. What was his assumption? His assumption was that he would mislead them all. Allah the Exalted said about him: ﴿He said, "By Your might, I will surely mislead them all, except Your sincere servants among them"﴾ [Sad 82–83]. He also said: ﴿"Because You have led me astray, I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path. Then I will certainly come to them from before them and from behind them and from their right and from their left, and You will not find most of them grateful"﴾ [al-A'raf 16–17]. This is what he hoped for and aspired to, and he assumed it either as a probable assumption (ẓann rājiḥ) or as a certain assumption. But he could not be certain; rather he assumed it as a probability. So here, ṣaddaqa his assumption: what was his assumption? That he would mislead them. So it was confirmed, because he did mislead them.

Or ﴿Iblis had confirmed his assumption about them﴾ means that when he assumed it, what he said came to pass, so ṣadaqa refers to the fact that he misled them. The summary is that the assumption Iblis held was what? Their misguidance. This is the assumption. It is either that by his misleading them he confirmed it, in that it first occurred from him by putting it into practice in action, or ﴿ṣadaqa ʿalayhim Iblis ẓannahu﴾ means that when he made that assumption, he carried it out and acted upon it.

The meaning is that what Satan anticipated and assumed regarding the misguidance of the unbelievers, including Saba', came to pass emphasized by the lam, qad, and the oath.

﴿So they followed him﴾: they followed Satan. And what, if we consider it, is the common thread of what Satan commands? He commands indecency: ﴿Satan threatens you with poverty and commands you to indecency﴾ [al-Baqarah 268]. So he commands indecency, wrongdoing, and every ugly deed. When a person follows him into indecency, wrongdoing, and ugly deeds, he has followed him and strayed from the right way. If he opposes him, then he has opposed him. For this reason He said: ﴿So they followed him, except a party of the believers﴾ (﴿illā﴾ here means "but," and ﴿a party of the believers﴾ is min for explanation).

The author said: ﴿illā﴾ means (but), indicating that the exception here is disjunctive (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ, an exception not of the same category as what precedes it), because when the exception carries the meaning of "but," it becomes disjunctive. What led the author to this is that His saying ﴿Iblis had confirmed his assumption about them, and they followed him, except a party of the believers﴾ apparently means that he confirmed it upon them all. In that case the believers were not included in this, so the exception here is disjunctive, because Iblis confirmed his assumption only upon the unbelievers. But if we make ﴿Iblis had confirmed his assumption about them﴾ general to the whole tribe, or to all the children of Adam, and then He says ﴿except a party of the believers﴾, the exception would be connected (istithnāʾ muttaṣil).

The summary is: if we make ﴿upon them﴾ refer to the unbelievers who followed Iblis, then the exception must be disjunctive here. If we make it general to the children of Adam or to the kind of this tribe (Saba'), the exception becomes connected.

As for His saying ﴿except a party of the believers﴾: the author, may Allah have mercy on him, says: (﴿of the believers﴾ is for explanation). How is it for explanation? It means that min is explanatory (bayāniyya), not partitive (tabʿīḍiyya), because if it were partitive the meaning would be "except a party of the believers, some of whom were saved from it and another party who were not saved," and this meaning is corrupt. Therefore min is explanatory.

Who are this party? The believers. The author said: (that is, they are the believers who did not follow him). Pay attention to this subtle meaning. The author, may Allah have mercy on him, is excellent in... I say again: ﴿except a party of the believers﴾. If you say: "A group of the people came," did they all come or not? No. So min is partitive. If we make min partitive as in your saying "a group of the people came," the meaning becomes corrupt, because all the believers did not follow him. For this reason the author needed to make min explanatory, with "the believers" serving as an explanation of ﴿a party﴾, as if he said: "So they followed him, except the believers." This is the meaning of the verse.

(﴿And he had no authority over them﴾ means dominion or power.) ﴿And he had no﴾: the pronoun refers to Iblis. ﴿Over them﴾ means over the people he misled. ﴿Any authority﴾: min is grammatically extra (zāʾida) in wording but not in meaning, and ﴿authority﴾ is the delayed subject of kāna (the noun of kāna placed after its predicate), meaning he had no authority over them. The intended meaning of authority here is domination or empowerment, and for this reason he said: "tasliṭ" (empowerment). So it is a verbal noun (ism maṣdar), and not the authority that is a meaning. The meaning is that Satan had no empowerment over them. On the author's interpretation that sulṭān means taslīṭ, the exception is connected, meaning: We did not give Satan empowerment over them except so that We would know. If we take sulṭān to mean domination or power, then the exception is disjunctive, meaning: he had no authority over them, but [We gave him this] so that We would know who follows him, and so on.

And His saying ﴿except that We would know who﴾: is the lam here for causation (taʿlīl) or for consequence (ʿāqiba)? It may be either. On both assumptions there is a difficulty. The difficulty is that its apparent meaning is the renewal of Allah's knowledge, whereas it is known that Allah's knowledge is eternal and everlasting, a qadīm (pre-eternal) continuing knowledge that must persist. So how is it correct for the lam here to be for causation or consequence?

The author explains it as: (knowledge of manifestation, ʿilm ẓuhūr). This is because God's knowledge of a thing has two states:
The first state: before its existence.
The second state: after its existence. So the attachment of God's knowledge to it after existence is called knowledge of manifestation, meaning His knowledge after it has appeared and become evident. God's knowledge before its existence is knowledge of decree (ʿilm taqdīr), meaning that He decreed that it should be. Knowledge of decree is established beyond doubt, for Allah has never ceased and will never cease to know everything that will happen.

Pay attention: if we say that knowledge is either knowledge of decree or knowledge of manifestation, the difficulty disappears, and God's knowledge of a thing after its occurrence is that it has become manifest and occurred, while His knowledge before its occurrence is knowledge that it will occur. There is a difference between the two objects of knowledge.

It was also said that what is meant by knowledge here is the knowledge upon which reward is based. That occurs only after the test, because God's knowledge of a thing before it occurs is knowledge upon which neither reward nor punishment is based, since the responsible person has not yet been commanded or forbidden. When he is commanded and obeys, or is commanded and does not obey, then he becomes rewarded or punished, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We will surely test you until We make evident those of you who strive and those who are patient﴾ [Muhammad 31], and ﴿Or do you think that you will enter Paradise while Allah has not yet made evident those of you who strove and made evident the patient?﴾ [Ali 'Imran 142]. On this view, God the Exalted has two kinds of knowledge:
A knowledge meaning that Allah knows this thing will occur, but no reward or punishment is based upon it.
And a knowledge upon which reward and punishment are based, which occurs only after the responsible person is tested, whether he acts or does not act, that is, whether he complies or does not comply.

Thus it becomes clear that in this matter, whose apparent meaning is the renewal of Allah's knowledge, there are two answers:
The first answer... Who knows the first answer? The knowledge by which the hidden is distinguished, because the matter has never ceased and will never cease to be clear and manifest before Allah, glorified is He.

He said: ﴿except that We would know who believes in the Hereafter from who is in doubt about it﴾. Here ﴿We would know﴾ is interpreted to mean (We would distinguish, numayyiz), and for this reason He said ﴿from who is﴾, meaning: except that We would distinguish who believes in the Hereafter from who is in doubt about it. People with regard to the Hereafter are divided into three categories:
A category that believed in it.
A category that disbelieved in it and denied it.
A category that is in doubt and hesitation.

As for those who believed in it, their situation is clear. And those who disbelieved and said: ﴿And they say, "When we are bones and crumbled remains, will we really be resurrected in a new creation?"﴾ [al-Isra' 49], this is impossible, and their situation is also clear. As for those who hesitated, they say: it may be true and it may be false. Which of the two categories do they belong to, the unbeliever or the believer? To the unbeliever, yes, because it is obligatory to believe. For this reason the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿from who is in doubt about it﴾. So how about one who denies it, rejects it, and disbelieves in it? Allah the Mighty and Majestic has given Satan authority over the children of Adam in order to test these people, so that He may know who believes in the Hereafter from who is in doubt about it. The one who is in doubt about the Hereafter follows whom? He follows Satan with certainty, because he does not believe that there is a Day on which people will be rewarded and punished. He thinks he has absolute freedom, but in reality it is freedom from something and bondage to something else. Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

"They fled from the bondage for which they were created ∗∗∗ ..........................."

What is the bondage for which we were created? Servitude to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

"..................... ∗∗∗ and they were afflicted with the bondage of the self and of Satan."

We ask Allah for well-being. They became slaves to their own selves and their devils. A person who thinks he has freed himself from worshipping Allah becomes a slave to others, to the self and to Satan. The summary is that those who were in doubt about the Hereafter cannot act or perform obedience to Allah, because the one who performs obedience is the one who believes that he will be gathered and rewarded or punished.

He said: (﴿from who is in doubt about it﴾, so We will recompense each of them ﴿and your Lord is Guardian over all things﴾). The sentence is declarative, conveying a meaning and what that meaning entails. It is declarative, indicating that Allah is a Guardian over all things, that is, He observes, knows, and watches over everything, whether it relates to His own action or to the actions of creation. He, may He be exalted, is a watcher over everything; nothing is hidden from Him in the earth or in the heavens. This meaning implies another meaning, which is a warning against disobedience, because when a person knows that Allah, glorified and exalted is He, is a Guardian over everything, he fears and does not disobey. But if he is in doubt about this, he acts as he wishes.

﴿Say: Call upon those you claimed besides Allah﴾. ﴿Say﴾: he said: (O Muhammad, to the unbelievers of Mecca). Here the author made the address specific in two respects: in terms of the one addressed and in terms of those called upon. The one addressed he said: (﴿Say﴾, O Muhammad), and those called upon: (the unbelievers of Mecca). But this is not accepted by the author or the exegete. Rather we say: ﴿Say﴾ can be addressed to you, and to whoever the address reaches from the Messenger ﷺ or others who inherited from him in his community; that is, say, O people. As for those called upon, we say: the more correct view is that it is general to everyone who called upon something besides Allah, from the unbelievers of Mecca and others.

Thus there must be a principle for us: "When the address is in doubt as to whether it is specific or general, it must be taken as general," because the general includes the specific but not vice versa, and the wider the meaning of the Quran, the more correct it is.

So we say: Say, O addressee, to those who call upon something other than Allah: Call upon those you claimed. (﴿Call upon those you claimed﴾ means you claimed them to be gods.) Call upon them. Is the intended calling here the calling of petition or the calling of summoning? "Call upon them" means summon them, or the calling of petition, that is, ask them, request needs from them, will they respond to you or not? Yes, it may have both meanings: summon them so that we may question them, or call upon them in petition, that is, ask them, as you say: "Call upon Allah," meaning ask Him.

The author's words: (that is, you claimed them to be gods). Look at what the author estimated: he supplied a pronoun and an explicit noun. The pronoun is "you claimed them" (the pronoun "them"), and the explicit noun is "gods." Thus he informed us that "claimed" (zaʿama) takes two objects, and that both objects are omitted, and the sentence's estimated form is "you claimed them gods," because zaʿama is among the verbs that take two objects whose original form is subject and predicate, so it belongs to the sisters of ẓanna. ﴿Besides Allah﴾: he said: (other than Him, that they may benefit you by your claim).

Is it possible for these polytheists that these gods benefit them? No, it is impossible for them to benefit them, because the causes of benefit are absent in several respects. First: they do not possess an atom's weight in the heavens or on the earth independently, nor do they possess it jointly. They have no assistance by which they help Allah, the Exalted. Fourth: they have no intercession except after Allah's permission. So Allah made clear that the causes of benefit in these gods are absent.

His saying ﴿they do not possess﴾ is a resumptive sentence (istiʾnāfiyya) explaining the state of these gods. (﴿They do not possess an atom's weight﴾, meaning the weight of an atom of good or evil, ﴿in the heavens or in the earth﴾.) This is correct: they do not possess an atom's weight in the heavens or on the earth. Do they possess less than an atom's weight? Or not less? Yes, because when the estimate is meant as emphasis, it has no implication, whether in quantity or in smallness. So here ﴿they do not possess an atom's weight﴾ means: not even less than it. Is that clear?

Fine. In terms of greater quantity: ﴿Even if you ask forgiveness for them seventy times, Allah will not forgive them﴾ [al-Tawbah 80]. Even if he asked more than seventy times, Allah would not forgive them. For this reason He said in the verse about the hypocrites: ﴿It is the same for them whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them; Allah will never forgive them﴾ [al-Munafiqun 6]. So when a restriction comes for emphasis, whether for smallness or greatness, it has no implication.

Therefore they do not possess an atom's weight, nor less than it, in the heavens or on the earth. If they possessed it, you would say: we cling to them, perhaps they will give us from what they possess. Is that correct or not? Fine. Do they have any share in the heavens or the earth? No. And if they had a share, you would say: perhaps they will give us from their portion. For this reason He said: (﴿And they have no share in them﴾, a partnership). The min here is grammatically extra but not in meaning. On this basis, ﴿share﴾ is the delayed subject, and its predicate is the prepositional phrase placed before it: ﴿And they have﴾, meaning they have no share in the heavens or the earth.

(﴿And for Him﴾, the Exalted: ﴿of them﴾, of the gods, ﴿is no supporter﴾). ﴿And for Him of them is no supporter﴾: ﴿of them﴾ is parsed in the same way as ﴿of share﴾; that is, min is extra in wording but not in meaning, ﴿supporter﴾ is the delayed subject, and the supporter means the helper, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say, "If mankind and the jinn gathered to produce the like of this Quran, they would not produce its like, even if they were to each other assistants"﴾ [al-Isra' 88]. So they have no assistance with Allah by which they might claim favor with Him, saying: give us in return for our assistance so that we may benefit those who call upon us. They have no help with Allah. (﴿And for Him of them is no supporter﴾, meaning helper.)

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 34, verse 20–23 (part 2 of 3):

(﴿And intercession will not benefit with Him﴾, a refutation of their claim that their gods would intercede with Him, ﴿except for one whom He permits﴾, with the hamza pronounced either as a fatha or a damma, ﴿and he is permitted﴾ to intercede.) If they say: "Yes, our gods do not own anything in the heavens or on the earth; our gods have no partnership with Allah; our gods did not assist Allah, but they intercede," as they said: ﴿They say, "These are our intercessors with Allah"﴾ [Yunus 18], intercession being their final claim, Allah cuts off this last means: ﴿And intercession will not benefit with Him except for one whom He permits.﴾ So these deities cannot intercede except after Allah's permission. And is it possible that He grants permission? No, it is not possible, because Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And how many an angel is there in the heavens whose intercession will not avail at all except after Allah gives permission to whom He wills and approves﴾ [an-Najm 26]. He, Mighty and Majestic, also says: ﴿And they do not intercede except for those whom He approves﴾ [al-Anbiya' 28]. It is known that He, Glorified and Exalted, does not approve of the disbelievers, so that they would intercede or be interceded for. Thus it is clear that everything the polytheists cling to in their associating partners with Allah is entirely false and entirely impossible. The means by which they could benefit are one of four matters, which we enumerate: sovereignty independently, sovereignty shared, assistance, and intercession. All four of these are absent in the worship of these invoked beings besides Allah, so every means to which the polytheists cling is cut off. In that case, worship and supplication must be directed to whom? To Allah the Exalted alone, for He is the One to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth.

Alright, what is intercession with Him? Linguistically, intercession (shafa'ah) is making a single thing into a pair (shaf'), or making an odd number (witr) into a pair, ﴿and the even and the odd﴾ [al-Fajr 3]. So one joins one to one? 
* Students: Shaf'.
* The Shaykh: And joins one to three?
* Students: Shaf'.
* The Shaykh: Shaf', and so on. But in terminology (istilah), it is mediating for another in bringing about a benefit or repelling a harm. This is intercession: that you mediate for someone else either to bring them a benefit or to repel a harm. Intercession for the people of Paradise to enter Paradise is bringing a benefit; intercession for one deserving the Fire not to enter it, and for one who has entered it to be taken out, is repelling a harm. Intercession does not go beyond these two matters: either to bring benefit or to repel harm.
Someone interceding for a person that his rank be elevated? That is bringing a benefit. Interceding for a person that a fine imposed on him be lifted? That is repelling a harm.
As for His saying: ﴿except for one whom He permits﴾ or ﴿he is permitted﴾, is the permission here the universal (kawni) or the legislative (shar'i)? The universal, meaning: except for one whom Allah has allowed to intercede, and the condition of permission is that Allah, the Exalted, be pleased with the intercessor and with the one interceded for. He grants permission for it, Glorified and Exalted, as an honour to the intercessor, a demonstration of his virtue, mercy toward the one interceded for, and kindness to him. And Allah (...).
﴿Besides Allah﴾: the supplication here (...).
Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And Iblis had already found his assumption true of them, so they followed him﴾ [Saba' 20]. From this it is derived that Iblis is described as truthful and described as lying, and what is the attribute necessarily his? Lying. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And Satan promises them nothing but delusion﴾ [an-Nisa' 120], and the Prophet ﷺ said: "He spoke the truth to you, though he is a liar"[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (2803) from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him).]]. But he may speak the truth.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of the wisdom of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in empowering Satan over the children of Adam, which is that He may know who believes in the Hereafter and acts for it, from among those who do not believe and are in doubt and so do not act; based on His saying: ﴿And he had no authority over them, except that We might make evident who believes in the Hereafter from one who is in doubt about it.﴾
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that faith is a barrier against following Satan; based on His saying: ﴿So they followed him, except for a group of the believers﴾. For this reason you often hear: "None of you believes until he does such-and-such," "Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him say such-and-such or let him do such-and-such," which indicates that faith is a barrier against following Satan and necessitates following the guidance of the Messengers, peace be upon them.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Satan is the leader of every astray person; based on His saying: ﴿So they followed him﴾; so all the misguided have Satan as their leader, and they are his followers.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse, if we say that ﴿from﴾ is for partitive meaning (tab'id), and that the following intended is absolute following: among its benefits is that some believers may follow Satan in some matters. This is because we said that the exception may be connected (muttasil), and ﴿from﴾ is partitive, since some believers may follow Satan in some matters. An example of this is: "None of you should eat with his left hand, nor drink with his left hand, for Satan eats with his left hand and drinks with his left hand."[[Narrated by Ibn Majah (3266) from Abu Hurayrah as a marfu' report with the wording: "Let one of you eat with his right hand, drink with his right hand, take with his right hand and give with his right hand, for Satan eats with his left hand, drinks with his left hand, gives with his left hand and takes with his left hand."]] Whoever does that becomes a follower of Satan. For this reason the preponderant view is that eating with the left hand and drinking with the left hand is forbidden, not merely disliked, and a person who does so is sinful, except if he is a modern, progressive, civilized "effendi", in which case he eats with the left hand.
* A student: With a fork.
* The Shaykh: No, the fork is not contrary; but the discussion is about the left hand. If you eat with the right hand, eat with three forks, it does not matter; but if you eat with the left, this is the problem, which those who do it claim makes them progressive and civilized. Yes, but not every advancement is praiseworthy, for Allah says about Pharaoh: ﴿He will lead his people on the Day of Resurrection and bring them down to the Fire, and wretched is the place to which they are brought﴾ [Hud 98]. Alright, so according to this last view, that ﴿from﴾ is partitive, the exception is connected, and some believers have a share of following Satan, though not complete following.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's knowledge; based on His saying: ﴿except that We may know﴾. The connection of Allah's knowledge to existing things, we previously mentioned yesterday, is of two kinds: a connection before their existence and a connection after their existence. The connection after existence is knowledge of an actual occurrence, while the first is knowledge of what will occur. By this the difficulty in such a verse is removed, since its apparent meaning suggests the renewal of Allah's knowledge, whereas we know that Allah, Glorified and Exalted, encompasses everything in knowledge, eternally and everlastingly, and whoever thinks that Allah does not know a thing until after its existence has disbelieved.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of the Hereafter and the obligation of believing in it. It is derived... from where is it derived?
* A student: ﴿except that We may know who believes in the Hereafter from one who is in doubt about it﴾.
* The Shaykh: So it contains the affirmation of the Hereafter and the obligation of believing in it.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that doubt regarding what must be held with certainty is disbelief; based on His saying: ﴿from one who is in doubt about it﴾. He did not say "from one who denies it," because one might say that the apparent meaning, since He said "who believes in the Hereafter," would be the opposite: "who disbelieves in the Hereafter." But He said: ﴿from one who is in doubt about it﴾ so that we benefit from it, namely that doubt regarding what is required to be certain is, like denial, disbelief.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the general care and watchfulness of Allah over everything. From where is it derived?
* A student: ﴿And your Lord is Guardian over all things﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿And your Lord is Guardian over all things﴾, correct.
* Among its benefits: that the lordship (rububiyyah) of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is divided into general and specific, and the specific into more specific and specific; based on His saying: ﴿And your Lord is Guardian over all things﴾, which is a lordship more specific than the specific. His lordship over His special servants, such as the prophets, is more specific than His lordship over believers in general, and His lordship over believers is more specific than His lordship over people in general. Look at ﴿I have only been commanded to worship the Lord of this city, which He has made sacred﴾ [an-Naml 91]: is it specific or general?
* A student: General.
* The Shaykh: O brothers, the Lord of this city is specific; how is it general? ﴿The Lord of this city which He has made sacred﴾: since specific lordship here may give the impression that His lordship is restricted to this city, after this He said: ﴿and to Him belongs everything﴾, which is general.

Then Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿Say, "Call upon those you claimed besides Allah"﴾ [Saba' 22]. In this is evidence that in debate it is proper to challenge the opponent regarding what is known not to be the case; based on His saying: ﴿Say, "Call upon those you claimed"﴾. So every caller to the truth must challenge these falsifiers by presenting, against their falsehood, some of the negation; and just as this applies to association with Allah, it also applies to what is less than it. The one calling to Allah the Mighty and Majestic should have knowledge of matters so that he can argue about them, for whoever lacks knowledge in them will be left bewildered and unable to confront the opponent.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that these idols invoked besides Allah own nothing for themselves, and therefore own nothing for others. They have no sovereignty, no share in sovereignty, no assistance in disposing of affairs, and no intercession. The matter here is clear: ﴿They do not possess an atom's weight in the heavens or in the earth, and they have no partnership in them, and He has no supporter among them﴾ [Saba' 22], meaning, no supporter for Allah from among them. ﴿And intercession will not benefit with Him except for one whom He permits﴾.
* Among its benefits: the affirmation of intercession by Allah's permission; based on His saying: ﴿And intercession will not benefit with Him except for one whom He permits﴾. Had intercession been of no benefit at all, the exception would not be valid; and had it benefited absolutely, the negation would not be valid. Note: if intercession absolutely benefited, whether or not Allah permitted it, the negation would not be valid; and if it absolutely benefited, the exception would not be valid. Therefore it benefits by Allah's permission.

* * *

﴿And intercession will not benefit with Him﴾, that is, with Allah, ﴿except for one whom He permits﴾. Here, ﴿intercession will not benefit with Him except for one whom He permits﴾ is due to the completeness of His dominion, so the negation here includes an affirmation, namely the completeness of sovereignty. For it is part of the completeness of sovereignty that no one speaks in the presence of the king to whom intercession is made except with his permission. For this reason, you find that when a person has awe among people and is in a gathering, people do not speak out of reverence for him; and when a ruler is awe-inspiring, no one dares to speak in his place of sitting, or even privately with his brother, because they stand in awe of him. So, because of the completeness of the sovereignty of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, no one can intercede except with His permission, even His most special servants, the prophets, and most special of them Muhammad ﷺ, cannot intercede except when Allah permits. Even in the station of mercy on the Day of Resurrection, when Allah makes one hundred mercies through which He shows mercy to creation, in the station of mercy and at the height of distress and grief which calls for Allah's mercy, the Messenger ﷺ cannot intercede at all except with Allah's permission. Why? Because of the completeness of the sovereignty of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. If intercession benefits only with Allah's permission, then can these idols, which are despised by Allah and lowly in rank before Him, intercede for their worshippers? Never. Even Jesus, peace be upon him, who was worshipped besides Allah, cannot intercede for his worshippers; for this reason he says on the Day of Resurrection: ﴿I said to them only what You commanded me: "Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord"﴾ [al-Ma'idah 117], and he cannot intercede for them.

﴿And intercession will not benefit with Him except for one whom He permits﴾. It was mentioned in the previous lesson that Allah does not permit except when both the intercessor and the one interceded for are among the people of intercession. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And how many an angel is there in the heavens whose intercession will not avail at all except after Allah gives permission to whom He wills and approves﴾ [an-Najm 26], and the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿And they do not intercede except for those whom He approves﴾ [al-Anbiya' 28]. For this reason the scholars said: the conditions of intercession are three: Allah's approval of the intercessor, His approval of the one interceded for, and the third, His permission for the intercession.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿until, when fear is removed from their hearts, they say, "What has your Lord said?"﴾. Here ﴿until﴾ is inceptive (ibtida'iyyah), not terminal (ghayatiyyah), because "until" (hatta) comes for limit, comes for beginning, and comes for causation, and it has several meanings. Whoever wishes to study them should refer to the book al-Mughni, meaning Mughni al-Labib by Ibn Hisham, may Allah have mercy on him, for it is beneficial for the student of knowledge.

He says: ﴿Until, when fear is removed﴾, in which there are two readings: ﴿fuzzi'a﴾ and ﴿fazza'a﴾, as the author said: (with the active and passive forms).
﴿From their hearts﴾, that is, the hearts of the creatures, or the hearts of the angels; there are two opinions among the scholars on this, and their explanation will come, Allah willing.
﴿Fuzzi'a 'an qulubihim﴾: he said: (the fear is uncovered from them by the permission concerning it). ﴿Fazza'a﴾ and ﴿fuzzi'a﴾ mean: removed the fear, and it is not ﴿fazza'a﴾ meaning to inflict fear, but rather meaning to remove it, and it is a verb used to express negation, because there are verbs used to express the removal of a meaning, that is, its opposite. They said: from this is their saying: qarrada al-ba'ir (he de-ticked the camel). What does qarrada mean? It removed the ticks from it. (...) Do you know the camel and the tick in it?
* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Known; the tick is known.
* A student: I don't know.
* The Shaykh: You know the camel. The tick is a thing that is in a camel's hide, a small insect that bites the camel and drinks its blood. What is its name?
* A student: Jarad.
* The Shaykh: Jarad? No, no.
* A student: Like lice, shaykh?
* The Shaykh: Like lice for humans; it is the lice of camels.
* The student: It grips (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. When it grips the skin, you can never release it, unless you grip it yourself and pull it off forcibly.
In any case, God willing, we may go out to the desert, see a camel with ticks, and show you them.
So the point is that qarrada al-ba'ir does not mean placing ticks on it; it means removing them from it. So ﴿fuzzi'a 'an qulubihim﴾ or ﴿fazza'a 'an qulubihim﴾ means: removed the fear.
﴿From their hearts﴾: the author said: (by the permission concerning it), that is, concerning the intercession. On this view, the pronoun here refers to the one interceded for; that is, when the one interceded for has been overtaken by distress, grief, and sorrow, as well as fear and dread, and then Allah permits the intercession, the fear is removed from the hearts, because relief is near.
He said: (﴿until, when fear is removed from their hearts﴾) by the permission concerning it, ﴿they say﴾, some of them to others, rejoicing, ﴿they say, "What has your Lord said?"﴾ concerning it, that is, concerning the intercession. ﴿They say﴾ the saying ﴿the truth﴾, that is, He has indeed permitted it, ﴿and He is the Most High﴾ above His creation by subjugation, ﴿the Great﴾, the Magnificent).
The author, may Allah have mercy on him, informed us that the pronoun in (from their hearts) refers to whom? To the one interceded for, for before intercession the one interceded for is overtaken by fear and dread because of his sins or other things; when permission for intercession is given, the fear is removed. And they say: "What did Allah say?" He describes that: one of them says to another: ﴿They say the truth﴾, that is, they say the true word, ﴿the truth﴾ meaning what is established and corresponds to its proper place.

Previously we established that truth in reports means truthfulness, and truth in rulings means justice, as God Most High says: ﴿The word of your Lord is fulfilled in truth and justice. None can alter His words, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ [al-An'am 115]. So this is the view the author (al-Sa'di) took: that the pronoun in "from their hearts" refers to those who were granted intercession, and that "tafzi'" means removing fear, which is fear of God's permission to intercede. Yes, the context does not reject this. However, it is established in a sound hadith from the Prophet ﷺ that the intended meaning is different, namely that it refers to the angels who are in the presence of God. When God speaks through revelation, they swoon. When they swoon, fear is removed from their hearts, meaning the fear is taken away, and then they ask one another, "What did your Lord say?" It is answered, "The Truth; and He is the Most High, the Great."

When the Sunnah explains the Quran, it takes precedence. We have also previously said that if the Quran indicates several meanings that do not contradict one another, it is understood to include all of them, because it is broader and greater than what human thought can reach. My thinking may reach one thing, another's thinking another, and a third's a third, and the verse as a whole allows all of these, so it is taken to include them. But if it allows only one meaning, then it must be understood in the sense supported by evidence.

Some scholars said: the fear is removed from their hearts at death, not on the Day of Resurrection when intercession is permitted. But this is weak. Although it is possible that fear is removed from the heart at death and a person acknowledges the truth, when Pharaoh was drowning, what did he say? ﴿Until, when drowning overtook him, he said: "I believe that there is no god except the One in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am among the Muslims"﴾ [Yunus 90]. And God the Glorified and Exalted says: ﴿So when they saw Our punishment, they said: "We believe in God alone, and we disbelieve in what we used to associate with Him"﴾ [Ghafir 84]. But this meaning is weak. The verse is therefore caught between what the author said and what the sound hadith establishes. The hadith definitively indicates what it reports, while what the author mentioned is possible and is not rejected by the verse.

God's words ﴿They say, "The truth"﴾: "the truth" (al-haqq). What is its i'rab (grammatical analysis)? What is it? It is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (masdar), meaning: they said the true statement. It cannot be an object of "qala" (said), because the verb "qala" (say) takes as its object only a sentence or something with the meaning of a sentence. "Qala" takes only a sentence or what is equivalent to one. A sentence, as in God's words: ﴿He said, "I am the servant of God"﴾ [Maryam 30]. Where is the object of "said"? ﴿I am the servant of God﴾ is a sentence. Or what has the meaning of a sentence, as when you say: "I said a poem," "I said a word." These have the meaning of a sentence, because a word, a poem, or a verse is only a sentence.

Now, if you say: What do you say about God's words: ﴿It is said to those who were mindful of God, "What has your Lord sent down?" They say, "Good"﴾ [al-Nahl 30]?

We say: this is not an object of "qala" but the object of an omitted verb. What is the estimated (implied) verb?

Student: "They said a good statement."

Shaykh: No.

Student: "He sent down good."

Shaykh: He sent down good: ﴿It is said to those who were mindful of God, "What has your Lord sent down?" They say, "Good."﴾

The author, may God have mercy on him, said: (﴿And He is the Most High﴾ above His creation by subjugation). This is either a deficiency or a shortcoming, because God's highness is not by subjugation alone. His highness has three types: the highness of subjugation, the highness of rank, and the highness of essence. But the author, may God pardon us and him, seems not to recognize the highness of essence. Those who deny the essential highness of God, the Glorified and Exalted, divide into two groups: the Hulūliyyah (those who hold that God is indwelling in creation), and the Mu'attilah (those who deny His attributes entirely).

The Hulūliyyah say: you must believe that God is in every place in His essence, and deny His highness above. Wherever you are, in the mosque, in the market, on land, or at sea, God the Glorified and Exalted is in that place in His essence. If you are in a latrine, He is in the latrine. The latrine is the place of relieving oneself, and God forbid, they did not exalt God above filth and defilement. We ask God for well-being. There is no doubt that this is pure disbelief, and no one doubts the disbelief of one who holds this belief.

The second group who deny the highness say: it is not permissible for us to say that God is above the world, nor beneath it, nor to the right or left, nor in front or behind, nor connected or separated. This is pure negation (ta'til). That is: if someone said to you, "Describe for us the nonexistent," you would find no description more comprehensive of the nonexistent than this description, which is neither above the world nor beneath it, neither to the right nor left, neither behind nor in front, neither connected nor separated. This is certainly not existent. As for the messengers and their followers, they believe that God the Mighty and Majestic is in His essence above everything. This is what reason, natural disposition (fitrah), consensus, the Book, and the Sunnah indicate. Let us review this matter. Although, praise be to God, the matter is clear, still the Book indicates that God in His essence is above His Throne in various ways: sometimes by mention of highness, as in ﴿He is the Most High, the Mighty﴾ [al-Baqarah 255]; sometimes by mention of aboveness, ﴿He is the Subduer over His servants﴾ [al-An'am 18]; sometimes by mention of things ascending to Him, ﴿To Him ascends good speech﴾ [Fatir 10]; and sometimes by mention of things descending from Him, ﴿He arranges the affair from the heaven to the earth﴾ [al-Sajdah 5]. The evidences in the Book of God for His highness, the Glorified and Exalted, are thus varied.

As for the Sunnah, it likewise indicates God's highness in His essence through the Prophet's ﷺ words, actions, and tacit approval. He ﷺ said: "Our Lord is God, who is in the heaven."[1] And he said: "Will you not trust me, when I am the trustworthy one of the One who is in the heaven?"[2]

As for his action: on the Day of 'Arafah, while delivering that great sermon, he said to the people: "Have I not conveyed?" They said: "Yes." He said: "O God, bear witness," raising his finger to the sky and pointing it toward the sky: "O God, bear witness." This is an action of the Sunnah, his gesture ﷺ when God was mentioned. As for tacit approval: he ﷺ was brought a slave girl, and he asked her: "Where is God?" She said: "In the heaven." He said: "Free her, for she is a believer."[3] He said this, and this is considered tacit approval. Thus the Sunnah varies in its indication of God's highness in His essence.

As for consensus: the early generations (salaf) from among the Companions, the Successors, and the leading scholars of the Ummah agreed that God the Most High is in the heaven in His essence. None of them said, not even a single letter, that God is not in the heaven, or that God is in every place in His essence, ever.

As for reason: ask your reason, is perfection in the highness of essence or in negating highness from it? The first, without doubt. Highness of essence indicates perfection; it is perfection itself. If highness is perfection, then it is known by reason that the Lord is characterized by perfection, and so highness is established for Him by reason. As for natural disposition: ask your nature when you ask God for something. Suppose you have not studied or attended mosques or anything. When you ask God the Mighty and Majestic for something, where does your heart turn? Upward. This is why Abu al-Ma'ali al-Juwayni used to argue, saying: "God existed and nothing was before Him, and His Throne was upon the water." He intended by this to deny God's istiwa' (settling) over the Throne, which necessarily entails affirming highness. Abu al-'Ala al-Hamadhani, may God have mercy on him, said to him: "Leave aside the mention of the Throne, and tell us about this innate necessity we find in ourselves. No knower has ever said 'O God' without finding in his heart a necessity to seek highness." That is correct. Al-Juwayni struck his head and cried out, saying: "Al-Hamadhani has bewildered me." Why? Because the natural evidence cannot be disputed. If a disputant contests it with you, you say: this man is insane.

Student: Is there in the hadith that was narrated (...)?

Shaykh: What?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: No, when he said: "His Throne was upon the water, and God existed and nothing was before Him." He did not mention "settled over the Throne." He did not mention His istiwa' over the Throne. He wanted to establish that God did not settle over the Throne, so His highness is negated.

Student: He omitted something from the hadith, then?

Shaykh: No, not at all. It is the same hadith, but he wanted to establish that God existed and nothing was before Him, and His Throne was upon the water. That is, there is no istiwa' or highness in it.

So now we say: the natural matter can never be denied by anyone. If someone denied that the hungry seek food, would he be believed? If he said the hungry do not seek food, would he be believed? No. This is why Abu al-Ma'ali al-Juwayni was bewildered and unable to answer, because this is a natural evidence that no one disputes.

Thus the evidences agree on God's highness in His essence. As for His highness in His attributes, whether attributes of decree or of subjugation, all who ascribe themselves to Islam acknowledge it, even the Jahmiyyah, the Ash'aris, and others acknowledge that God the Glorified and Exalted is high with a non-literal, metaphorical highness, which is the highness of attributes.

The author, may God have mercy on him, said: (﴿And He is the Most High﴾ above His creation by subjugation; ﴿the Great﴾, the Mighty). There is no doubt that this is not an exact tafsir. But it seems the author took it from pairing "the Mighty" with "the Most High" in the Verse of the Throne, where He said: ﴿and He is the Most High, the Mighty﴾ [al-Baqarah 255], and here He said: ﴿the Most High, the Great﴾. He explained ﴿the Great﴾ as what? As the Mighty. But the correct view is that ﴿al-Kabir﴾ does not mean the Mighty. Rather, it means the Possessor of Greatness (al-Kibriya'), and it means that nothing resembles God in His essence. The seven heavens and the seven earths in His hand, the Glorified and Exalted, are like a mustard seed in the hand of one of us. That is, the seven heavens with their greatness and the seven earths are like what would be if a person put a mustard seed in his hand. You know the mustard seed; the mustard seed is small. How big is it?

Student: Sesame.

Another student: Lentil seeds.

Shaykh: As big as sesame. This mustard seed, if you put it in your hand, is nothing. This too is an illustration for the sake of approximation. God is greater and more majestic, and all creatures are nothing compared to Him, the Glorified and Exalted. So we should say that ﴿al-Kabir﴾ does not mean the Mighty, but conveys another meaning: the One who possesses greatness, who is not likened to any of His creation. The seven heavens and the seven earths in His hand are like a mustard seed in the hand of one of us.

(...) In this verse is evidence for affirming intercession, because of His words: ﴿and intercession does not benefit with Him except for whom He permits﴾. If you say: what is the basis for establishing intercession, given that it is a negation? ﴿intercession will not benefit﴾. (...) He did not say: "and intercession will not be." ﴿and intercession will not benefit﴾ indicates its affirmation, but it does not benefit except with His permission.

Among the benefits of the noble verse: the greatness of God the Most High and the strength of His sovereignty. From where is this derived?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: What is the basis of that: it indicates God's greatness and the strength of His sovereignty. What is the basis of the indication?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: That is not in it... He did not say that God is strong, possessor of authority, or great, possessor of authority. But it indicates that by necessary implication. What is the basis of the indication?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: (...).

Student: (...).

Shaykh: Unlike created beings, however great their kingdom, where an intercessor enters upon the king or ruler and intercedes without permission. The greater the sovereign, the greater the awe, and no one speaks except by God's permission, as He said in Surat "Amma yatasa'alun": ﴿and the angels in ranks, none speak except one whom the Most Merciful permits, and he speaks rightly﴾ [al-Naba' 38].

Among the benefits of the noble verse: cutting off every means by which the polytheists hold on to their gods. What is its basis?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: Yes, cutting off all the means by which they argue that these gods benefit them, which are:

Student: (...).

Shaykh: Yes, and that intercession does not benefit. This is the last possible means, and yet God negated it.

Among the benefits of the noble verse: the demonstration of God the Mighty and Majestic's generosity toward both the intercessor and the one for whom intercession is made. From where do you derive God's generosity toward the intercessor and the one interceded for?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: Well done.

Among the benefits of the noble verse: that God the Glorified and Exalted speaks with audible speech. We now derive these benefits based on the preferred view regarding His words: ﴿until, when fear is removed from their hearts﴾.

Student: (...).

Shaykh: How?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: It is possible that ﴿except for whom He permits﴾, but I meant in the verse: ﴿when fear is removed from their hearts﴾.

Student: (...).

Shaykh: What is between them?

Student: (...) the angels swooned.

Shaykh: The angels swooned, and had they not heard His speech, they would not have swooned.

Among the other benefits of the noble verse: that the speech of God the Mighty and Majestic is not like the speech of created beings, but greater, because whoever hears it swoons unless God the Mighty and Majestic strengthens him, by His words: ﴿until, when fear is removed from their hearts﴾.

Among its benefits: that the word of God the Mighty and Majestic is entirely true, by His words: ﴿They say, "The truth"﴾.

Among its benefits: the affirmation of Lordship, by His words: ﴿What has your Lord said?﴾

Among its benefits: the affirmation of His highness, the Glorified and Exalted, by His words: ﴿And He is the Most High﴾. It is divided into the highness of essence and the highness of attributes, and both are established for God the Mighty and Majestic.

Among its benefits: the affirmation of greatness for God the Glorified and Exalted, by His words: ﴿the Most High, the Great﴾.

Among its benefits also: that the angels have intellects, understanding, perception, and hearts, by His words: ﴿until, when fear is removed from their hearts﴾. But are their hearts like the hearts of human beings? God knows best. We do not know their modality. The angels are a light-created people who do not eat or drink, and have no bodily cavities or intestines, because only one who eats and drinks needs a body cavity and intestines.

Student: (...)?

Shaykh: No. They speak. Did I say they do not speak? They speak. What I said is that they do not eat or drink.

Among the benefits of the verse: that the angels speak: ﴿They say, "What has your Lord said?" They say, "The truth, and He is the Most High, the Great."﴾

---

[1] Abu Dawud (3892) from Abu al-Darda', who said: I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say: "Whoever among you suffers a pain, or a brother of his suffers it, let him say: Our Lord is God, who is in the heaven..." the hadith.

[2] Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (4351) and Muslim (1064/144), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may God be pleased with him.

[3] Narrated by Muslim (537/33) from the hadith of Mu'awiyah ibn al-Hakam al-Sulami, may God be pleased with him.

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Say: Who provides for you from the heavens and the earth?﴾ [Saba' 24] ﴿Man﴾ is an interrogative particle, and what is meant by it is a challenge: a challenge to these polytheists who worship other than Allah. Are these idols providing for them from the heavens and the earth? No. Rather, it is Allah who provides, so He challenges them with the question: ﴿Who provides for you from the heavens and the earth?﴾

As for His saying ﴿from the heavens﴾, ﴿min﴾ (from) indicates the starting point; that is, provision comes from the heavens. Provision (rizq) means giving. So what is the provision from the heavens? The author said: (By rain), for rain is a provision that descends to the earth so that things grow. As for provision from the earth, its matter is evident: ﴿It is He who created for you all that is on the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah 29]. Then we may also say that provision from the heavens is more comprehensive than rain, for from the heavens descends rain, and from them descended the manna and the quails; and perhaps we may also say that birds in the air of the sky are of the provision of the sky, because they come from above, so everything that comes from above truly qualifies as provision from the heavens.

﴿Who provides for you from the heavens and the earth?﴾ The address in His saying ﴿Say﴾ is to the Messenger ﷺ. Who is the addressee in His saying ﴿provides for you﴾?

* The student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, the addressee is Allah! How? ﴿Who provides for you﴾: the polytheists and disbelievers. So how do they answer? Sometimes they answer correctly, as in His saying in Surah Yunus: ﴿Say: Who provides for you from the heaven and the earth, or who owns hearing and sight, and who brings forth the living from the dead and brings forth the dead from the living, and who arranges the affair? They will say, "Allah."﴾ [Yunus 31]. This is a correct answer. Sometimes they do not answer; they stammer, or they refuse to speak out of obstinacy and fear of being compelled, because if they say "Allah," they would be compelled to worship none but Allah: how can you worship one who does not provide? So sometimes they answer correctly and say, "Allah."
