Another benefit of this noble verse: affirmation of resurrection (al-ba'th), based on His words ﴿And on the Day when He will gather them all together﴾.

Another benefit of this noble verse also: the gathering is general for everyone, even for one who was eaten by beasts or burned by fire. From where is this derived? From His words ﴿all together﴾, and so it is. The one eaten by beasts or burned by fire must be gathered on the Day of Resurrection, as Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿As We began the first creation, We will repeat it﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:104].

Another benefit of this noble verse: affirmation that Allah speaks: ﴿Then We will say﴾. This, meaning the affirmation of speech and words to Allah, Glorified and Exalted, is the doctrine of Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah (the people of the Sunnah and the community), and the doctrine of the Ash'ariyyah, and the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah. Yes, but they differ in the explanation of this speech. For Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah, speech is real speech with letters and audible sounds, and it is uncreated.

For the Mu'tazilah, speech is speech with letters and audible sounds, but it is not one of the attributes of Allah; it is created according to them. They say that Allah, Exalted, creates speech and attributes it to Himself as an honor and glorification, like the attribution of the House (of Allah), the attribution of the mosques to Him, the attribution of the she-camel to Him, the attribution of the souls to Him, and similar things.

The Ash'ariyyah affirm that Allah has speech, but they say that it is without letters and without audible sounds; rather, it is a meaning subsisting in His essence. As for what is heard, which Musa heard, and which Muhammad (ﷺ) heard, and which people will hear on the Day of Resurrection, these are sounds that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, creates to express what is in His essence, and they are not the speech of Allah; rather, they are an expression of it.

As for Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah, they say: the speech of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, is real speech with letters and audible sound, but this sound does not resemble the sounds of created beings, because it is the speech of Allah, and His speech is one of His attributes, which do not resemble the attributes of created beings.

Another benefit of this noble verse: rebuke and reproach of those polytheists, by questioning those whom they claim to be gods, in order that they may show their disavowal of them, based on His words ﴿Did these used to worship you?﴾ and ﴿They will say: "Glory be to You! You are our Protector, not them"﴾ [Saba' 34:40-41]. Questioning the worshipped ones about the worship of the worshippers is intended for what? For rebuke and reproach of those worshippers, and to show that these worshipped ones disowned them and said: ﴿Glory be to You! You are our Protector, not them﴾. This is among the most severe forms of humiliation, reproach and regret, because it exposes the lies and fabrications of those worshippers.

Another benefit of it: affirmation of the angels, and that among people there are those who worshipped them besides Allah, based on His words, saying to the angels: ﴿Did these used to worship you?﴾.

Another benefit of it also: clarification of what the angels, upon them be peace, have of glorification of Allah, in that they said: ﴿Glory be to You﴾, meaning, exalted above having any partner, neither from us nor from anyone else.

And among its benefits: affirmation of the lordship of Allah, Glorified and Exalted, over the angels, in that they said: ﴿You are our Protector, not them﴾.

Another benefit of the verse: affirmation of the jinn, based on His words: ﴿Rather, they used to worship the jinn﴾. The jinn are an unseen world, created from fire, among whom are believers and disbelievers, obedient and disobedient, as in Surat al-Jinn.

Another benefit of this noble verse: the obligation to disbelieve in the jinn.

Student: The opposite.

Shaykh: The opposite?

Student: Yes, indeed.

Shaykh: Good. Now, His words ﴿Most of them were believers in them﴾: is this an affirmation or a denial?

Students: A denial.

Shaykh: Good. So the intended meaning of belief here is belief in their being worshipped, not belief in their existence, because belief in their existence is obligatory. But belief that they have a right to worship...

Thus we understand what passed us and what you found difficult in the Book of Monotheism (Kitab al-Tawhid), that one who affirms (witchcraft) as true will not enter Paradise, even though sorcery is a reality, and affirming it is a factual matter. But what is intended is affirming it in the sense of practicing it and believing in it, that is, in what it produces, such that a person practices it himself. As for affirming that sorcery has effects, this is a matter that cannot be denied.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 34, verses 38–41 (part 1 of 3):

(...) When He mentioned the reward of the believers, He mentioned the reward of others, because the Qur'an is *mathani* (oft-repeated), in which meanings are repeated and paired. When reward is mentioned, punishment is mentioned; when the believer is mentioned, the disbeliever is mentioned. This is so that the soul does not grow weary when it remains on a single subject, and so that a person, while reciting the Qur'an, moves between fear and hope. We all know that when the subject is one, the soul becomes bored and tired of it, but when it is varied, this gives it renewed energy.

He says: ﴿And those who strive against Our signs﴾. The author said: (the Qur'an, by nullifying it). ﴿Strive (yas'awna)﴾: *al-sa'y* is used for mere movement, and it is also used for running with intensity. In the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, when the call is made for prayer on the day of Jumu'ah, then proceed (fas'aw) to the remembrance of Allah﴾ [al-Jumu'ah 9], what is meant is general movement, not that one should run. But when you say, "He strives (yas'a) between al-Safa and al-Marwah, he strives between the two green markers," what is meant is running. Here, ﴿they strive against Our signs﴾ may mean general movement, or it may mean movement with intensity and determination, and the latter is more eloquent. That is, these people strive earnestly against the signs of Allah.

The author's statement ﴿against Our signs﴾, i.e., (the Qur'an), its basis is that the disbelievers do not deny the cosmic signs of Allah. Rather, they deny His legislative signs, although at times they ask for cosmic signs in order to make the Messenger ﷺ incapable (of bringing them). As Allah relates about them in His saying: ﴿And they say, "We will not believe you until you cause to gush forth for us from the earth a spring, or you have a garden of palms and grapes and make rivers gush forth within it in profusion, or you cause the sky to fall upon us in fragments as you have claimed, or you bring Allah and the angels before us in group, or you have a house of gold, or you ascend into the sky. And we will not believe in your ascension until you bring down to us a book we can read." Say, "Exalted is my Lord! Am I but a human messenger?"﴾ [al-Isra' 90–93]. How many signs did they request from the cosmic signs here? Yet Allah, Glorified and Exalted, said: ﴿Say, "Glory be to my Lord"﴾, meaning: exalting Him above sending a messenger without signs by which humans could believe, and I am but a human messenger. The point is that the author here restricted the signs to the legislative signs and said that what is meant is the Qur'an. It is possible that what is meant is both the cosmic signs and the legislative signs together, because just as these people are unable to match the Qur'an, they are also unable to match the cosmic signs.

The Qur'an was itself a sign from the signs of Allah, because it contains what humans cannot produce. Indeed, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, challenged mankind and the jinn: ﴿Say, "If mankind and the jinn gathered together to produce the like of this Qur'an, they could not produce its like, even if they were to one another assistants"﴾ [al-Isra' 88]. And He, Exalted, said: ﴿And they say, "Why has a sign not been sent down to him from his Lord?" Say, "Indeed, the signs are with Allah, and I am only a clear warner." Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book which is recited to them?﴾ [al-'Ankabut 50–51].

He says: (﴿And those who strive against Our signs, seeking to cause failure﴾ to Us, thinking that they have made Our power ineffective, and that they will escape Us).

﴿Mu'ajizin (seeking to cause failure)﴾: *al-mu'jiz* is the one who seeks to make another incapable. It is (ʿājazahu), like (qātalahu). So the meaning is that they seek to make Allah incapable, i.e., they seek, in their claim, what would demonstrate incapacity. That is why the author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: (i.e., thinking that they have made Our power ineffective, and that they will escape Us).

Those who did this seek to make Allah incapable and ask for what they claim would show incapacity, and they say: ﴿O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky or bring us a painful punishment﴾ [al-Anfal 32]. This is an attempt to make Allah, Mighty and Majestic, incapable. But Allah, Glorified and Exalted, is All-Wise and does not grant them what they want. Rather, He does these matters according to what wisdom requires.

Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿Those will be brought into the punishment﴾. I told you a little while ago: this sentence is the predicate of what? ﴿Those who strive﴾ is the predicate of the subject. Now, it is a declarative sentence. And His saying: ﴿Those will be brought into the punishment (muhdarun)﴾ means: they will be brought into the punishment itself, not merely toward it. Rather, they will be brought so that they fall into the very punishment. And *al-'adhab* means punishment and retribution. This statement is meant as a threat, not merely to inform us that these people will be brought into punishment and tormented. Rather, the purpose is a threat and a warning against their conduct.

Then He said: ﴿Say, "Indeed, my Lord extends provision for whom He wills of His servants and restricts [it] for him"﴾. ﴿Say﴾: the address is to the Prophet ﷺ, and it is permissible that what is meant is: the address can be directed to him, or to anyone to whom address is appropriate. He addresses those who strive against Our signs, seeking to cause failure, and who claim that Allah is incapable in what they assert.

(﴿Indeed, my Lord extends the provision﴾, expands it.) This is the meaning of ﴿extends (yabsuṭu)﴾, from *al-bast*, which is expansion. That is why it is said: "He expanded (basaṭa) the speech and abridged the speech," meaning he extended it and lengthened it. And *al-rizq* means provision and giving.

(﴿for whom He wills﴾ of His servants, as a trial, ﴿and restricts﴾ it, narrows it after expansion, or ﴿for whom He wills﴾, as a test.) Pay attention: ﴿He extends the provision for whom He wills of His servants﴾. His saying ﴿for whom He wills﴾ has come to us many times: every act that Allah attaches to His will is accompanied by wisdom. ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ [al-Insan 30]. So His will, Glorified and Exalted, follows His wisdom. If His wisdom requires that He expand the provision for someone, He expands it; and if His wisdom requires that He restrict it, He restricts it.

His saying ﴿of His servants﴾: "servants" here means general servitude, because it is observed that disbelievers and believers alike are subject to this: some of them Allah expands provision for, and some He restricts it for. So "servants" here means general servitude.

It has already been explained to us that servitude is divided into general and specific. The general, which includes all creation, is the cosmic servitude about which Allah said: ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾ [Maryam 93]. As for the specific, it is the servitude of legislative obedience, about which He said: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility﴾ [al-Furqan 63], and so on.

﴿of His servants﴾: the author said: (as a trial). What is the meaning of trial? It means a test that He tests: will he be thankful or ungrateful? That is why Sulayman, peace be upon him, said: ﴿This is of the bounty of my Lord to test me whether I will be grateful or ungrateful﴾ [al-Naml 40], when he saw the throne of Bilqis present before him in such a short time. He said: ﴿This is of the bounty of my Lord to test me whether I will be grateful or ungrateful﴾ [al-Naml 40]. And Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿And We test you with evil and with good as a trial﴾ [al-Anbiya' 35], meaning a trial and a test. How many a person was in a state of poverty that was better for him than after wealth, and how many a person was the reverse: poor, extravagant toward himself, and when Allah made him wealthy, Allah guided him. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, extends provision for whom He wills according to what wisdom requires.

He says: ﴿and restricts for him﴾. Does ﴿for him (lahu)﴾ refer back to the one for whom provision was expanded, or does it refer to whoever He wills in general? The author, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned both meanings. He said: ﴿restricts (yaqdiru)﴾: narrows it for him after expansion. That is, Mighty and Majestic, He expands provision for whom He wills and then narrows it for him in order to test him. He gives blessings and then removes them as a trial and a test. Allah bestows children on a person and they die; wealth, and it perishes. This is restriction after what? After expansion. Or the meaning is: ﴿He extends﴾ and ﴿restricts for him﴾, i.e., for whom He wills, not for the one who was given expanded provision. That is, He, Glorified and Exalted, extends provision to some people and restricts it for others. Do the two meanings contradict each other? No. And since the two meanings do not contradict each other, it has already been explained to us that the rule in tafsir (exegesis) is that when two meanings do not contradict each other, the verse is understood to include both of them.

﴿He extends the provision for whom He wills of His servants and restricts [it] for him﴾ [Saba' 39]. (﴿And whatever you spend of anything﴾ in good ﴿He will replace it, and He is the best of providers﴾. He replaces it for the person. It is said that every person provides for his family, i.e., from the provision of Allah.)

﴿And whatever you spend of anything, He will replace it﴾. ﴿Ma (whatever)﴾ here is conditional. The conditional verb is (anfaqa, you spend), and its response is ﴿fahuwa yukhlifuhu (He will replace it)﴾, and it is joined with the *fa'* because it is a nominal sentence. The response of the conditional is joined with *fa'* in seven situations. Our brother recites for us the verse in which they were versified...

* Student:
Nominal, imperative, and with the indeclinable...

* Shaykh: No.

* Student:
Nominal, imperative, and with the indeclinable, and with *ma*, and with *qad*, and with *lan*, and with the future particle.

* Shaykh: And with *ma*. No, (...) the order.

* The student:
.................. ∗∗∗ and with *ma*, *qad*, and with *lan*, and with the future particle.

* Shaykh: Yes.

Nominal, imperative, and with the indeclinable ∗∗∗ and with *ma*, *qad*, and with *lan*, and with the future particle.

Which of the seven categories is this verse from? Nominal.

And His saying, Exalted: (﴿And whatever you spend of anything, then He﴾, i.e., Allah, ﴿will replace it﴾, i.e., will bring its replacement.) Know that there is a difference between *yakhluf* and *yukhlif*. *Yakhluf* refers to a thing that succeeds another. Allah said about Musa when he appointed Harun as his successor: ﴿Be my successor among my people and reform﴾ [al-A'raf 142], meaning: be my successor among my people. As for the quadriliteral *akhlafa*, it means to give a successor. So the one who gives a successor is *mukhlif*, and the one who succeeds another is *khalif*. Pay attention to the difference between the triliteral and the quadriliteral: the triliteral means what? It means succeeded another. The quadriliteral means gave a successor. And from this is the hadith of Abu Salamah, who said: "And grant me a successor in my posterity" [[We have not located this text; perhaps what is intended is what Muslim (920/7) transmitted with his chain from Umm Salamah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ entered upon Abu Salamah when his eyes were open. He closed them and said: "Indeed, when the soul is taken, the eye follows it." Some of his family cried out, and he said: "Do not invoke against yourselves except for good, for the angels say Amen to what you say." Then he said: "O Allah, forgive Abu Salamah, raise his rank among those guided, grant him a successor among those who remain behind, forgive us and him, O Lord of the worlds, widen his grave for him, and illuminate it for him."]]. And the hadith of Umm Salamah, the same thing: she said: "And grant me something better than it" [[Muslim (918/4) transmitted with his chain from Umm Salamah, wife of the Prophet ﷺ, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "No servant who is afflicted by a calamity and says: ﴿Indeed we belong to Allah and to Him we return﴾, O Allah, reward me in my affliction and grant me something better than it, except that Allah will reward him in his affliction."]]. It is not "and make it succeed for me" (*wa-ukhlif*). "And grant me something better than it, except that Allah will reward him in his affliction and will grant him something better than it." Good. Here, is it from the quadriliteral or the triliteral? It is from the quadriliteral: ﴿fahuwa yukhlifuhu﴾, i.e., He gives what becomes a successor to it.

His saying ﴿and whatever you spend﴾: *al-infaq* means spending wealth. The author, may Allah have mercy on him, restricted it with his statement: (﴿whatever you spend﴾ in good). This restriction the author mentioned is indicated by many verses, as Allah said: ﴿And whatever good you spend, it is for yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah 272].

﴿And whatever good you spend will be repaid to you in full, and you will not be wronged﴾ [al-Baqarah 272]. The verses on this are numerous, because whoever spends in what is not good, the replacement is not guaranteed for him, but whoever spends in good, the replacement is guaranteed for him. This includes obligatory expenditures, such as a person's spending on his wife, mother, father, son, daughter, and what is similar. It also includes spending in zakah, because it is the mother of expenditures, since spending in zakah is one of the pillars of Islam. It includes spending in jihad in the way of Allah, and it includes spending in avenues of good, such as kindness to people and other things.

His saying: ﴿And whatever you spend of anything, He will replace it﴾: is this replacement in quantity or in quality? That is, does Allah give you a replacement for it in quantity, so that if you spend ten, He gives you ten? Or in quality, meaning that Allah sends blessing upon what remains, so that it becomes equivalent to what you spent and more? The apparent meaning is that it includes both: Allah replaces it, giving you a successor in quantity, so when you spend ten, Allah opens the door of provision for you and gives you ten; or it is a successor in quality. If you spend ten out of a hundred and ninety remain, these ninety stand in place of a hundred or more by the blessing that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, places in them. That is why it has come in the authentic hadith: "Charity does not decrease wealth" [[Muslim (2588/69) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]], meaning that charity does not diminish wealth but increases it, as Allah says here: ﴿He will replace it﴾.

He says: ﴿And He is the best of providers﴾. ﴿Khayr (best)﴾ originally was *akhyar*, because it is a superlative noun, but the hamzah was dropped for lightness, due to its frequent use.

And ﴿al-raziqin (providers)﴾ means those who give. How can we say ﴿the best of providers﴾ when the one who extends provision and gives provision is Allah?

We say: because others provide, but their provision is limited. It is said: he provided for his family. Allah said: ﴿And when the division is present, the relatives, the orphans, and the needy, then provide for them from it and speak to them a kind word﴾ [al-Nisa' 8]. So provision comes from Allah and comes from others, but from Allah it is comprehensive and general, while from others it is deficient and specific. So a person, as the author, may Allah have mercy on him, said, is said to "provide for his family", meaning he gives to them. But a person's giving to his family, or providing for those other than his family, from where is it? From the provision of Allah. Were it not that Allah gave you, you would not have given to others. So the meaning returns to: provision belongs to whom? To Allah, Glorified and Exalted. Yes: ﴿and He is the best of providers﴾.

He says: (And mention the day when We will gather them all together, then We will say to the angels...).

(And mention) the author supplied this as an implied verb because (إذ, "when") is an adverb of time, and an adverb, like a prepositional phrase, must have a governing element (mutaʿallaq). This element may be stated or implied. An example is the verse ﴿And if you could see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death﴾ [al-An'am 6:93]. Is the governing verb stated or implied? In ﴿And if you could see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death﴾, it is stated: "see" (ترى). In ﴿And if only you could see when the angels take those who disbelieve﴾ [al-Anfal 8:50], the governing element here is stated. It may also be omitted, and this is common in the Qur'an. Here, the governing element of "the Day" (يوم) is omitted. The implied meaning is: "Remember" the Day ﴿when He will gather them﴾, mention that day as a warning and a threat, because this day is a great day. As for His saying ﴿We will gather them all﴾: ﴿We will gather them﴾ means We will assemble them, and ﴿all﴾ is a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the pronoun in ﴿We will gather them﴾. When does this happen? Allah says: ﴿The Day He will assemble you for the Day of Assembly, that is the Day of Mutual Loss﴾ [al-Taghabun 64:9]. This is the Day of Resurrection, when Allah gathers the first and the last. Allah says: ﴿Say, "Indeed, the former and the latter (49) will surely be gathered for the appointed time of a known Day"﴾ [al-Waqiʿah 56:49–50]. And He says: ﴿That is a Day for which mankind will be gathered, and that is a Day witnessed﴾ [Hud 11:103].

(﴿We will gather them all﴾ meaning: the polytheists. ﴿Then We will say to the angels, "Did these [people] used to worship you?"﴾) His saying ﴿Did these [people] used to worship you?﴾: the hamzah is the interrogative particle. What is the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of ﴿these﴾? It is either a fronted object of (yaʿbudūn, "they worship"), or it is the subject (mubtada') with ﴿you﴾ (ʾiyyākum) as the object. This is because ﴿they worship﴾ here is mufarragha (a transitive verb whose object is not yet expressed), meaning it has not taken its object; when it has not taken its object, what precedes it becomes the object.

Now, may the object of the predicate of (kāna, "was") be placed before it?

The answer: Yes, it is permitted. This was covered earlier in the chapter on (kāna and its sisters), that its predicate may be placed first, and that the complement of its predicate may be placed first. Allah says: ﴿Unquestionably, the Day it comes to them, it will not be turned away from them﴾ [Hud 11:8]. Here the governing element of the predicate was placed before the particle. Here, ﴿you﴾ (ʾiyyākum) is the object of ﴿they worship﴾; that is, "Did these [people] used to worship you?" But it separated the pronoun because it was placed first.

He said: (﴿Ahāʾulāʾ iyyākum﴾ with the two hamzahs made clear, and changing the first into a yāʾ or dropping it.) We have two hamzahs: the hamzah of ﴿these﴾ and the hamzah of ﴿you﴾ (ʾiyyākum). There are three readings:
The first reading: (making both hamzahs clear), pronounced: ﴿ʾa-hāʾulāʾ ʾiyyākum﴾.
The second reading, he says: (changing the first into a yāʾ): ﴿ʾa-hāʾulāy ʾiyyākum﴾, where the hamzah is made a yāʾ.
The third: (dropping the first hamzah): ﴿ʾa-hāʾulā ʾiyyākum﴾ without a hamzah.

* The student: Dropping the first (hā'ulāʾ), without (ʾa-hāʾulāʾ).
* The Shaykh: No, I mean the first hamzah, that is, the first of the two adjacent hamzahs, which is the hamzah of (ʾulāʾ, "these") and the hamzah of (ʾiyyākum). These are three readings, and whichever of them you recite (...).

He says: ﴿they used to worship﴾. When is ﴿used to﴾? In the world. Allah says this as a rebuke and reproach to those worshippers who used to worship the angels. The angels are often presented to us as the plural of malak (angel), and the origin of malak is malʾak, and the origin of malʾak is maʾlak. Is this so? There are roots, but through usage it reached this form.

﴿They will say﴾: the pronoun refers to the angels. (﴿Glory be to You﴾: exalting You above having partners.) That is, we exalt You above our being partners with You, neither we nor anyone else. The exaltation of Allah the Mighty and Majestic concerns two things: the first is imperfection, and the second is resemblance to created beings. Although resemblance to created beings is itself an imperfection, this is a matter of detail in speech. Allah is exalted above imperfection, so, for example, Allah is not described as blind, deaf, incapable, weak, or the like. He is exalted above resembling created beings in attributes of perfection, so it is not said that His knowledge is like the knowledge of created beings, or His face like the faces of created beings, or His hand like the hands of created beings, or the like. He is exalted above both of these matters.

Here, He is exalted above having a partner, because if He had a partner, He would be deficient, since a partner is either a helper to the one he partners with or an owner of what that one owns. Allah, glorified be He, is exalted above this. The angels say, "Glory be to You," meaning exalting You above having a partner. The author, by his saying "exalting," informs us that ﴿Glory﴾ (subḥāna) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (ism maṣdar), so it is an absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq). It is always in the accusative as an absolute object and always tied to a genitive, so it does not occur as a noun in the nominative, or otherwise it is in the accusative as its absolute object.

(﴿Glory be to You; You are our Guardian, not them﴾: meaning, there is no alliance between us and them on our part.) That is, this affirmative statement ﴿You are our Guardian, not them﴾ means in effect a negative statement: we do not take them as allies; rather, You are our Guardian, not them. There is no alliance between us and them. When alliance is negated, its opposite is established, which is enmity. That is: these are our enemies, and You are our Guardian, not them. This is like His saying: ﴿Allah is the Guardian of those who believe; He brings them out of darkness into light. And those who disbelieve – their guardians are taghut; they bring them out of the light into darkness﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:257].

(﴿But﴾ marks a transition, ﴿they used to worship the jinn﴾: meaning the devils; that is, they obeyed them in their worship of us, ﴿most of them were believers in them﴾: affirming and believing what they say.)

﴿But﴾ marks a transition, because (bal) is used for two kinds of disengagement (iḍrāb): the transitional (intiqālī) and the cancelling (ibṭālī). If the purpose is to cancel what came before and establish what follows, the disengagement is cancelling. If the purpose is to move from one meaning to another, higher or lower, it is called transitional.

Here, the author says that this disengagement is transitional: that is, they did not cancel what came before. They still hold to their statement, "Glory be to You; You are our Guardian, not them," and there is no alliance between us and them; we do not take them as allies, nor do they take us. Rather, we add to that: ﴿they used to worship the jinn﴾. By "the jinn" here is meant the devils, because the jinn are in fact the devils. Allah says: ﴿And [mention] when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," and they prostrated, except Iblis. He was of the jinn and departed from the command of his Lord﴾ [al-Kahf 18:50]. So how do they worship the jinn? If the meaning is (...).

If they used to worship the angels, what is the apparent context? Then how is their worship of the jinn here? Their worship of the jinn is the worship of obedience: they obey them in associating partners with Allah. The jinn command them to make the angels partners with Allah in worship, and they obey them. Whoever obeys other than Allah in disobedience to Allah has taken that one as a god. Allah says: ﴿They took their rabbis and their monks as lords besides Allah, and [also] the Messiah, son of Mary﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:31]. It is related that when they made lawful what Allah had prohibited, they made it lawful, and when they prohibited what Allah had made lawful, they prohibited it. So they made them gods alongside Allah, glorified and exalted be He, in legislating, prohibiting, and obeying. Thus the meaning of His saying ﴿But they used to worship the jinn﴾ is: they obeyed them in worshipping whom? In worshipping the angels. Whoever obeys another in disobedience to Allah has taken that one as a god. ﴿But they used to worship the jinn; most of them were believers in them.﴾

(﴿Most of them were believers in them﴾: affirming what they say to them.) He said ﴿most of them﴾ and did not say "all of them," although all of them worship the angels out of obedience to the jinn. Why did He express it as ﴿most of them﴾ rather than "all of them"?

The answer is that these polytheists divide into two groups:
One group is the general followers, who know nothing, found their fathers upon a religion, and walked in its path.
The other group is the deliberate ones, who know the matter but believe in these jinn, affirm them, and disbelieve in the messengers. These are the majority. Nevertheless, the followers, who are the first group, if the truth becomes clear to them and they insist on following these and say what the nations said, ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers upon a religion, and we are following in their footsteps﴾ [al-Zukhruf 43:22], they deserve punishment, because they disbelieved with insight.

﴿So today, none of you will possess for another benefit or harm﴾ [Saba' 34:42]. In ﴿So today﴾, the (al-) is for the known (lil-ʿahd); what type is it?
* A student: The mental (dhihnī).
* The Shaykh: No, not the mental, nor the presential. The presential would mean "today." This is the anaphoric (dhikrī) "al-," referring back to what was mentioned, which is His saying ﴿And the Day We gather them﴾. That is, on the Day when We gather them, none of you will possess for another any benefit or harm.

And His saying ﴿today﴾: why is it in the accusative, or what governs its accusative?
* A student: Apposition (badal).
* The Shaykh: No.
* A student: "We warn today."
* The Shaykh: No.
* A student: As an adverb of time (ẓarf).
* The Shaykh: As an adverb of time, and what governs it is His saying ﴿does not possess﴾, meaning: none of you will possess for another any benefit or harm today.

(﴿So today none of you will possess for another﴾: meaning some of the worshipped for some of the worshippers ﴿benefit﴾: intercession ﴿or harm﴾: punishment.) ﴿None of you will possess for another﴾: whose possession is negated? The worshippers or the worshipped?
* Students: The worshipped.
* The Shaykh: The one who does not possess is the worshipped, because the worshipper hopes from the worshipped for benefit or harm. So we say: the worshipper does not possess for the worshipped any harm or benefit, just as the worshipped does not possess for the worshipper any harm or benefit. I believe this, and Allah knows best, is the wisdom: Allah the Mighty and Majestic said ﴿So today none of you will possess for another﴾ and made it indefinite to include the worshipper and the worshipped, the follower and the followed. So every person on the Day of Resurrection does not possess benefit or harm for anyone.

The author says: (intercession). Although the word "benefit" is more general than intercession, it seems that God have mercy on him restricted it to intercession, because of their saying: ﴿We only worship them that they may bring us nearer to Allah in position﴾ [al-Zumar 39:3]. They claimed that their worship of them was so that they would intercede for them with Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, and bring them closer to Him.

﴿So today none of you will possess for another benefit or harm﴾: meaning benefit in your worship of them through intercession, and it is more correct to say, and in other matters as well; ﴿or harm﴾ by your not worshipping them. That is, if you do not worship them, they will not harm you. Just as they do not possess benefit or harm on that Day, so they do not possess benefit or harm in this world.

If you say: a person may worship other than Allah and call upon it to remove a harm, and the harm is removed. What is the answer to this verse and others like it?

We say: what occurred did not happen through the supplication or the worship, but happened in his presence, not through it. So it is not a cause. If you say: your saying that it happened in his presence, not through it, is a claim that requires proof; otherwise it would be obligatory to attribute the matter to the thing or the apparent cause, which is the supplication to these idols. Do you understand this objection or not?

That is, you may say: this thing happened at the time of the supplication, not by means of it. Then it is said to you: this is your claim. Since he supplicated this idol to heal him and he was healed, the default is to attribute the ruling to the apparent cause, which is this supplication. The claim that it happened through something other than this apparent cause requires evidence. The answer is that we have evidence for this, which is His saying: ﴿And they worship besides Allah that which neither harms them nor benefits them, and they say, "These are our intercessors with Allah"﴾ [Yunus 10:18]. And He says: ﴿And who is more astray than one who calls upon other than Allah, one who will not respond to him until the Day of Resurrection, and they are unaware of their supplication?﴾ [al-Ahqaf 46:5]. These two verses and what resembles them all show that these idols benefit neither by bringing benefit nor by repelling harm. If something is found that happened after the supplication, it happened in their presence, not through them.

If you say: how can this thing be? And what is the wisdom in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, making the occurrence of this benefit or the removal of this harm happen at the supplication of these idols? We say: it is a trial and a test, for Allah may test the servant with a forbidden thing, which he persists in, or afflict him with a forbidden thing from which he refrains, and Allah is over all things capable (...).

* * *

Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And those who strive against Our verses, seeking to cause failure – those will be brought into the punishment﴾ [Saba' 34:38].

* Among the benefits of these verses:
* First: that among the servants of Allah are those who strive to nullify the verses of Allah with all the strength they can muster. The evidence is that Allah affirmed this and affirmed His punishment, saying: ﴿those will be brought into the punishment﴾, and it is not a supposed or hypothetical matter, but a real occurrence.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: showing how far human arrogance and tyranny may go, as he strives against the verses of Allah, seeking to defeat Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Who are you that you should try to defeat Allah, seek to make Him helpless, and challenge Him?!
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that these defeaters who strive against the verses of Allah seeking to defeat Him will on the Day of Resurrection be in punishment, by His saying: ﴿those will be brought into the punishment﴾. Someone may say: they are brought into punishment even in this world, and "punishment" here means inner punishment, because the disbeliever, however much he is given comfort in this world, is in pain and torment in his heart, since the disbeliever is never satisfied with the world. He is in sorrow, fearing the loss of what he has, and in anxiety, seeking what he lacks, because he wants his worldly life to grow and flourish, and he also fears that it may slip away. This differs from the believer.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: affirmation of recompense and punishment, by His saying: ﴿those will be brought into the punishment﴾.

Then Allah, glorified and exalted be He, said: ﴿Say, "Indeed, my Lord extends provision to whom He wills and restricts [it for whom He wills]"﴾ [Saba' 34:39].
* Among the benefits of this verse: the command to make it known that all matters, expansion and restriction alike, are in the hand of Allah. Evidence: His saying ﴿Say﴾, since the intent is not that you say it to yourself alone, but that you say it to yourself and to others as well.
* Among its benefits: that provision is in the hand of Allah, by His saying ﴿He extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it for him﴾. From this follows a benefit: that we should seek provision from whom? From Allah, since He is the one who extends and restricts provision. From this follows another benefit: that we should not seek Allah's provision through His disobedience, since seeking Allah's provision through disobedience to Him contradicts good manners. How can you seek provision from the One in whose hand is provision by disobeying Him?! For this reason the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, warned against this, saying: "Indeed, no soul will die until it has completed its provision and its term, so fear Allah and seek [provision] graciously."[[Al-Ḥākim (2163) related with his chain from Jabir, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed, none of you will die until he has completed his provision, so do not be impatient for provision. O people, fear Allah and seek [provision] graciously..." The hadith.]] That is: seek provision graciously, which means in accordance with the Sharia. Accordingly, is seeking provision through cheating, lying, and wrongdoing a lawful seeking or not? It is not lawful; rather, it contradicts good manners with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the completeness of Allah's lordship, glorified and exalted be He, and His authority, since He extends and restricts. No one can object to Him, and even if someone objects, will that objection benefit him? It does not benefit, because Allah directs what He wills.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: encouragement to spend (in charity), based on His words: ﴿And whatever you spend, He will replace it﴾. The reasoning is that when a person spends, his commanding self (al-nafs al-ammarah bi'l-su') tells him: "If you spend from your wealth, you will lose some of it, so do not spend." Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Whatever you spend, He will replace it﴾.

Another benefit: spending, even if it is little, will be replaced. From where is this derived? From His words ﴿of anything﴾ (min shay'), for it is an indefinite noun (nakirah) in a conditional context, emphasized by the extra (ziyadah) "min." This holds unless "min" is an explanatory "min" (bayaniyyah) for "má" in His words ﴿whatever you spend﴾.

Another benefit: Allah, Glorified and Exalted, is the best of providers in abundance of giving and continuity of giving. Anyone other than Allah among providers does not give much, and if he gives much, he tires and does not continue in his giving. As for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, He is the best of providers in His giving, both in abundance and in continuity.

Another benefit: affirmation of a provider other than Allah. From where is this derived? From His words ﴿the best of providers﴾, for this indicates the existence of one who is superior and one who is surpassed, both sharing the root of that in which superiority lies, which is provision. However, the provision of others is from the provision of Allah, because the one who gave me, for example, from where does he have his giving? From Allah. So his giving to me is from the provision of Allah which He gave him. Also, the provision of others is limited provision; it does not encompass everyone, nor does it encompass every time.

Another benefit of this noble verse: the actions of servants are created by Allah. Therefore it refutes whom? The Qadariyyah (those who deny divine decree). From where is this benefit taken? From His words ﴿whatever you spend﴾. We know that the provision that comes to us is largely from our earning: we trade, we farm, we work, and we obtain provision. So in this there is evidence that the act of the servant is created by Allah, Glorified and Exalted. In it there is also a refutation of the Jabriyyah (determinists), who are also the Jahmiyyah, based on His words ﴿whatever you spend﴾, where He attributes the act to the servant. The Jabriyyah say that man is deprived of power and choice, and that his act is ascribed to him only in a figurative sense, for in reality he has no choice in his act.

Then He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And on the Day when He will gather them all together, then He will say to the angels, "Did these used to worship you?"﴾ [Saba' 34:40].

From this noble verse it is derived: that one should remind people of the Day of Return (yawm al-ma'ad). The evidence is that ﴿the day when He gathers them﴾ is connected to an omitted verb whose estimated form is: "Remember the day when He gathers them." Does this include reminding oneself? That is, if your soul becomes heedless, should you remind it of the Day of Gathering and the Day of Death, or not? Yes, it includes that, because the implied "remember" (udhkur) may mean: remember this day within yourself, or remember this day to others. Both are true. So a person should remind himself of his destination. Whenever he inclines toward this world and wants to plunge into it, let him remind himself of the day of departure from this world, and remind himself of peoples who departed from this world while they were stronger than him, with more wealth and more children. Then let him remind himself of what lies beyond that: the reckoning and the punishment, and the witnessed Day for which people will be gathered.

Another benefit of this noble verse: affirmation of resurrection (al-ba'th), based on His words ﴿And on the Day when He will gather them all together﴾.

Another benefit of this noble verse also: the gathering is general for everyone, even for one who was eaten by beasts or burned by fire. From where is this derived? From His words ﴿all together﴾, and so it is. The one eaten by beasts or burned by fire must be gathered on the Day of Resurrection, as Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿As We began the first creation, We will repeat it﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:104].

Another benefit of this noble verse: affirmation that Allah speaks: ﴿Then We will say﴾. This, meaning the affirmation of speech and words to Allah, Glorified and Exalted, is the doctrine of Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah (the people of the Sunnah and the community), and the doctrine of the Ash'ariyyah, and the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah. Yes, but they differ in the explanation of this speech. For Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah, speech is real speech with letters and audible sounds, and it is uncreated.

For the Mu'tazilah, speech is speech with letters and audible sounds, but it is not one of the attributes of Allah; it is created according to them. They say that Allah, Exalted, creates speech and attributes it to Himself as an honor and glorification, like the attribution of the House (of Allah), the attribution of the mosques to Him, the attribution of the she-camel to Him, the attribution of the souls to Him, and similar things.

The Ash'ariyyah affirm that Allah has speech, but they say that it is without letters and without audible sounds; rather, it is a meaning subsisting in His essence. As for what is heard, which Musa heard, and which Muhammad (ﷺ) heard, and which people will hear on the Day of Resurrection, these are sounds that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, creates to express what is in His essence, and they are not the speech of Allah; rather, they are an expression of it.

As for Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah, they say: the speech of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, is real speech with letters and audible sound, but this sound does not resemble the sounds of created beings, because it is the speech of Allah, and His speech is one of His attributes, which do not resemble the attributes of created beings.

Another benefit of this noble verse: rebuke and reproach of those polytheists, by questioning those whom they claim to be gods, in order that they may show their disavowal of them, based on His words ﴿Did these used to worship you?﴾ and ﴿They will say: "Glory be to You! You are our Protector, not them"﴾ [Saba' 34:40-41]. Questioning the worshipped ones about the worship of the worshippers is intended for what? For rebuke and reproach of those worshippers, and to show that these worshipped ones disowned them and said: ﴿Glory be to You! You are our Protector, not them﴾. This is among the most severe forms of humiliation, reproach and regret, because it exposes the lies and fabrications of those worshippers.

Another benefit of it: affirmation of the angels, and that among people there are those who worshipped them besides Allah, based on His words, saying to the angels: ﴿Did these used to worship you?﴾.

Another benefit of it also: clarification of what the angels, upon them be peace, have of glorification of Allah, in that they said: ﴿Glory be to You﴾, meaning, exalted above having any partner, neither from us nor from anyone else.

And among its benefits: affirmation of the lordship of Allah, Glorified and Exalted, over the angels, in that they said: ﴿You are our Protector, not them﴾.

Another benefit of the verse: affirmation of the jinn, based on His words: ﴿Rather, they used to worship the jinn﴾. The jinn are an unseen world, created from fire, among whom are believers and disbelievers, obedient and disobedient, as in Surat al-Jinn.

Another benefit of this noble verse: the obligation to disbelieve in the jinn.

Student: The opposite.

Shaykh: The opposite?

Student: Yes, indeed.

Shaykh: Good. Now, His words ﴿Most of them were believers in them﴾: is this an affirmation or a denial?

Students: A denial.

Shaykh: Good. So the intended meaning of belief here is belief in their being worshipped, not belief in their existence, because belief in their existence is obligatory. But belief that they have a right to worship...

Thus we understand what passed us and what you found difficult in the Book of Monotheism (Kitab al-Tawhid), that one who affirms (witchcraft) as true will not enter Paradise, even though sorcery is a reality, and affirming it is a factual matter. But what is intended is affirming it in the sense of practicing it and believing in it, that is, in what it produces, such that a person practices it himself. As for affirming that sorcery has effects, this is a matter that cannot be denied.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 34, verses 38–41 (part 1 of 3):

(...) When He mentioned the reward of the believers, He mentioned the reward of others, because the Qur'an is *mathani* (oft-repeated), in which meanings are repeated and paired. When reward is mentioned, punishment is mentioned; when the believer is mentioned, the disbeliever is mentioned. This is so that the soul does not grow weary when it remains on a single subject, and so that a person, while reciting the Qur'an, moves between fear and hope. We all know that when the subject is one, the soul becomes bored and tired of it, but when it is varied, this gives it renewed energy.

He says: ﴿And those who strive against Our signs﴾. The author said: (the Qur'an, by nullifying it). ﴿Strive (yas'awna)﴾: *al-sa'y* is used for mere movement, and it is also used for running with intensity. In the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, when the call is made for prayer on the day of Jumu'ah, then proceed (fas'aw) to the remembrance of Allah﴾ [al-Jumu'ah 9], what is meant is general movement, not that one should run. But when you say, "He strives (yas'a) between al-Safa and al-Marwah, he strives between the two green markers," what is meant is running. Here, ﴿they strive against Our signs﴾ may mean general movement, or it may mean movement with intensity and determination, and the latter is more eloquent. That is, these people strive earnestly against the signs of Allah.

The author's statement ﴿against Our signs﴾, i.e., (the Qur'an), its basis is that the disbelievers do not deny the cosmic signs of Allah. Rather, they deny His legislative signs, although at times they ask for cosmic signs in order to make the Messenger ﷺ incapable (of bringing them). As Allah relates about them in His saying: ﴿And they say, "We will not believe you until you cause to gush forth for us from the earth a spring, or you have a garden of palms and grapes and make rivers gush forth within it in profusion, or you cause the sky to fall upon us in fragments as you have claimed, or you bring Allah and the angels before us in group, or you have a house of gold, or you ascend into the sky. And we will not believe in your ascension until you bring down to us a book we can read." Say, "Exalted is my Lord! Am I but a human messenger?"﴾ [al-Isra' 90–93]. How many signs did they request from the cosmic signs here? Yet Allah, Glorified and Exalted, said: ﴿Say, "Glory be to my Lord"﴾, meaning: exalting Him above sending a messenger without signs by which humans could believe, and I am but a human messenger. The point is that the author here restricted the signs to the legislative signs and said that what is meant is the Qur'an. It is possible that what is meant is both the cosmic signs and the legislative signs together, because just as these people are unable to match the Qur'an, they are also unable to match the cosmic signs.

The Qur'an was itself a sign from the signs of Allah, because it contains what humans cannot produce. Indeed, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, challenged mankind and the jinn: ﴿Say, "If mankind and the jinn gathered together to produce the like of this Qur'an, they could not produce its like, even if they were to one another assistants"﴾ [al-Isra' 88]. And He, Exalted, said: ﴿And they say, "Why has a sign not been sent down to him from his Lord?" Say, "Indeed, the signs are with Allah, and I am only a clear warner." Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book which is recited to them?﴾ [al-'Ankabut 50–51].

He says: (﴿And those who strive against Our signs, seeking to cause failure﴾ to Us, thinking that they have made Our power ineffective, and that they will escape Us).

﴿Mu'ajizin (seeking to cause failure)﴾: *al-mu'jiz* is the one who seeks to make another incapable. It is (ʿājazahu), like (qātalahu). So the meaning is that they seek to make Allah incapable, i.e., they seek, in their claim, what would demonstrate incapacity. That is why the author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: (i.e., thinking that they have made Our power ineffective, and that they will escape Us).

Those who did this seek to make Allah incapable and ask for what they claim would show incapacity, and they say: ﴿O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky or bring us a painful punishment﴾ [al-Anfal 32]. This is an attempt to make Allah, Mighty and Majestic, incapable. But Allah, Glorified and Exalted, is All-Wise and does not grant them what they want. Rather, He does these matters according to what wisdom requires.

Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿Those will be brought into the punishment﴾. I told you a little while ago: this sentence is the predicate of what? ﴿Those who strive﴾ is the predicate of the subject. Now, it is a declarative sentence. And His saying: ﴿Those will be brought into the punishment (muhdarun)﴾ means: they will be brought into the punishment itself, not merely toward it. Rather, they will be brought so that they fall into the very punishment. And *al-'adhab* means punishment and retribution. This statement is meant as a threat, not merely to inform us that these people will be brought into punishment and tormented. Rather, the purpose is a threat and a warning against their conduct.

Then He said: ﴿Say, "Indeed, my Lord extends provision for whom He wills of His servants and restricts [it] for him"﴾. ﴿Say﴾: the address is to the Prophet ﷺ, and it is permissible that what is meant is: the address can be directed to him, or to anyone to whom address is appropriate. He addresses those who strive against Our signs, seeking to cause failure, and who claim that Allah is incapable in what they assert.

(﴿Indeed, my Lord extends the provision﴾, expands it.) This is the meaning of ﴿extends (yabsuṭu)﴾, from *al-bast*, which is expansion. That is why it is said: "He expanded (basaṭa) the speech and abridged the speech," meaning he extended it and lengthened it. And *al-rizq* means provision and giving.

(﴿for whom He wills﴾ of His servants, as a trial, ﴿and restricts﴾ it, narrows it after expansion, or ﴿for whom He wills﴾, as a test.) Pay attention: ﴿He extends the provision for whom He wills of His servants﴾. His saying ﴿for whom He wills﴾ has come to us many times: every act that Allah attaches to His will is accompanied by wisdom. ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ [al-Insan 30]. So His will, Glorified and Exalted, follows His wisdom. If His wisdom requires that He expand the provision for someone, He expands it; and if His wisdom requires that He restrict it, He restricts it.

His saying ﴿of His servants﴾: "servants" here means general servitude, because it is observed that disbelievers and believers alike are subject to this: some of them Allah expands provision for, and some He restricts it for. So "servants" here means general servitude.

It has already been explained to us that servitude is divided into general and specific. The general, which includes all creation, is the cosmic servitude about which Allah said: ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾ [Maryam 93]. As for the specific, it is the servitude of legislative obedience, about which He said: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility﴾ [al-Furqan 63], and so on.

﴿of His servants﴾: the author said: (as a trial). What is the meaning of trial? It means a test that He tests: will he be thankful or ungrateful? That is why Sulayman, peace be upon him, said: ﴿This is of the bounty of my Lord to test me whether I will be grateful or ungrateful﴾ [al-Naml 40], when he saw the throne of Bilqis present before him in such a short time. He said: ﴿This is of the bounty of my Lord to test me whether I will be grateful or ungrateful﴾ [al-Naml 40]. And Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿And We test you with evil and with good as a trial﴾ [al-Anbiya' 35], meaning a trial and a test. How many a person was in a state of poverty that was better for him than after wealth, and how many a person was the reverse: poor, extravagant toward himself, and when Allah made him wealthy, Allah guided him. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, extends provision for whom He wills according to what wisdom requires.

He says: ﴿and restricts for him﴾. Does ﴿for him (lahu)﴾ refer back to the one for whom provision was expanded, or does it refer to whoever He wills in general? The author, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned both meanings. He said: ﴿restricts (yaqdiru)﴾: narrows it for him after expansion. That is, Mighty and Majestic, He expands provision for whom He wills and then narrows it for him in order to test him. He gives blessings and then removes them as a trial and a test. Allah bestows children on a person and they die; wealth, and it perishes. This is restriction after what? After expansion. Or the meaning is: ﴿He extends﴾ and ﴿restricts for him﴾, i.e., for whom He wills, not for the one who was given expanded provision. That is, He, Glorified and Exalted, extends provision to some people and restricts it for others. Do the two meanings contradict each other? No. And since the two meanings do not contradict each other, it has already been explained to us that the rule in tafsir (exegesis) is that when two meanings do not contradict each other, the verse is understood to include both of them.

﴿He extends the provision for whom He wills of His servants and restricts [it] for him﴾ [Saba' 39]. (﴿And whatever you spend of anything﴾ in good ﴿He will replace it, and He is the best of providers﴾. He replaces it for the person. It is said that every person provides for his family, i.e., from the provision of Allah.)

﴿And whatever you spend of anything, He will replace it﴾. ﴿Ma (whatever)﴾ here is conditional. The conditional verb is (anfaqa, you spend), and its response is ﴿fahuwa yukhlifuhu (He will replace it)﴾, and it is joined with the *fa'* because it is a nominal sentence. The response of the conditional is joined with *fa'* in seven situations. Our brother recites for us the verse in which they were versified...

* Shaykh: And with *ma*. No, (...) the order.

Which of the seven categories is this verse from? Nominal.

And His saying, Exalted: (﴿And whatever you spend of anything, then He﴾, i.e., Allah, ﴿will replace it﴾, i.e., will bring its replacement.) Know that there is a difference between *yakhluf* and *yukhlif*. *Yakhluf* refers to a thing that succeeds another. Allah said about Musa when he appointed Harun as his successor: ﴿Be my successor among my people and reform﴾ [al-A'raf 142], meaning: be my successor among my people. As for the quadriliteral *akhlafa*, it means to give a successor. So the one who gives a successor is *mukhlif*, and the one who succeeds another is *khalif*. Pay attention to the difference between the triliteral and the quadriliteral: the triliteral means what? It means succeeded another. The quadriliteral means gave a successor. And from this is the hadith of Abu Salamah, who said: "And grant me a successor in my posterity" [[We have not located this text; perhaps what is intended is what Muslim (920/7) transmitted with his chain from Umm Salamah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ entered upon Abu Salamah when his eyes were open. He closed them and said: "Indeed, when the soul is taken, the eye follows it." Some of his family cried out, and he said: "Do not invoke against yourselves except for good, for the angels say Amen to what you say." Then he said: "O Allah, forgive Abu Salamah, raise his rank among those guided, grant him a successor among those who remain behind, forgive us and him, O Lord of the worlds, widen his grave for him, and illuminate it for him."]]. And the hadith of Umm Salamah, the same thing: she said: "And grant me something better than it" [[Muslim (918/4) transmitted with his chain from Umm Salamah, wife of the Prophet ﷺ, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "No servant who is afflicted by a calamity and says: ﴿Indeed we belong to Allah and to Him we return﴾, O Allah, reward me in my affliction and grant me something better than it, except that Allah will reward him in his affliction."]]. It is not "and make it succeed for me" (*wa-ukhlif*). "And grant me something better than it, except that Allah will reward him in his affliction and will grant him something better than it." Good. Here, is it from the quadriliteral or the triliteral? It is from the quadriliteral: ﴿fahuwa yukhlifuhu﴾, i.e., He gives what becomes a successor to it.

His saying ﴿and whatever you spend﴾: *al-infaq* means spending wealth. The author, may Allah have mercy on him, restricted it with his statement: (﴿whatever you spend﴾ in good). This restriction the author mentioned is indicated by many verses, as Allah said: ﴿And whatever good you spend, it is for yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah 272].

﴿And whatever good you spend will be repaid to you in full, and you will not be wronged﴾ [al-Baqarah 272]. The verses on this are numerous, because whoever spends in what is not good, the replacement is not guaranteed for him, but whoever spends in good, the replacement is guaranteed for him. This includes obligatory expenditures, such as a person's spending on his wife, mother, father, son, daughter, and what is similar. It also includes spending in zakah, because it is the mother of expenditures, since spending in zakah is one of the pillars of Islam. It includes spending in jihad in the way of Allah, and it includes spending in avenues of good, such as kindness to people and other things.

His saying: ﴿And whatever you spend of anything, He will replace it﴾: is this replacement in quantity or in quality? That is, does Allah give you a replacement for it in quantity, so that if you spend ten, He gives you ten? Or in quality, meaning that Allah sends blessing upon what remains, so that it becomes equivalent to what you spent and more? The apparent meaning is that it includes both: Allah replaces it, giving you a successor in quantity, so when you spend ten, Allah opens the door of provision for you and gives you ten; or it is a successor in quality. If you spend ten out of a hundred and ninety remain, these ninety stand in place of a hundred or more by the blessing that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, places in them. That is why it has come in the authentic hadith: "Charity does not decrease wealth" [[Muslim (2588/69) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]], meaning that charity does not diminish wealth but increases it, as Allah says here: ﴿He will replace it﴾.

He says: ﴿And He is the best of providers﴾. ﴿Khayr (best)﴾ originally was *akhyar*, because it is a superlative noun, but the hamzah was dropped for lightness, due to its frequent use.

And ﴿al-raziqin (providers)﴾ means those who give. How can we say ﴿the best of providers﴾ when the one who extends provision and gives provision is Allah?

We say: because others provide, but their provision is limited. It is said: he provided for his family. Allah said: ﴿And when the division is present, the relatives, the orphans, and the needy, then provide for them from it and speak to them a kind word﴾ [al-Nisa' 8]. So provision comes from Allah and comes from others, but from Allah it is comprehensive and general, while from others it is deficient and specific. So a person, as the author, may Allah have mercy on him, said, is said to "provide for his family", meaning he gives to them. But a person's giving to his family, or providing for those other than his family, from where is it? From the provision of Allah. Were it not that Allah gave you, you would not have given to others. So the meaning returns to: provision belongs to whom? To Allah, Glorified and Exalted. Yes: ﴿and He is the best of providers﴾.

He says: (And mention the day when We will gather them all together, then We will say to the angels...).

(And mention) the author supplied this as an implied verb because (إذ, "when") is an adverb of time, and an adverb, like a prepositional phrase, must have a governing element (mutaʿallaq). This element may be stated or implied. An example is the verse ﴿And if you could see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death﴾ [al-An'am 6:93]. Is the governing verb stated or implied? In ﴿And if you could see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death﴾, it is stated: "see" (ترى). In ﴿And if only you could see when the angels take those who disbelieve﴾ [al-Anfal 8:50], the governing element here is stated. It may also be omitted, and this is common in the Qur'an. Here, the governing element of "the Day" (يوم) is omitted. The implied meaning is: "Remember" the Day ﴿when He will gather them﴾, mention that day as a warning and a threat, because this day is a great day. As for His saying ﴿We will gather them all﴾: ﴿We will gather them﴾ means We will assemble them, and ﴿all﴾ is a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the pronoun in ﴿We will gather them﴾. When does this happen? Allah says: ﴿The Day He will assemble you for the Day of Assembly, that is the Day of Mutual Loss﴾ [al-Taghabun 64:9]. This is the Day of Resurrection, when Allah gathers the first and the last. Allah says: ﴿Say, "Indeed, the former and the latter (49) will surely be gathered for the appointed time of a known Day"﴾ [al-Waqiʿah 56:49–50]. And He says: ﴿That is a Day for which mankind will be gathered, and that is a Day witnessed﴾ [Hud 11:103].

(﴿We will gather them all﴾ meaning: the polytheists. ﴿Then We will say to the angels, "Did these [people] used to worship you?"﴾) His saying ﴿Did these [people] used to worship you?﴾: the hamzah is the interrogative particle. What is the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of ﴿these﴾? It is either a fronted object of (yaʿbudūn, "they worship"), or it is the subject (mubtada') with ﴿you﴾ (ʾiyyākum) as the object. This is because ﴿they worship﴾ here is mufarragha (a transitive verb whose object is not yet expressed), meaning it has not taken its object; when it has not taken its object, what precedes it becomes the object.

Now, may the object of the predicate of (kāna, "was") be placed before it?

The answer: Yes, it is permitted. This was covered earlier in the chapter on (kāna and its sisters), that its predicate may be placed first, and that the complement of its predicate may be placed first. Allah says: ﴿Unquestionably, the Day it comes to them, it will not be turned away from them﴾ [Hud 11:8]. Here the governing element of the predicate was placed before the particle. Here, ﴿you﴾ (ʾiyyākum) is the object of ﴿they worship﴾; that is, "Did these [people] used to worship you?" But it separated the pronoun because it was placed first.

He said: (﴿Ahāʾulāʾ iyyākum﴾ with the two hamzahs made clear, and changing the first into a yāʾ or dropping it.) We have two hamzahs: the hamzah of ﴿these﴾ and the hamzah of ﴿you﴾ (ʾiyyākum). There are three readings:
The first reading: (making both hamzahs clear), pronounced: ﴿ʾa-hāʾulāʾ ʾiyyākum﴾.
The second reading, he says: (changing the first into a yāʾ): ﴿ʾa-hāʾulāy ʾiyyākum﴾, where the hamzah is made a yāʾ.
The third: (dropping the first hamzah): ﴿ʾa-hāʾulā ʾiyyākum﴾ without a hamzah.

* The student: Dropping the first (hā'ulāʾ), without (ʾa-hāʾulāʾ).
* The Shaykh: No, I mean the first hamzah, that is, the first of the two adjacent hamzahs, which is the hamzah of (ʾulāʾ, "these") and the hamzah of (ʾiyyākum). These are three readings, and whichever of them you recite (...).

He says: ﴿they used to worship﴾. When is ﴿used to﴾? In the world. Allah says this as a rebuke and reproach to those worshippers who used to worship the angels. The angels are often presented to us as the plural of malak (angel), and the origin of malak is malʾak, and the origin of malʾak is maʾlak. Is this so? There are roots, but through usage it reached this form.

﴿They will say﴾: the pronoun refers to the angels. (﴿Glory be to You﴾: exalting You above having partners.) That is, we exalt You above our being partners with You, neither we nor anyone else. The exaltation of Allah the Mighty and Majestic concerns two things: the first is imperfection, and the second is resemblance to created beings. Although resemblance to created beings is itself an imperfection, this is a matter of detail in speech. Allah is exalted above imperfection, so, for example, Allah is not described as blind, deaf, incapable, weak, or the like. He is exalted above resembling created beings in attributes of perfection, so it is not said that His knowledge is like the knowledge of created beings, or His face like the faces of created beings, or His hand like the hands of created beings, or the like. He is exalted above both of these matters.

Here, He is exalted above having a partner, because if He had a partner, He would be deficient, since a partner is either a helper to the one he partners with or an owner of what that one owns. Allah, glorified be He, is exalted above this. The angels say, "Glory be to You," meaning exalting You above having a partner. The author, by his saying "exalting," informs us that ﴿Glory﴾ (subḥāna) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (ism maṣdar), so it is an absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq). It is always in the accusative as an absolute object and always tied to a genitive, so it does not occur as a noun in the nominative, or otherwise it is in the accusative as its absolute object.

(﴿Glory be to You; You are our Guardian, not them﴾: meaning, there is no alliance between us and them on our part.) That is, this affirmative statement ﴿You are our Guardian, not them﴾ means in effect a negative statement: we do not take them as allies; rather, You are our Guardian, not them. There is no alliance between us and them. When alliance is negated, its opposite is established, which is enmity. That is: these are our enemies, and You are our Guardian, not them. This is like His saying: ﴿Allah is the Guardian of those who believe; He brings them out of darkness into light. And those who disbelieve – their guardians are taghut; they bring them out of the light into darkness﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:257].

(﴿But﴾ marks a transition, ﴿they used to worship the jinn﴾: meaning the devils; that is, they obeyed them in their worship of us, ﴿most of them were believers in them﴾: affirming and believing what they say.)

﴿But﴾ marks a transition, because (bal) is used for two kinds of disengagement (iḍrāb): the transitional (intiqālī) and the cancelling (ibṭālī). If the purpose is to cancel what came before and establish what follows, the disengagement is cancelling. If the purpose is to move from one meaning to another, higher or lower, it is called transitional.

Here, the author says that this disengagement is transitional: that is, they did not cancel what came before. They still hold to their statement, "Glory be to You; You are our Guardian, not them," and there is no alliance between us and them; we do not take them as allies, nor do they take us. Rather, we add to that: ﴿they used to worship the jinn﴾. By "the jinn" here is meant the devils, because the jinn are in fact the devils. Allah says: ﴿And [mention] when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," and they prostrated, except Iblis. He was of the jinn and departed from the command of his Lord﴾ [al-Kahf 18:50]. So how do they worship the jinn? If the meaning is (...).

If they used to worship the angels, what is the apparent context? Then how is their worship of the jinn here? Their worship of the jinn is the worship of obedience: they obey them in associating partners with Allah. The jinn command them to make the angels partners with Allah in worship, and they obey them. Whoever obeys other than Allah in disobedience to Allah has taken that one as a god. Allah says: ﴿They took their rabbis and their monks as lords besides Allah, and [also] the Messiah, son of Mary﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:31]. It is related that when they made lawful what Allah had prohibited, they made it lawful, and when they prohibited what Allah had made lawful, they prohibited it. So they made them gods alongside Allah, glorified and exalted be He, in legislating, prohibiting, and obeying. Thus the meaning of His saying ﴿But they used to worship the jinn﴾ is: they obeyed them in worshipping whom? In worshipping the angels. Whoever obeys another in disobedience to Allah has taken that one as a god. ﴿But they used to worship the jinn; most of them were believers in them.﴾

(﴿Most of them were believers in them﴾: affirming what they say to them.) He said ﴿most of them﴾ and did not say "all of them," although all of them worship the angels out of obedience to the jinn. Why did He express it as ﴿most of them﴾ rather than "all of them"?

The answer is that these polytheists divide into two groups:
One group is the general followers, who know nothing, found their fathers upon a religion, and walked in its path.
The other group is the deliberate ones, who know the matter but believe in these jinn, affirm them, and disbelieve in the messengers. These are the majority. Nevertheless, the followers, who are the first group, if the truth becomes clear to them and they insist on following these and say what the nations said, ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers upon a religion, and we are following in their footsteps﴾ [al-Zukhruf 43:22], they deserve punishment, because they disbelieved with insight.

﴿So today, none of you will possess for another benefit or harm﴾ [Saba' 34:42]. In ﴿So today﴾, the (al-) is for the known (lil-ʿahd); what type is it?
* A student: The mental (dhihnī).
* The Shaykh: No, not the mental, nor the presential. The presential would mean "today." This is the anaphoric (dhikrī) "al-," referring back to what was mentioned, which is His saying ﴿And the Day We gather them﴾. That is, on the Day when We gather them, none of you will possess for another any benefit or harm.

And His saying ﴿today﴾: why is it in the accusative, or what governs its accusative?
* A student: Apposition (badal).
* The Shaykh: No.
* A student: "We warn today."
* The Shaykh: No.
* A student: As an adverb of time (ẓarf).
* The Shaykh: As an adverb of time, and what governs it is His saying ﴿does not possess﴾, meaning: none of you will possess for another any benefit or harm today.

(﴿So today none of you will possess for another﴾: meaning some of the worshipped for some of the worshippers ﴿benefit﴾: intercession ﴿or harm﴾: punishment.) ﴿None of you will possess for another﴾: whose possession is negated? The worshippers or the worshipped?
* Students: The worshipped.
* The Shaykh: The one who does not possess is the worshipped, because the worshipper hopes from the worshipped for benefit or harm. So we say: the worshipper does not possess for the worshipped any harm or benefit, just as the worshipped does not possess for the worshipper any harm or benefit. I believe this, and Allah knows best, is the wisdom: Allah the Mighty and Majestic said ﴿So today none of you will possess for another﴾ and made it indefinite to include the worshipper and the worshipped, the follower and the followed. So every person on the Day of Resurrection does not possess benefit or harm for anyone.

The author says: (intercession). Although the word "benefit" is more general than intercession, it seems that God have mercy on him restricted it to intercession, because of their saying: ﴿We only worship them that they may bring us nearer to Allah in position﴾ [al-Zumar 39:3]. They claimed that their worship of them was so that they would intercede for them with Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, and bring them closer to Him.

﴿So today none of you will possess for another benefit or harm﴾: meaning benefit in your worship of them through intercession, and it is more correct to say, and in other matters as well; ﴿or harm﴾ by your not worshipping them. That is, if you do not worship them, they will not harm you. Just as they do not possess benefit or harm on that Day, so they do not possess benefit or harm in this world.

If you say: a person may worship other than Allah and call upon it to remove a harm, and the harm is removed. What is the answer to this verse and others like it?

We say: what occurred did not happen through the supplication or the worship, but happened in his presence, not through it. So it is not a cause. If you say: your saying that it happened in his presence, not through it, is a claim that requires proof; otherwise it would be obligatory to attribute the matter to the thing or the apparent cause, which is the supplication to these idols. Do you understand this objection or not?

That is, you may say: this thing happened at the time of the supplication, not by means of it. Then it is said to you: this is your claim. Since he supplicated this idol to heal him and he was healed, the default is to attribute the ruling to the apparent cause, which is this supplication. The claim that it happened through something other than this apparent cause requires evidence. The answer is that we have evidence for this, which is His saying: ﴿And they worship besides Allah that which neither harms them nor benefits them, and they say, "These are our intercessors with Allah"﴾ [Yunus 10:18]. And He says: ﴿And who is more astray than one who calls upon other than Allah, one who will not respond to him until the Day of Resurrection, and they are unaware of their supplication?﴾ [al-Ahqaf 46:5]. These two verses and what resembles them all show that these idols benefit neither by bringing benefit nor by repelling harm. If something is found that happened after the supplication, it happened in their presence, not through them.

If you say: how can this thing be? And what is the wisdom in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, making the occurrence of this benefit or the removal of this harm happen at the supplication of these idols? We say: it is a trial and a test, for Allah may test the servant with a forbidden thing, which he persists in, or afflict him with a forbidden thing from which he refrains, and Allah is over all things capable (...).

* * *

Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And those who strive against Our verses, seeking to cause failure – those will be brought into the punishment﴾ [Saba' 34:38].

* Among the benefits of these verses:
* First: that among the servants of Allah are those who strive to nullify the verses of Allah with all the strength they can muster. The evidence is that Allah affirmed this and affirmed His punishment, saying: ﴿those will be brought into the punishment﴾, and it is not a supposed or hypothetical matter, but a real occurrence.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: showing how far human arrogance and tyranny may go, as he strives against the verses of Allah, seeking to defeat Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Who are you that you should try to defeat Allah, seek to make Him helpless, and challenge Him?!
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that these defeaters who strive against the verses of Allah seeking to defeat Him will on the Day of Resurrection be in punishment, by His saying: ﴿those will be brought into the punishment﴾. Someone may say: they are brought into punishment even in this world, and "punishment" here means inner punishment, because the disbeliever, however much he is given comfort in this world, is in pain and torment in his heart, since the disbeliever is never satisfied with the world. He is in sorrow, fearing the loss of what he has, and in anxiety, seeking what he lacks, because he wants his worldly life to grow and flourish, and he also fears that it may slip away. This differs from the believer.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: affirmation of recompense and punishment, by His saying: ﴿those will be brought into the punishment﴾.

Then Allah, glorified and exalted be He, said: ﴿Say, "Indeed, my Lord extends provision to whom He wills and restricts [it for whom He wills]"﴾ [Saba' 34:39].
