Rather, what is intended is that you stand for Allah together, whether you are two, three, four, five, or ten. This is the apparent meaning.

Some of the commentators said: the meaning of "mathna" here is literally two, and they gave as reason that when people are many, their opinions become confused, disputes multiply, and the goal is lost. For if you put forward an opinion among ten people, how many opinions will come to you? Ten opinions. Between two, two opinions will come to you. They said: two is closer to limitation and closer to grasping the matter than when they are more than two.

But it may be said: this is literal, yet sometimes three or four give a sounder opinion than two alone. So the verse is taken to mean that "mathna" refers to plurality in general, whether they are two or more.

"Mathna" may be used to mean plurality in general, as in His words: ﴿Then return your gaze; do you see any flaw? Then return your gaze twice﴾ [al-Mulk 3–4]. That is, repeatedly, one glance after another, not literally two.

Like a person saying, while reciting the talbiyah for Hajj or 'Umrah: "Labbayk," meaning, "I answer You twice"? Or is the meaning answering after answering, even if many times? The latter. Yes indeed, and Allah knows best.

* * *

Allah, glorified is He, says: ﴿And when Our clear verses are recited to them﴾ to the end [Saba' 43].

* This verse contains many benefits. First: revelation is one of the signs of Allah, mighty and majestic. The way it is a sign is in several respects:

First: it defeats humankind and other than humankind, and this is evidence that it is from Allah.

Second: its rulings are just, beneficial for hearts and bodies, for individuals and communities, in every time and every place. This cannot exist in human speech. Human laws, however great, are suitable only within a limited scope, and you find in them harmful matters that may outweigh the benefits they contain. This is unlike the signs of Allah.

Third: what revelation, or the Qur'an itself, contains of true reports, in which there is nothing contrary to reality in any respect, whether those reports concern the past, the present, or the future. This is one aspect of its being a sign of Allah.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: Allah's signs, mighty and majestic, are clear, with nothing obscure in them. Accordingly, when some rulings of Allah, exalted is He, are difficult for some scholars, the source of that is not that revelation is obscure, but the shortcoming of the one who considers the revelation, or his negligence: his shortcoming, or his negligence.

His shortcoming: such that he does not have knowledge, or does not have understanding.

Or his negligence: such that he does not seek knowledge or seek understanding. Do you understand? Otherwise, Allah's signs are clear. No event can occur until the Day of Resurrection without its explanation being in the Book of Allah, exalted is He. But not everyone can discern it from the Qur'an. You find one verse recited by a group who reflect on it, one of them deriving from it many issues, and another deriving from it only one or two. This is an obvious matter. Often a question is difficult for us, and we review the books of the scholars, jurists and others, and then upon reflection on the Book and the Sunnah we find that it is near and present, either included in the generality of a word, or in an allusion, an indication, or something similar.

The explanation of the verses is either by themselves, or by way of the Sunnah. That is, the explanation of the verses in the Qur'an is either by themselves, being clear and manifest, or by way of the Sunnah, which explains the mujmal (the general, unspecified), clarifies the mushkil (the obscure), restricts the mutlaq (the unrestricted), specifies the 'amm (the general), and abrogates the muhkam (the established ruling). Is that not so?

This is a point of disagreement among the scholars, and the correct view is that it abrogates it, because all of it is from Allah.

So we have understood the meaning of "clear" (bayyinat), whether by itself or by the explanation of the Sunnah. Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿And We sent down to you the Reminder so that you may explain to people what was sent down to them﴾ [al-Nahl 44]. The Messenger ﷺ explained the Qur'an, both its wording and its meaning, whether by his words or by his deeds.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of the obstinacy (utuww) of those who denied the Messenger ﷺ. Their obstinacy is shown in that, despite these clear verses, they made this false claim: that the Messenger ﷺ wants only to turn them away from what their fathers used to worship.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: these deniers of the Messenger ﷺ had no excuse. Their denial was only aggression through false claims, for the most they could say is: "This is what our fathers were upon." But this is not a proof, since truth is what agrees with the Shari'ah, whether or not the fathers were upon it.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the harshness of these deniers in devising expressions or phrases that belittle the Prophet ﷺ, as shown by their saying: ﴿This is only a man who wants to turn you away﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: these deniers were, they and their fathers, in misguidance, since they worshipped what neither benefits nor harms them, for they worshipped trees and stones, claiming that they could benefit or harm, either by their own nature or by their intercession.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse also: they claimed that the Prophet ﷺ fabricated lies against Allah, as shown by their saying: ﴿And they said: This is nothing but a fabricated lie﴾. Yet they themselves would deny this claim, for they used to call the Messenger ﷺ "the trustworthy" (al-Amin) before revelation came to him, and they regarded him as the greatest of people in trustworthiness and truthfulness. What, then, changed him from that description, which you acknowledged, until you said that he fabricates against Allah, mighty and majestic!

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: we should not be surprised at one who disputes falsely and claims false sayings. There are people today who, when they reject something, begin to say and attribute to the one who said it what he never said. They say: "He is a liar, he is contradictory, he did such and such, he did such and such," while he is innocent of that. So these have a predecessor among those disbelievers.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: what the Prophet ﷺ brought of verses is among the most eloquent, most forceful, and most clear speech. This is shown by their saying: ﴿And those who disbelieved said of the truth when it came to them: This is nothing but obvious magic﴾. They described him as a sorcerer only because he takes hold of hearts and draws people to himself by force, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed, among eloquence there is magic."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (5146) from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar.]]

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: whoever attributes falsehood to the Messenger ﷺ regarding what Allah revealed to him is a disbeliever, as shown by His words: ﴿And those who disbelieved said of the truth when it came to them: This is nothing but obvious magic﴾.

* Among the benefits of this verse also: these people claimed that revelation was magic after it reached them and they recognized it, as shown by His words: ﴿when it came to them﴾. They recognized that it was true, to the extent that their leaders used to slip away secretly at night to the Messenger ﷺ to listen to the Qur'an, because it had seized the hearts and they came to love listening to it. But zealotry and fanaticism, may Allah protect us, prevented them from being guided by this Qur'an.

Then He, mighty and majestic, says: ﴿And We did not give them books which they could study, nor did We send to them any warner before you﴾ [Saba' 44]. We will explain it on the basis that the meaning is that Allah, glorified is He, did not give the Quraysh, indeed the Arabs altogether, books, nor did He send to them a messenger. We take the benefits on this meaning, saying:

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of the great favor of Allah, glorified is He, upon the Arabs by sending to them Muhammad ﷺ. The way it shows this is that they were an ignorant nation, with no books to study, and no warner had come to them to inform and teach them. So they were the most in need of the Messenger, and when need is intense and then something comes that removes that need, this is a greater favor.

So in the verse there is a great demonstration of the favor of Allah, mighty and majestic, upon the Arabs, in that He sent among them this noble Messenger ﷺ.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse also: the Arabs were among the most ignorant of people before the mission of the Messenger ﷺ. From where is this derived? ﴿And We did not give them books﴾ and ﴿nor did We send to them any warner before you﴾. Hence Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿Certainly did Allah confer favor upon the believers when He sent among them a messenger from themselves, reciting to them His verses, purifying them, and teaching them the Book and wisdom, although they were before in manifest error﴾ [Ali 'Imran 164].

* One of the benefits of the noble verse: there is no messenger among the Arabs except Muhammad ﷺ, and that is so. As for what some historians have mentioned, that there existed in the Jahiliyyah (the period of ignorance before Islam) messengers from among them, such as Khalid ibn Sinan, this has no basis and the report is not sound; for Allah says: ﴿O People of the Scripture, there has certainly come to you Our Messenger, making clear to you [the truth] after a gap in [the sending of] messengers﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 19]. And the Prophet ﷺ informed that there was no messenger between him and 'Isa (Jesus). Accordingly, no messenger was sent to them — i.e., to the Arabs — except Muhammad ﷺ.
* One of the benefits of the noble verse: the essence of prophethood (risalah) is warning, and likewise giving glad tidings: warning those who oppose with punishment, and giving glad tidings to those who comply with reward and recompense.
* Also in it — according to the second meaning — it is derived from the verse that those who denied the Messenger ﷺ have no basis on which they rely in their denial; for they have not read books that indicate their falsehood, and no messenger has come to them whose message would necessitate that Muhammad ﷺ is a liar. This is according to the second meaning.
Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And those before them denied, and they did not reach a tenth of what We had given them; but they denied My messengers, so how was My reproach?﴾ [Saba' 45]
* In this noble verse: a warning to the one who denies the Messenger ﷺ. Its aspect: Allah informed that He denied those before them, although they were stronger and had more wealth and children than these deniers of the Messenger ﷺ.
* One of its benefits: whoever denies the messengers, the word of punishment has become due against him; by His saying: ﴿so they denied My messengers, so how was My reproach?﴾
* One of its benefits: the nobility of the prophets, or the nobility of the messengers, upon them be prayers and peace; because Allah attributed their messengership to Himself, saying: ﴿they denied My messengers﴾. And it is known that the rank of messengership is the highest rank of humanity.
For the ranks of mankind are four: prophethood, which includes messengership; siddiqiyyah (truthfulness); martyrdom; and righteousness. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger — those are with the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed favour of the prophets, the steadfast of truth, the martyrs, and the righteous﴾ [An-Nisa' 69]. So the highest rank is prophethood, then siddiqiyyah, then martyrdom, then righteousness — in contrast to the heretics (zanadiqah) who say that the saints (awliya') are better than the prophets, and the prophets are better than the messengers. One of them says:
"The station of prophethood is in a barzakh (isthmus)
above the messenger and below the saint"
They claim — may Allah disfigure them — that the saints are better than the messengers and prophets. Indeed, it is so in their view, since their saints are the taghut (false objects of worship), and the taghut dictates to them that it is better than the messengers and prophets.
* One of the benefits of the noble verse: the demonstration of the wisdom of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in that He made the punishment of the same kind as the deed. Since the deed of these people was grave — namely, denying the messengers of Allah, glorified and exalted is He — their recompense was grave and astonishing: ﴿so how was My reproach?﴾ [Saba' 45], meaning: how great it was and how severe.
* One of the benefits of the noble verse: that denial (inkar) may be by action as it may be by speech. Its aspect: Allah's denunciation of them was not by speech only, but by action and the imposition of punishment; so this is denunciation by action.
This also exists in our own affairs: when your child disobeys you in some matter, sometimes you rebuke him, saying: "Why do you do this? Did I not command you to leave it?" And sometimes, when you come and find he has done it, you strike him. This denunciation — by what is it? It is by action.
So the denunciation of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is by speech and by action; the punishment of the criminals is denunciation by what? By action. And in this verse and others that attribute the action to the doer, in refutation of whom? As in ﴿so they denied My messengers﴾ and ﴿And those before them denied﴾ and what is similar to that — a refutation of whom?
* Students: The Qadariyyah.
* The Shaykh: No, it is not the Qadariyyah. It is a refutation of the Jabriyyah, who say that the act is the act of the servant, compelled upon him, with no choice in it for him.
* One of the benefits of the noble verse: the use of qiyas al-awla (analogy from the stronger). From where is it derived? ﴿And those before them denied, and they did not reach a tenth of what We had given them; but they denied My messengers, so how was My reproach?﴾ That is: if Allah seized those strong, mighty ones, who had more wealth and children, for their crime, then those who are beneath them are more deserving of it.
There is no doubt that qiyas is a sound proof whose validity is established by the Book, the Sunnah and reason; but qiyas is of two kinds: sound and corrupt.
The corrupt: the Book, the Sunnah and reason indicate that it is not to be relied upon.
The sound: the Book, the Sunnah and reason indicate that it is to be relied upon.
An example of the corrupt: the statement of Iblis, using qiyas al-awla when Allah commanded him to prostrate to Adam: he said: ﴿I am better than him; You created me from fire and You created him from clay﴾ [Al-A'raf 12]. How would the superior be a servant to one beneath him?
And an example of qiyas al-mithliyyah (analogy of equivalence) is their saying: ﴿Trade is only like usury﴾ [Al-Baqarah 275]. This is corrupt qiyas, because it equates what Allah has forbidden with what Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has permitted.
The point is that qiyas has been established as valid by the Book, the Sunnah and reason, and whoever denies it has denied what the Book and the Sunnah indicate. Yes, what is rejected is the corrupt qiyas, fine.
Can we derive from this verse that denying the messengers is denying Allah? Yes, that is the apparent meaning; for He said in the first part: ﴿And those before them denied﴾ without mentioning the one denied.
Then He said: ﴿so they denied My messengers﴾, which indicates that denying the messengers is denying Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. And upon reflection this is so; for when a messenger comes to you and says that he is a messenger of Allah, and Allah has supported him with signs, and then you deny him, you have denied Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; for the signs that Allah gives the messenger are nothing but proofs indicating his truthfulness. So it is as if the denier is saying that these signs are false, since he denies the messenger whom He has supported.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 34, verse 42–45 (part 1 of 3):

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So on that Day none of you will have power to benefit or harm one another﴾ [Saba' 42].

In it there is something we wish to draw attention to, namely His saying: ﴿Were these the ones you used to worship?﴾ [Saba' 40] (with both hamzas pronounced as hamzas, and the first changed to a yā'). Some of the commentators (muhashshin) have noted that the author (al-mu'allif) erred in this, and that the changing of the hamza to yā' applies only to the second, not the first. Be attentive to this. That is, there is no reading in which the first is changed to yā'; the changing to yā' is only in the second and not the first. So this is an error on the part of the author, may Allah have mercy on him, or a slip of the pen.

* Student: How is it pronounced if the second is a yā'?
* The Shaykh: ﴿ahaؤlaa'i ayyaakum﴾ [pronounced as written].
* The Student: So it is assimilated (idghām) into the second?
* The Shaykh: No, it is not assimilated, because the second is vowelled, so there is no need... ﴿ahaؤlaa'i ayyaakum﴾.

Also, the author, may Allah have mercy on him, says: ﴿And We will say to those who did wrong, "Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny."﴾ [Saba' 42].

His saying: ﴿And We will say﴾ is conjoined to His saying: ﴿will have power﴾, meaning: "And on that Day We will say: to those who did wrong..." Injustice (ẓulm) linguistically means deficiency; this is the original meaning. From it is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Each of the two gardens brought forth its produce and did not fall short therein at all﴾ [al-Kahf 33], i.e., it did not diminish.

As for the technical or legal meaning: it is the depriving of those entitled to their right, either by procrastinating in what is obligatory, or by violating what is forbidden. Depriving those entitled of their right by procrastinating in what is obligatory is like the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The procrastination of the wealthy is injustice" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2287) and Muslim (1564/33) from Abu Hurayrah].

Or by transgressing against their right, like the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿The blame is only upon those who wrong people and transgress upon the earth without right﴾ [al-Shura 42].

So, the original meaning of injustice is deficiency. What is your evidence?

* Students: ﴿Each of the two gardens brought forth its produce and did not fall short therein at all﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿and did not fall short therein at all﴾.

As for the legal meaning, it is the depriving of those entitled of their right, either by violating a prohibition concerning their right or by procrastinating in an obligation.

His saying: ﴿to those who did wrong﴾ — the author explained it as (disbelieved). Is this an explanation of the meaning or of the intended referent? It is of the intended referent, because injustice in meaning is more general than disbelief.

But the author says: the intended meaning of injustice here is the injustice of disbelief, like the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And the disbelievers are the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah 254], His saying: ﴿Indeed, association [with Allah] is a great injustice﴾ [Luqman 13], and His saying: ﴿Those who believed and did not mix their belief with injustice﴾ [al-An'am 82].

So injustice may be intended to mean disbelief, and it seems the author, may Allah have mercy on him, restricted injustice here to disbelief by the context: ﴿And We will say to those who did wrong, "Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny."﴾ This shows that the intended injustice here is the injustice of disbelief, because whoever denies the Fire is a disbeliever, due to his denial of the report of Allah and His Messenger.

﴿Taste the punishment of the Fire﴾: ﴿Taste﴾ is an imperative verb but it is meant as humiliation. That is, they are told in humiliation: "Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny," meaning the Fire will reach you until you taste it as you taste food.

His saying: ﴿the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny﴾ — how did they deny the Fire? Because they denied the resurrection, and the Fire is only after the resurrection, and they denied that. It follows, a fortiori, that they denied what occurs in the grave of punishment. So they denied completely, and they say: when the soul leaves the body it will never return to it. Here He said: ﴿which you used to deny﴾, while in Surah As-Sajdah He said: ﴿Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny﴾ [al-Sajdah 20]. Accordingly, in the two verses, the description of denial is once with respect to the Fire and once with respect to its punishment. So sometimes they deny the Fire itself, saying there is no Fire, no Hereafter, nothing at all, and sometimes they deny the punishment by the Fire, saying: "How can we be punished by the Fire? How can we remain for ages while in the Fire? When a person enters the Fire he is burnt and finished." So they deny the punishment, and sometimes they deny the Fire itself.

His saying: ﴿which you used to deny﴾ — the prepositional phrase here is connected to ﴿deny﴾, but it was placed first for restriction or for the rhyme (fawāṣil)? Yes, for the rhyme, undoubtedly; this is one aspect, and for restriction. But if we say it is for restriction, a problem arises: they denied the Fire and other things. It is said: since the punishment was by the Fire, they were reminded of their denial of it specifically, because they were punished by it. It is as if they were told: "You are punished by something you used to deny, and otherwise they have another denial."

(﴿And when Our verses are recited to them, clear [in evidence]﴾ — the Quran — ﴿clear﴾: plain, in the tongue of our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) — ﴿they say﴾).

In this conditional sentence, the protasis is ﴿when﴾ [idhā], the verb of the condition is ﴿are recited﴾, and its response is ﴿they say, "This is not but a man..."﴾.

His saying: ﴿This is not but a man﴾ — this ﴿mā﴾ is the negative particle, and here it did not operate. Why? Because of the nullification of the negation. Ibn Malik said in his Alfiyya:

The operation of laysa is given to mā, [only] as long as in [its] negation... [remains]

So when the negation is nullified, there is no operation. And Allah knows best.

* * *

﴿For those who did wrong﴾ [Saba' 42] (...).
﴿So on that Day none of you will have power to benefit or harm one another, and We will say﴾ [Saba' 42] to you.

He said: ﴿And We will say to those who did wrong﴾, and the explicit mention in place of the pronoun, as we have mentioned, has a constant and continuous benefit, which is to draw attention.

It also has a specific benefit in each context according to what it is. Here it is intended for generality, meaning: to those who did wrong, from among these people and others.

It also indicates the cause of the ruling, which is His saying: ﴿And We will say to those who did wrong, "Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny."﴾ What remains? The generality and the indication of the cause of the ruling, which is injustice; for if He had only said "We will say to them," we would not have learned that the reason for Allah's saying to them and rebuking them is injustice.

He said: ﴿And when Our verses are recited to them, clear [in evidence]﴾. We begin with the grammatical analysis first:

His saying: ﴿Our verses, clear﴾ — ﴿clear﴾ is a ḥāl (circumstantial qualifier) of ﴿Our verses﴾, because it is a qualifier after a definite noun; and a qualifier after a definite noun, when it is indefinite or a clause, is a ḥāl. Likewise, qualifiers after definite nouns that are definite are a na't (adjective). A ḥāl and a na't are both descriptions, but if it agrees with its antecedent in definiteness and indefiniteness, it is a na't; otherwise, if the antecedent is definite and the second is indefinite or a clause, it is a ḥāl.

His saying: ﴿They say, "This is not..."﴾ — this is the response of the condition, to the end.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿When Our verses are recited to them, clear﴾, i.e., when Our verses are read to them, and the reader is not specified, so it includes the reader being the Prophet (ﷺ) or others. When the verses of Allah are recited to them, ﴿clear﴾, meaning manifest. What is their manifestness here? Is it that they are plainly the speech of Allah, since they are unable to match them; or that they are clear in what they indicate of lofty meanings that no human could produce; or both? It includes both. They are clear in themselves, plainly not the speech of humans, and clear in their subject matter and in what they indicate, that they are not of human composition, because they do not contradict one another, and do not refute one another. This indicates they are from Allah. If these verses were obscure, they would have some excuse in rejecting them, but they are clear verses, and they have no excuse for rejecting them. Yet, despite this, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿They say, "This is not but a man who wants to turn you away from what your fathers used to worship."﴾ The author, in explaining it, says: (clear in the tongue of our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ)).

﴿They say, "This is not but a man who wants to turn you away from what your fathers used to worship."﴾ ﴿This﴾ refers to the one who brought them and claimed they were from Allah: ﴿not but a man who wants to turn you away﴾. And consider how this sentence carries the contempt and denial that is well known.

Their saying ﴿This﴾ is in the form of the present, though he was absent, for contempt.

Their saying ﴿not but a man﴾ is for denial, because they used the indefinite form, as if they did not know him, as if he were a foreign man among them. ﴿They say, "This is not but a man"﴾ — they did not say, "That man is only a man," but ﴿This is not but a man﴾, out of contempt and denial.

﴿who wants to turn you away﴾ means: he does not want to guide you to the right path, but ﴿wants to turn you away﴾, to divert and prevent you ﴿from what your fathers used to worship﴾. And what did their fathers worship? Idols, of trees, stones and others. This is the aim of this man who brought these verses recited to them; his aim is neither righteousness nor reform. Thus they rejected the truth with this false claim.

His saying ﴿from what your fathers used to worship﴾, and not "from what you used to worship," is to stir zeal in their souls, because a person finds it hard to abandon what his fathers were upon, especially such ignorant people. Had they said "from what you used to worship," it could be said that they worshipped without foundation. But when He said ﴿from what your fathers used to worship﴾, it is as if this worship of these idols were a settled matter upon which the fathers stood, and you should not abandon the creed of your fathers. This is why they say, as Allah related about them in another verse: ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers upon a religion, and indeed we are following in their footsteps, guided﴾ [al-Zukhruf 22], or ﴿following their example﴾ [al-Zukhruf 23], two verses.

﴿from what your fathers used to worship﴾ — of idols; and "fathers" here means what includes the father of the loins (the immediate father) and the forefathers above him, namely the grandfathers and higher ancestors.

His saying ﴿your fathers﴾ — do their mothers count likewise? But a person is moved by zeal for his father more than for his mother, because it is known that the father is a man, and a man is more rational than a woman. So if your fathers worshipped these idols and insisted on worshipping them, and they were the rational ones, then you should not follow this man who wanted to turn you away from what your fathers worshipped.

(And ﴿they said﴾ in the Quran: ﴿This is not but a fabrication, a lie, ﴿invented﴾ against Allah.) I seek refuge in Allah! They slandered the Messenger and they slandered the Quran. Against the Messenger they slandered by what? By his evil intention, and that he does not intend reform, but wants to turn you away from what your fathers worshipped. And they slandered the revelation that this Messenger brought, saying: ﴿This is not but a fabrication, invented﴾. You know that this form is a form of restriction, so by their claim there is nothing true in the Quran; the whole Quran, in totality and in detail, is fabricated invention.

﴿Fabrication﴾ means lie: it is itself a lie, and against whom? Invented against Allah. Because there is an absolute lie that a person utters without attributing it to anyone, and here is a lie that a person fabricates against another. So they say the Quran is a lie and that it is fabricated against Allah. There is no doubt that this claim is false. The Quran, as Allah described it: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice﴾ [al-An'am 115]. Likewise, the Quran is from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as proven by the fact that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, challenged these people to produce its like, and they did not. So this is evidence that it is from Allah, and all its reports are true and correct, contrary to what these people slandered.

﴿And they said, "This is not but a fabrication, invented."﴾ They slandered the Messenger, and slandered what was brought by him, and slandering both is slandering Allah, Mighty and Majestic. How? Because Allah's enabling this Messenger, His support of him, His sending down verses upon him, while he is a liar — is it wisdom or foolishness? Foolishness. And Allah, Mighty and Majestic, supports His Messenger with what He sends down to him and testifies that he is right, and the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, calls people openly and secretly. So if he were lying against Allah, Mighty and Majestic, while Allah supported and enabled him, Allah's enabling him would be in the utmost foolishness, and this is a slander against Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿And those who disbelieved said of the truth when it came to them, "Indeed, [what] this is but evident magic."﴾ This is also a third false claim, but He used the explicit mention in place of the pronoun; He did not say "and they said," but ﴿And those who disbelieved said﴾, to include these and others, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Likewise, no messenger came to those before them but they said, "A magician or a madman."﴾ [al-Dhariyat 52]. So His saying ﴿And those who disbelieved said﴾ includes these and others, and indicates that those who said this statement are disbelievers, since He described them with disbelief, attributing this statement to them, and that would be the cause of their disbelief.

The author said regarding ﴿in﴾ [in], explaining it as (mā) — how is ﴿in﴾ (mā)? That is, ﴿in﴾ is negative.

Now, can ﴿in﴾ occur as a negative? Is it a condition for it to be negative that ﴿illā﴾ come after it?

The answer: No. But when ﴿illā﴾ comes after it, it is negative. Whenever ﴿illā﴾ comes after ﴿in﴾, ﴿in﴾ is negative. We do not say it is negative only when ﴿illā﴾ follows it, because it may come negative without ﴿illā﴾ following it, as in the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿You have no authority for this﴾ [Yunus 68], i.e., you have no authority for this; and yet that sentence has no ﴿illā﴾.

Summary: when ﴿illā﴾ comes after ﴿in﴾, ﴿in﴾ is negative, and it is not necessary that ﴿illā﴾ follow it, because it may be negative without ﴿illā﴾.

We may digress to mention the meanings of ﴿in﴾: it comes negative as here.

It comes conditional, like His saying: ﴿Say, "Whether you conceal what is within your breasts or reveal it, Allah will know it."﴾ [Ali 'Imran 29].

It comes superfluous (zā'idah), like the saying of the poet:

"Banū Ghudāna, mā in antum dhahabun / wa lā ṣarīfun wa lākin antumu l-kha<u>z</u>afu"

It comes as the light form of the heavy (mukhaffafah min al-thaqīlah), like:

"... wa in Mālikun kānat kirāmu l-ma'ādini"

This one is the light form of the heavy.

So it is used in the Arabic language in four ways.

Now, ﴿in hādhā illā siḥrun mubīn﴾ [Saba' 43] (clear). ﴿Magic﴾ (siḥr): linguistically, it is everything hidden. It was called siḥr because it corresponds to al-saḥar, which is the last part of the night, since in the last part of the night things occur hidden, because people are concealed in their houses. So siḥr linguistically is a hidden thing whose matter and cause are concealed. This is why, when clocks first appeared, it was said they were siḥr, and when strange things come upon people that break habit, they say: "This is magic."

So they say that what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought is magic: in their view Moses' staff was magic, and Jesus' raising of the dead by Allah's permission was magic, and this speech that Muhammad (ﷺ) brought is magic — "indeed, there is magic in eloquence" — and they said: this is eloquent speech that bewitches people's minds.

His saying ﴿mubīn﴾ is of the category of deception, meaning that it is evident magic that should not be disputed because of its clarity and manifestness. This is like when you emphasize a thing, saying: "This is a clear, evident matter," even if it is not clearly evident. Indeed, what the Messengers brought of signs is not evidently magic; rather, what is evident is that it is truth and genuine signs. But the deniers, may Allah protect us, dispute the truth.

His saying ﴿mubīn﴾ — the author said it means (clear), because abāna is used intransitively and transitively: you say abāna al-fajr meaning the dawn became manifest, and you say bāna al-fajr.

So here the word ﴿mubīn﴾ means clear (bayyin). This is the closer meaning. As for mubīn meaning abāna, i.e., to make clear and manifest, that is in such a saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿It is only a reminder and a clear Quran﴾ [Ya Sin 69], because the Quran makes the truth clear; so mubīn there is from the transitive abāna, while mubīn here is from the intransitive abāna.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We did not give them any books which they study, nor did We send to them before you any warner﴾ [Saba' 44] (so from where did they deny you).

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 34, verses 42–45 (part 2 of 3)**

The Almighty said: ﴿And We did not give them books which they could study, nor did We send to them any warner before you.﴾ The commentators (mufassirun) differed over its meaning. Some of them said: ﴿And We did not give them books which they could study, nor did We send to them any warner before you﴾ contradicts what you have said. For if they have no knowledge from books they study, and no knowledge from a warner who came to them, then how can they oppose what you are upon? How, then, do they deny you? Accordingly, the meaning of this verse is that their denial of you comes from what?

* A student: From knowledge.
* The Shaykh: No.
* The students: From ignorance.
* The Shaykh: From ignorance, arising from ignorance. For He says, ﴿We did not give them books﴾. He does not say, "We gave them." Pay attention.

﴿We did not give them books which they could study﴾ indicates that what they said about you is true.

﴿Nor did We send to them any warner before you﴾ contradicts what you brought, so that they could say: You are what? A liar and a sorcerer.

So the meaning of the verse is that these people who denied you did not base their denial on what? On knowledge. Not from books, nor from revelation. Not from books which they study and understand, and so know that what you brought contradicts them. Nor from a warner who warned them and cautioned them against what you brought, saying that a lying, fabricating impostor would come, so do not obey him.

Now, if a prophet came to us and said that he is a prophet from Allah, would we deny him?

* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Why? Because we have been warned about these people, as the Prophet ﷺ informed us. But when the Prophet ﷺ came, did those who denied him receive a warning about him and take heed of it? No. Is there any book these people studied that shows the Messenger ﷺ to be upon falsehood? No. This is one aspect, and it is the one the author followed. That is why he said: (So from where did they deny you?)

The second view: Allah, exalted is He, sent Muhammad ﷺ among a people who were unlettered (ummiyyun), who could not read, and to whom no prophet had been sent before. As Allah, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿It is He who sent among the unlettered a messenger from among themselves, reciting to them His verses﴾ [al-Jumu'ah 2]. And Allah, glorified is He, says: ﴿That you may warn a people to whom no warner had come before you﴾ [al-Qasas 46]. That is, it would have been most fitting for these people to rejoice at your message and to accept what you brought. Why? Because they had no books to study, as the Jews and Christians had, and no prophet had been sent to them before you. So they were in the greatest need of you. Whoever is in need of something rejoices in it more, and is more ready to believe its report. Accordingly, the meaning of this sentence is a rebuke of these people for denying the Prophet ﷺ, and that it would have been most fitting for them to rejoice in this and to believe: since they had no books to study, and had no ﴿trace of knowledge﴾, and no warner had come to them before you, they were in the greatest need of what? Of your confirmation and acceptance of what you brought. Thus this verse contains a rebuke of these people for denying the Prophet ﷺ. Which of the two is more preferable? ﴿And We did not give them books which they could study, nor did We send to them any warner before you.﴾ Which of the two is preferable?

* Students: The first view.
* The Shaykh: Our brother says the second view. Can the verse bear two meanings?
* A student: It can bear them.
* The Shaykh: Let us examine the situation of these people. If it applies to their situation under both aspects, we take it in both senses and say: these people did not study books which indicate the falsehood of Muhammad ﷺ (...).

Nor did anyone warn them about him. Likewise, they did not have knowledge of the earlier books, and no messenger had been sent to them.

So their situation admits of both aspects. That is, applying the verse to both aspects does not conflict with the situation of these people who denied the Messenger ﷺ. Both aspects apply to them. When both aspects apply to them, there is no obstacle to saying that the verse is intended to convey both this and that, because the situation of those who denied the Messenger ﷺ admits of both together.

Allah, exalted is He, says: (﴿And those before them denied, and they have not attained one-tenth of what We gave them﴾), that is, these people (﴿one-tenth of what We gave them﴾), meaning its tenth (in strength, long life, and abundance of wealth). This contains consolation for the Messenger ﷺ and a threat to the deniers. So it has two meanings: consolation and threat.

﴿Those before them denied﴾ like whom? Like 'Ad, Thamud, Pharaoh, the people of the thicket (al-Aykah), and many others. These earlier deniers were far stronger than these people and had more wealth and children. Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿Have they not traveled through the earth and seen what was the end of those before them? They were more numerous than these and greater in strength﴾ [Ghafir 82]. And: ﴿and more in wealth and children﴾ [al-Tawbah 69]. So these verses indicate that those who denied the earlier messengers were greater than those who denied the Messenger ﷺ in physical strength, abundance of wealth, and number of sons. And did that avail them anything? No, it availed them nothing.

That is why Allah, exalted is He, said: (﴿So they denied My messengers﴾, to them, ﴿then how was My rejection?﴾, My disapproval through punishment and destruction). That is, these earlier people denied the messengers of Allah, so what happened? There came upon them the disapproval of Allah, exalted is He, through punishment and destruction. Allah did not approve of their denial; rather He disapproved of them. Was that disapproval by deed or by word? By deed: He destroyed and annihilated them. Accordingly, the interrogative in His words ﴿then how was My rejection?﴾ is for magnification and emphasis, meaning: how great was My disapproval of them, since it was a disapproval that led them to destruction.

As for the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of ﴿then how was My rejection?﴾, it is adopted by our brother (...).

That is why the author said: (That is, it falls in their place).

Then Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿Say: I only admonish you with one thing﴾ [Saba' 46]. Note the fairness, the fairness of Allah, mighty and majestic, in addressing creation.

﴿Say﴾, that is, O Muhammad, directing the address to these deniers.

﴿I only admonish you with one thing﴾. This sentence contains restriction (hasr), and its implied meaning is: I do not admonish you except with one thing. That is, I do not call you as an admonisher and sincere advisor except to this one thing alone.

So ﴿admonish﴾ here implies: I advise you. That is, I call you as a sincere advisor and admonisher to this one trait.

﴿With one thing: that you stand﴾. He said: it is that you stand. So ﴿that you stand﴾ is in the genitive position as an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan) to ﴿one thing﴾. That is, He explained this one thing by His words: ﴿that you stand for Allah﴾, and so on to the end.

And ﴿that you stand﴾ here means that you hold firm to something, not standing in the sense of the opposite of sitting. It is like His words: ﴿and that you stand for orphans with justice﴾ [al-Nisa' 127]. It does not mean that you stand up for orphans, as in one person standing. Likewise ﴿that you stand for Allah﴾ does not mean that you stand up in the sense of rising, but that you be steadfast and reflect on the matter.

As for His words ﴿that you stand for Allah﴾, the author said: (that is, for His sake). So the lam here is for sincerity (ikhlas), meaning: that you stand sincerely for Allah, not blindly following your fathers nor fanatically defending your opinions. Purify your intentions of everything except Allah. That you stand for Allah alone, not for me. Not out of regard for me, nor for your fathers, nor for your partisan zeal, but for Allah.

﴿Two by two (mathna)﴾. The author said: (two by two). Is the real meaning of duality intended? That is, that they stand in pairs of two? Or is the mere meaning of more than one intended, that it is "mathna" but the real meaning of two is not intended? Rather, what is intended is that you stand for Allah together, whether you are two, three, four, five, or ten. This is the apparent meaning.

Some of the commentators said: the meaning of "mathna" here is literally two, and they gave as reason that when people are many, their opinions become confused, disputes multiply, and the goal is lost. For if you put forward an opinion among ten people, how many opinions will come to you? Ten opinions. Between two, two opinions will come to you. They said: two is closer to limitation and closer to grasping the matter than when they are more than two.

But it may be said: this is literal, yet sometimes three or four give a sounder opinion than two alone. So the verse is taken to mean that "mathna" refers to plurality in general, whether they are two or more.

"Mathna" may be used to mean plurality in general, as in His words: ﴿Then return your gaze; do you see any flaw? Then return your gaze twice﴾ [al-Mulk 3–4]. That is, repeatedly, one glance after another, not literally two.

Like a person saying, while reciting the talbiyah for Hajj or 'Umrah: "Labbayk," meaning, "I answer You twice"? Or is the meaning answering after answering, even if many times? The latter. Yes indeed, and Allah knows best.

* * *

Allah, glorified is He, says: ﴿And when Our clear verses are recited to them﴾ to the end [Saba' 43].

* This verse contains many benefits. First: revelation is one of the signs of Allah, mighty and majestic. The way it is a sign is in several respects:

First: it defeats humankind and other than humankind, and this is evidence that it is from Allah.

Second: its rulings are just, beneficial for hearts and bodies, for individuals and communities, in every time and every place. This cannot exist in human speech. Human laws, however great, are suitable only within a limited scope, and you find in them harmful matters that may outweigh the benefits they contain. This is unlike the signs of Allah.

Third: what revelation, or the Qur'an itself, contains of true reports, in which there is nothing contrary to reality in any respect, whether those reports concern the past, the present, or the future. This is one aspect of its being a sign of Allah.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: Allah's signs, mighty and majestic, are clear, with nothing obscure in them. Accordingly, when some rulings of Allah, exalted is He, are difficult for some scholars, the source of that is not that revelation is obscure, but the shortcoming of the one who considers the revelation, or his negligence: his shortcoming, or his negligence.

His shortcoming: such that he does not have knowledge, or does not have understanding.

Or his negligence: such that he does not seek knowledge or seek understanding. Do you understand? Otherwise, Allah's signs are clear. No event can occur until the Day of Resurrection without its explanation being in the Book of Allah, exalted is He. But not everyone can discern it from the Qur'an. You find one verse recited by a group who reflect on it, one of them deriving from it many issues, and another deriving from it only one or two. This is an obvious matter. Often a question is difficult for us, and we review the books of the scholars, jurists and others, and then upon reflection on the Book and the Sunnah we find that it is near and present, either included in the generality of a word, or in an allusion, an indication, or something similar.

The explanation of the verses is either by themselves, or by way of the Sunnah. That is, the explanation of the verses in the Qur'an is either by themselves, being clear and manifest, or by way of the Sunnah, which explains the mujmal (the general, unspecified), clarifies the mushkil (the obscure), restricts the mutlaq (the unrestricted), specifies the 'amm (the general), and abrogates the muhkam (the established ruling). Is that not so?

This is a point of disagreement among the scholars, and the correct view is that it abrogates it, because all of it is from Allah.

So we have understood the meaning of "clear" (bayyinat), whether by itself or by the explanation of the Sunnah. Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿And We sent down to you the Reminder so that you may explain to people what was sent down to them﴾ [al-Nahl 44]. The Messenger ﷺ explained the Qur'an, both its wording and its meaning, whether by his words or by his deeds.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of the obstinacy (utuww) of those who denied the Messenger ﷺ. Their obstinacy is shown in that, despite these clear verses, they made this false claim: that the Messenger ﷺ wants only to turn them away from what their fathers used to worship.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: these deniers of the Messenger ﷺ had no excuse. Their denial was only aggression through false claims, for the most they could say is: "This is what our fathers were upon." But this is not a proof, since truth is what agrees with the Shari'ah, whether or not the fathers were upon it.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the harshness of these deniers in devising expressions or phrases that belittle the Prophet ﷺ, as shown by their saying: ﴿This is only a man who wants to turn you away﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: these deniers were, they and their fathers, in misguidance, since they worshipped what neither benefits nor harms them, for they worshipped trees and stones, claiming that they could benefit or harm, either by their own nature or by their intercession.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse also: they claimed that the Prophet ﷺ fabricated lies against Allah, as shown by their saying: ﴿And they said: This is nothing but a fabricated lie﴾. Yet they themselves would deny this claim, for they used to call the Messenger ﷺ "the trustworthy" (al-Amin) before revelation came to him, and they regarded him as the greatest of people in trustworthiness and truthfulness. What, then, changed him from that description, which you acknowledged, until you said that he fabricates against Allah, mighty and majestic!

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: we should not be surprised at one who disputes falsely and claims false sayings. There are people today who, when they reject something, begin to say and attribute to the one who said it what he never said. They say: "He is a liar, he is contradictory, he did such and such, he did such and such," while he is innocent of that. So these have a predecessor among those disbelievers.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: what the Prophet ﷺ brought of verses is among the most eloquent, most forceful, and most clear speech. This is shown by their saying: ﴿And those who disbelieved said of the truth when it came to them: This is nothing but obvious magic﴾. They described him as a sorcerer only because he takes hold of hearts and draws people to himself by force, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed, among eloquence there is magic."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (5146) from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar.]]

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: whoever attributes falsehood to the Messenger ﷺ regarding what Allah revealed to him is a disbeliever, as shown by His words: ﴿And those who disbelieved said of the truth when it came to them: This is nothing but obvious magic﴾.

* Among the benefits of this verse also: these people claimed that revelation was magic after it reached them and they recognized it, as shown by His words: ﴿when it came to them﴾. They recognized that it was true, to the extent that their leaders used to slip away secretly at night to the Messenger ﷺ to listen to the Qur'an, because it had seized the hearts and they came to love listening to it. But zealotry and fanaticism, may Allah protect us, prevented them from being guided by this Qur'an.

Then He, mighty and majestic, says: ﴿And We did not give them books which they could study, nor did We send to them any warner before you﴾ [Saba' 44]. We will explain it on the basis that the meaning is that Allah, glorified is He, did not give the Quraysh, indeed the Arabs altogether, books, nor did He send to them a messenger. We take the benefits on this meaning, saying:

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of the great favor of Allah, glorified is He, upon the Arabs by sending to them Muhammad ﷺ. The way it shows this is that they were an ignorant nation, with no books to study, and no warner had come to them to inform and teach them. So they were the most in need of the Messenger, and when need is intense and then something comes that removes that need, this is a greater favor.

So in the verse there is a great demonstration of the favor of Allah, mighty and majestic, upon the Arabs, in that He sent among them this noble Messenger ﷺ.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse also: the Arabs were among the most ignorant of people before the mission of the Messenger ﷺ. From where is this derived? ﴿And We did not give them books﴾ and ﴿nor did We send to them any warner before you﴾. Hence Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿Certainly did Allah confer favor upon the believers when He sent among them a messenger from themselves, reciting to them His verses, purifying them, and teaching them the Book and wisdom, although they were before in manifest error﴾ [Ali 'Imran 164].

* One of the benefits of the noble verse: there is no messenger among the Arabs except Muhammad ﷺ, and that is so. As for what some historians have mentioned, that there existed in the Jahiliyyah (the period of ignorance before Islam) messengers from among them, such as Khalid ibn Sinan, this has no basis and the report is not sound; for Allah says: ﴿O People of the Scripture, there has certainly come to you Our Messenger, making clear to you [the truth] after a gap in [the sending of] messengers﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 19]. And the Prophet ﷺ informed that there was no messenger between him and 'Isa (Jesus). Accordingly, no messenger was sent to them — i.e., to the Arabs — except Muhammad ﷺ.
* One of the benefits of the noble verse: the essence of prophethood (risalah) is warning, and likewise giving glad tidings: warning those who oppose with punishment, and giving glad tidings to those who comply with reward and recompense.
* Also in it — according to the second meaning — it is derived from the verse that those who denied the Messenger ﷺ have no basis on which they rely in their denial; for they have not read books that indicate their falsehood, and no messenger has come to them whose message would necessitate that Muhammad ﷺ is a liar. This is according to the second meaning.
Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And those before them denied, and they did not reach a tenth of what We had given them; but they denied My messengers, so how was My reproach?﴾ [Saba' 45]
* In this noble verse: a warning to the one who denies the Messenger ﷺ. Its aspect: Allah informed that He denied those before them, although they were stronger and had more wealth and children than these deniers of the Messenger ﷺ.
* One of its benefits: whoever denies the messengers, the word of punishment has become due against him; by His saying: ﴿so they denied My messengers, so how was My reproach?﴾
* One of its benefits: the nobility of the prophets, or the nobility of the messengers, upon them be prayers and peace; because Allah attributed their messengership to Himself, saying: ﴿they denied My messengers﴾. And it is known that the rank of messengership is the highest rank of humanity.
For the ranks of mankind are four: prophethood, which includes messengership; siddiqiyyah (truthfulness); martyrdom; and righteousness. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger — those are with the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed favour of the prophets, the steadfast of truth, the martyrs, and the righteous﴾ [An-Nisa' 69]. So the highest rank is prophethood, then siddiqiyyah, then martyrdom, then righteousness — in contrast to the heretics (zanadiqah) who say that the saints (awliya') are better than the prophets, and the prophets are better than the messengers. One of them says:
"The station of prophethood is in a barzakh (isthmus)
above the messenger and below the saint"
They claim — may Allah disfigure them — that the saints are better than the messengers and prophets. Indeed, it is so in their view, since their saints are the taghut (false objects of worship), and the taghut dictates to them that it is better than the messengers and prophets.
* One of the benefits of the noble verse: the demonstration of the wisdom of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in that He made the punishment of the same kind as the deed. Since the deed of these people was grave — namely, denying the messengers of Allah, glorified and exalted is He — their recompense was grave and astonishing: ﴿so how was My reproach?﴾ [Saba' 45], meaning: how great it was and how severe.
* One of the benefits of the noble verse: that denial (inkar) may be by action as it may be by speech. Its aspect: Allah's denunciation of them was not by speech only, but by action and the imposition of punishment; so this is denunciation by action.
This also exists in our own affairs: when your child disobeys you in some matter, sometimes you rebuke him, saying: "Why do you do this? Did I not command you to leave it?" And sometimes, when you come and find he has done it, you strike him. This denunciation — by what is it? It is by action.
So the denunciation of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is by speech and by action; the punishment of the criminals is denunciation by what? By action. And in this verse and others that attribute the action to the doer, in refutation of whom? As in ﴿so they denied My messengers﴾ and ﴿And those before them denied﴾ and what is similar to that — a refutation of whom?
* Students: The Qadariyyah.
* The Shaykh: No, it is not the Qadariyyah. It is a refutation of the Jabriyyah, who say that the act is the act of the servant, compelled upon him, with no choice in it for him.
* One of the benefits of the noble verse: the use of qiyas al-awla (analogy from the stronger). From where is it derived? ﴿And those before them denied, and they did not reach a tenth of what We had given them; but they denied My messengers, so how was My reproach?﴾ That is: if Allah seized those strong, mighty ones, who had more wealth and children, for their crime, then those who are beneath them are more deserving of it.
There is no doubt that qiyas is a sound proof whose validity is established by the Book, the Sunnah and reason; but qiyas is of two kinds: sound and corrupt.
The corrupt: the Book, the Sunnah and reason indicate that it is not to be relied upon.
The sound: the Book, the Sunnah and reason indicate that it is to be relied upon.
An example of the corrupt: the statement of Iblis, using qiyas al-awla when Allah commanded him to prostrate to Adam: he said: ﴿I am better than him; You created me from fire and You created him from clay﴾ [Al-A'raf 12]. How would the superior be a servant to one beneath him?
And an example of qiyas al-mithliyyah (analogy of equivalence) is their saying: ﴿Trade is only like usury﴾ [Al-Baqarah 275]. This is corrupt qiyas, because it equates what Allah has forbidden with what Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has permitted.
The point is that qiyas has been established as valid by the Book, the Sunnah and reason, and whoever denies it has denied what the Book and the Sunnah indicate. Yes, what is rejected is the corrupt qiyas, fine.
Can we derive from this verse that denying the messengers is denying Allah? Yes, that is the apparent meaning; for He said in the first part: ﴿And those before them denied﴾ without mentioning the one denied.
Then He said: ﴿so they denied My messengers﴾, which indicates that denying the messengers is denying Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. And upon reflection this is so; for when a messenger comes to you and says that he is a messenger of Allah, and Allah has supported him with signs, and then you deny him, you have denied Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; for the signs that Allah gives the messenger are nothing but proofs indicating his truthfulness. So it is as if the denier is saying that these signs are false, since he denies the messenger whom He has supported.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 34, verse 42–45 (part 1 of 3):

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So on that Day none of you will have power to benefit or harm one another﴾ [Saba' 42].

In it there is something we wish to draw attention to, namely His saying: ﴿Were these the ones you used to worship?﴾ [Saba' 40] (with both hamzas pronounced as hamzas, and the first changed to a yā'). Some of the commentators (muhashshin) have noted that the author (al-mu'allif) erred in this, and that the changing of the hamza to yā' applies only to the second, not the first. Be attentive to this. That is, there is no reading in which the first is changed to yā'; the changing to yā' is only in the second and not the first. So this is an error on the part of the author, may Allah have mercy on him, or a slip of the pen.

* Student: How is it pronounced if the second is a yā'?
* The Shaykh: ﴿ahaؤlaa'i ayyaakum﴾ [pronounced as written].
* The Student: So it is assimilated (idghām) into the second?
* The Shaykh: No, it is not assimilated, because the second is vowelled, so there is no need... ﴿ahaؤlaa'i ayyaakum﴾.

Also, the author, may Allah have mercy on him, says: ﴿And We will say to those who did wrong, "Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny."﴾ [Saba' 42].

His saying: ﴿And We will say﴾ is conjoined to His saying: ﴿will have power﴾, meaning: "And on that Day We will say: to those who did wrong..." Injustice (ẓulm) linguistically means deficiency; this is the original meaning. From it is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Each of the two gardens brought forth its produce and did not fall short therein at all﴾ [al-Kahf 33], i.e., it did not diminish.

As for the technical or legal meaning: it is the depriving of those entitled to their right, either by procrastinating in what is obligatory, or by violating what is forbidden. Depriving those entitled of their right by procrastinating in what is obligatory is like the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The procrastination of the wealthy is injustice" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2287) and Muslim (1564/33) from Abu Hurayrah].

Or by transgressing against their right, like the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿The blame is only upon those who wrong people and transgress upon the earth without right﴾ [al-Shura 42].

So, the original meaning of injustice is deficiency. What is your evidence?

* Students: ﴿Each of the two gardens brought forth its produce and did not fall short therein at all﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿and did not fall short therein at all﴾.

As for the legal meaning, it is the depriving of those entitled of their right, either by violating a prohibition concerning their right or by procrastinating in an obligation.

His saying: ﴿to those who did wrong﴾ — the author explained it as (disbelieved). Is this an explanation of the meaning or of the intended referent? It is of the intended referent, because injustice in meaning is more general than disbelief.

But the author says: the intended meaning of injustice here is the injustice of disbelief, like the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And the disbelievers are the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah 254], His saying: ﴿Indeed, association [with Allah] is a great injustice﴾ [Luqman 13], and His saying: ﴿Those who believed and did not mix their belief with injustice﴾ [al-An'am 82].

So injustice may be intended to mean disbelief, and it seems the author, may Allah have mercy on him, restricted injustice here to disbelief by the context: ﴿And We will say to those who did wrong, "Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny."﴾ This shows that the intended injustice here is the injustice of disbelief, because whoever denies the Fire is a disbeliever, due to his denial of the report of Allah and His Messenger.

﴿Taste the punishment of the Fire﴾: ﴿Taste﴾ is an imperative verb but it is meant as humiliation. That is, they are told in humiliation: "Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny," meaning the Fire will reach you until you taste it as you taste food.

His saying: ﴿the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny﴾ — how did they deny the Fire? Because they denied the resurrection, and the Fire is only after the resurrection, and they denied that. It follows, a fortiori, that they denied what occurs in the grave of punishment. So they denied completely, and they say: when the soul leaves the body it will never return to it. Here He said: ﴿which you used to deny﴾, while in Surah As-Sajdah He said: ﴿Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny﴾ [al-Sajdah 20]. Accordingly, in the two verses, the description of denial is once with respect to the Fire and once with respect to its punishment. So sometimes they deny the Fire itself, saying there is no Fire, no Hereafter, nothing at all, and sometimes they deny the punishment by the Fire, saying: "How can we be punished by the Fire? How can we remain for ages while in the Fire? When a person enters the Fire he is burnt and finished." So they deny the punishment, and sometimes they deny the Fire itself.

His saying: ﴿which you used to deny﴾ — the prepositional phrase here is connected to ﴿deny﴾, but it was placed first for restriction or for the rhyme (fawāṣil)? Yes, for the rhyme, undoubtedly; this is one aspect, and for restriction. But if we say it is for restriction, a problem arises: they denied the Fire and other things. It is said: since the punishment was by the Fire, they were reminded of their denial of it specifically, because they were punished by it. It is as if they were told: "You are punished by something you used to deny, and otherwise they have another denial."

(﴿And when Our verses are recited to them, clear [in evidence]﴾ — the Quran — ﴿clear﴾: plain, in the tongue of our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) — ﴿they say﴾).

In this conditional sentence, the protasis is ﴿when﴾ [idhā], the verb of the condition is ﴿are recited﴾, and its response is ﴿they say, "This is not but a man..."﴾.

His saying: ﴿This is not but a man﴾ — this ﴿mā﴾ is the negative particle, and here it did not operate. Why? Because of the nullification of the negation. Ibn Malik said in his Alfiyya:

The operation of laysa is given to mā, [only] as long as in [its] negation... [remains]

So when the negation is nullified, there is no operation. And Allah knows best.

* * *

﴿For those who did wrong﴾ [Saba' 42] (...).
﴿So on that Day none of you will have power to benefit or harm one another, and We will say﴾ [Saba' 42] to you.

He said: ﴿And We will say to those who did wrong﴾, and the explicit mention in place of the pronoun, as we have mentioned, has a constant and continuous benefit, which is to draw attention.

It also has a specific benefit in each context according to what it is. Here it is intended for generality, meaning: to those who did wrong, from among these people and others.

It also indicates the cause of the ruling, which is His saying: ﴿And We will say to those who did wrong, "Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny."﴾ What remains? The generality and the indication of the cause of the ruling, which is injustice; for if He had only said "We will say to them," we would not have learned that the reason for Allah's saying to them and rebuking them is injustice.

He said: ﴿And when Our verses are recited to them, clear [in evidence]﴾. We begin with the grammatical analysis first:

His saying: ﴿Our verses, clear﴾ — ﴿clear﴾ is a ḥāl (circumstantial qualifier) of ﴿Our verses﴾, because it is a qualifier after a definite noun; and a qualifier after a definite noun, when it is indefinite or a clause, is a ḥāl. Likewise, qualifiers after definite nouns that are definite are a na't (adjective). A ḥāl and a na't are both descriptions, but if it agrees with its antecedent in definiteness and indefiniteness, it is a na't; otherwise, if the antecedent is definite and the second is indefinite or a clause, it is a ḥāl.

His saying: ﴿They say, "This is not..."﴾ — this is the response of the condition, to the end.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿When Our verses are recited to them, clear﴾, i.e., when Our verses are read to them, and the reader is not specified, so it includes the reader being the Prophet (ﷺ) or others. When the verses of Allah are recited to them, ﴿clear﴾, meaning manifest. What is their manifestness here? Is it that they are plainly the speech of Allah, since they are unable to match them; or that they are clear in what they indicate of lofty meanings that no human could produce; or both? It includes both. They are clear in themselves, plainly not the speech of humans, and clear in their subject matter and in what they indicate, that they are not of human composition, because they do not contradict one another, and do not refute one another. This indicates they are from Allah. If these verses were obscure, they would have some excuse in rejecting them, but they are clear verses, and they have no excuse for rejecting them. Yet, despite this, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿They say, "This is not but a man who wants to turn you away from what your fathers used to worship."﴾ The author, in explaining it, says: (clear in the tongue of our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ)).

﴿They say, "This is not but a man who wants to turn you away from what your fathers used to worship."﴾ ﴿This﴾ refers to the one who brought them and claimed they were from Allah: ﴿not but a man who wants to turn you away﴾. And consider how this sentence carries the contempt and denial that is well known.

Their saying ﴿This﴾ is in the form of the present, though he was absent, for contempt.

Their saying ﴿not but a man﴾ is for denial, because they used the indefinite form, as if they did not know him, as if he were a foreign man among them. ﴿They say, "This is not but a man"﴾ — they did not say, "That man is only a man," but ﴿This is not but a man﴾, out of contempt and denial.

﴿who wants to turn you away﴾ means: he does not want to guide you to the right path, but ﴿wants to turn you away﴾, to divert and prevent you ﴿from what your fathers used to worship﴾. And what did their fathers worship? Idols, of trees, stones and others. This is the aim of this man who brought these verses recited to them; his aim is neither righteousness nor reform. Thus they rejected the truth with this false claim.

His saying ﴿from what your fathers used to worship﴾, and not "from what you used to worship," is to stir zeal in their souls, because a person finds it hard to abandon what his fathers were upon, especially such ignorant people. Had they said "from what you used to worship," it could be said that they worshipped without foundation. But when He said ﴿from what your fathers used to worship﴾, it is as if this worship of these idols were a settled matter upon which the fathers stood, and you should not abandon the creed of your fathers. This is why they say, as Allah related about them in another verse: ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers upon a religion, and indeed we are following in their footsteps, guided﴾ [al-Zukhruf 22], or ﴿following their example﴾ [al-Zukhruf 23], two verses.

﴿from what your fathers used to worship﴾ — of idols; and "fathers" here means what includes the father of the loins (the immediate father) and the forefathers above him, namely the grandfathers and higher ancestors.

His saying ﴿your fathers﴾ — do their mothers count likewise? But a person is moved by zeal for his father more than for his mother, because it is known that the father is a man, and a man is more rational than a woman. So if your fathers worshipped these idols and insisted on worshipping them, and they were the rational ones, then you should not follow this man who wanted to turn you away from what your fathers worshipped.

(And ﴿they said﴾ in the Quran: ﴿This is not but a fabrication, a lie, ﴿invented﴾ against Allah.) I seek refuge in Allah! They slandered the Messenger and they slandered the Quran. Against the Messenger they slandered by what? By his evil intention, and that he does not intend reform, but wants to turn you away from what your fathers worshipped. And they slandered the revelation that this Messenger brought, saying: ﴿This is not but a fabrication, invented﴾. You know that this form is a form of restriction, so by their claim there is nothing true in the Quran; the whole Quran, in totality and in detail, is fabricated invention.

﴿Fabrication﴾ means lie: it is itself a lie, and against whom? Invented against Allah. Because there is an absolute lie that a person utters without attributing it to anyone, and here is a lie that a person fabricates against another. So they say the Quran is a lie and that it is fabricated against Allah. There is no doubt that this claim is false. The Quran, as Allah described it: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice﴾ [al-An'am 115]. Likewise, the Quran is from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as proven by the fact that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, challenged these people to produce its like, and they did not. So this is evidence that it is from Allah, and all its reports are true and correct, contrary to what these people slandered.

﴿And they said, "This is not but a fabrication, invented."﴾ They slandered the Messenger, and slandered what was brought by him, and slandering both is slandering Allah, Mighty and Majestic. How? Because Allah's enabling this Messenger, His support of him, His sending down verses upon him, while he is a liar — is it wisdom or foolishness? Foolishness. And Allah, Mighty and Majestic, supports His Messenger with what He sends down to him and testifies that he is right, and the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, calls people openly and secretly. So if he were lying against Allah, Mighty and Majestic, while Allah supported and enabled him, Allah's enabling him would be in the utmost foolishness, and this is a slander against Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿And those who disbelieved said of the truth when it came to them, "Indeed, [what] this is but evident magic."﴾ This is also a third false claim, but He used the explicit mention in place of the pronoun; He did not say "and they said," but ﴿And those who disbelieved said﴾, to include these and others, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Likewise, no messenger came to those before them but they said, "A magician or a madman."﴾ [al-Dhariyat 52]. So His saying ﴿And those who disbelieved said﴾ includes these and others, and indicates that those who said this statement are disbelievers, since He described them with disbelief, attributing this statement to them, and that would be the cause of their disbelief.

The author said regarding ﴿in﴾ [in], explaining it as (mā) — how is ﴿in﴾ (mā)? That is, ﴿in﴾ is negative.

Now, can ﴿in﴾ occur as a negative? Is it a condition for it to be negative that ﴿illā﴾ come after it?

The answer: No. But when ﴿illā﴾ comes after it, it is negative. Whenever ﴿illā﴾ comes after ﴿in﴾, ﴿in﴾ is negative. We do not say it is negative only when ﴿illā﴾ follows it, because it may come negative without ﴿illā﴾ following it, as in the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿You have no authority for this﴾ [Yunus 68], i.e., you have no authority for this; and yet that sentence has no ﴿illā﴾.

Summary: when ﴿illā﴾ comes after ﴿in﴾, ﴿in﴾ is negative, and it is not necessary that ﴿illā﴾ follow it, because it may be negative without ﴿illā﴾.

We may digress to mention the meanings of ﴿in﴾: it comes negative as here.

It comes conditional, like His saying: ﴿Say, "Whether you conceal what is within your breasts or reveal it, Allah will know it."﴾ [Ali 'Imran 29].

It comes superfluous (zā'idah), like the saying of the poet:

"Banū Ghudāna, mā in antum dhahabun / wa lā ṣarīfun wa lākin antumu l-kha<u>z</u>afu"

It comes as the light form of the heavy (mukhaffafah min al-thaqīlah), like:

"... wa in Mālikun kānat kirāmu l-ma'ādini"

This one is the light form of the heavy.

So it is used in the Arabic language in four ways.

Now, ﴿in hādhā illā siḥrun mubīn﴾ [Saba' 43] (clear). ﴿Magic﴾ (siḥr): linguistically, it is everything hidden. It was called siḥr because it corresponds to al-saḥar, which is the last part of the night, since in the last part of the night things occur hidden, because people are concealed in their houses. So siḥr linguistically is a hidden thing whose matter and cause are concealed. This is why, when clocks first appeared, it was said they were siḥr, and when strange things come upon people that break habit, they say: "This is magic."

So they say that what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought is magic: in their view Moses' staff was magic, and Jesus' raising of the dead by Allah's permission was magic, and this speech that Muhammad (ﷺ) brought is magic — "indeed, there is magic in eloquence" — and they said: this is eloquent speech that bewitches people's minds.

His saying ﴿mubīn﴾ is of the category of deception, meaning that it is evident magic that should not be disputed because of its clarity and manifestness. This is like when you emphasize a thing, saying: "This is a clear, evident matter," even if it is not clearly evident. Indeed, what the Messengers brought of signs is not evidently magic; rather, what is evident is that it is truth and genuine signs. But the deniers, may Allah protect us, dispute the truth.

His saying ﴿mubīn﴾ — the author said it means (clear), because abāna is used intransitively and transitively: you say abāna al-fajr meaning the dawn became manifest, and you say bāna al-fajr.

So here the word ﴿mubīn﴾ means clear (bayyin). This is the closer meaning. As for mubīn meaning abāna, i.e., to make clear and manifest, that is in such a saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿It is only a reminder and a clear Quran﴾ [Ya Sin 69], because the Quran makes the truth clear; so mubīn there is from the transitive abāna, while mubīn here is from the intransitive abāna.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We did not give them any books which they study, nor did We send to them before you any warner﴾ [Saba' 44] (so from where did they deny you).

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 34, verses 42–45 (part 2 of 3)**

The Almighty said: ﴿And We did not give them books which they could study, nor did We send to them any warner before you.﴾ The commentators (mufassirun) differed over its meaning. Some of them said: ﴿And We did not give them books which they could study, nor did We send to them any warner before you﴾ contradicts what you have said. For if they have no knowledge from books they study, and no knowledge from a warner who came to them, then how can they oppose what you are upon? How, then, do they deny you? Accordingly, the meaning of this verse is that their denial of you comes from what?

* A student: From knowledge.
* The Shaykh: No.
* The students: From ignorance.
* The Shaykh: From ignorance, arising from ignorance. For He says, ﴿We did not give them books﴾. He does not say, "We gave them." Pay attention.

﴿We did not give them books which they could study﴾ indicates that what they said about you is true.

﴿Nor did We send to them any warner before you﴾ contradicts what you brought, so that they could say: You are what? A liar and a sorcerer.

So the meaning of the verse is that these people who denied you did not base their denial on what? On knowledge. Not from books, nor from revelation. Not from books which they study and understand, and so know that what you brought contradicts them. Nor from a warner who warned them and cautioned them against what you brought, saying that a lying, fabricating impostor would come, so do not obey him.

Now, if a prophet came to us and said that he is a prophet from Allah, would we deny him?

* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Why? Because we have been warned about these people, as the Prophet ﷺ informed us. But when the Prophet ﷺ came, did those who denied him receive a warning about him and take heed of it? No. Is there any book these people studied that shows the Messenger ﷺ to be upon falsehood? No. This is one aspect, and it is the one the author followed. That is why he said: (So from where did they deny you?)

The second view: Allah, exalted is He, sent Muhammad ﷺ among a people who were unlettered (ummiyyun), who could not read, and to whom no prophet had been sent before. As Allah, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿It is He who sent among the unlettered a messenger from among themselves, reciting to them His verses﴾ [al-Jumu'ah 2]. And Allah, glorified is He, says: ﴿That you may warn a people to whom no warner had come before you﴾ [al-Qasas 46]. That is, it would have been most fitting for these people to rejoice at your message and to accept what you brought. Why? Because they had no books to study, as the Jews and Christians had, and no prophet had been sent to them before you. So they were in the greatest need of you. Whoever is in need of something rejoices in it more, and is more ready to believe its report.
