He said: ﴿My reward is only from Allah﴾, Glorified and Exalted (﴿and He is Witness over all things﴾, Observer who knows my sincerity). ﴿and He is Witness over all things﴾: over everything Allah is a witness, meaning He observes it, and this includes my state with you. He observes that I have delivered and warned you, and He observes that you denied me and opposed me. So my reward is upon Allah, and your punishment is upon Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as He said: ﴿So remind, for you are only a reminder. You are not over them a controller. Except one who turns away and disbelieves. And Allah will punish him with the greatest punishment. Indeed, to Us is their return. Then indeed, upon Us is their account﴾ [al-Ghashiyah 21-26]. Does Allah, Mighty and Majestic, witness what is in a person's soul? Yes, He is a witness even over what no one observes, so Allah, Exalted, is a witness over it.

Then He said: (﴿Say: Indeed, my Lord casts the truth﴾, He throws it to His prophets, ﴿Knower of the unseen﴾ [Saba' 48], of what is hidden from His creation).

His saying: ﴿Indeed, my Lord casts﴾ is a declarative sentence emphasized by "inna," the subject of "inna" being "Rabb" (Lord), and its predicate is the clause "yaqdhifu" (casts). "'Allam al-ghuyub" (Knower of the unseen) is a second predicate, meaning He is also the Knower of the unseen.

His saying: ﴿casts with the truth﴾: qadhf (casting) is throwing with force; throwing with force is called qadhf. And His saying: ﴿with the truth﴾ means with the true word, which is the revelation Allah sent down to His prophets. The apparent meaning of the author's statement is that "qadhf" here is intransitive, not extending beyond the prophets, and that what is meant is the revelation sent down to the messengers. However, the author's statement is open to question, and the correct view is that this verse is explained by the next verse, His saying: ﴿Rather, We cast the truth against falsehood, so it crushes it, and thereupon it departs and vanishes﴾ [al-Anbiya' 18], and that the meaning of the verse is: Say, indeed my Lord casts the truth against falsehood. This is an indication that His truth will wipe out their falsehood, dispel it, and destroy it. As evidence, He also said afterward: ﴿Say: The truth has come, and falsehood can neither originate nor restore﴾ [Saba' 49].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 34, verse 46 (part 2 of 3):

He said: ﴿Says: "He [Allah] casts down the truth; He is the Knower of the unseen."﴾ He said: ﴿ʿAllām﴾ is in the intensive form (sigha al-mubalagha), because the unseen things (al-ghuyub) are many, so it was fitting that knowledge be attributed to them in an intensive manner. There is also intensiveness in it in terms of quality, not only in terms of quantity. In terms of quality, the knowledge of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, concerning the unseen is not superficial knowledge; rather it is deep knowledge that reaches the most hidden of the unseen things. Allah, Exalted, says: ﴿Indeed, nothing is hidden from Allah on the earth or in the heaven﴾ [Ali 'Imran 5]. The word "ghuyub" is the plural of "ghayb," which is that which is absent from a person. Is this limited to the future, or does it also apply to the present and the past?

As for the future, it is clear: no one can know the unseen of the future. Whoever claims knowledge of the unseen in the future is a disbeliever, because Allah says: ﴿Say: No one in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah﴾ [al-Naml 65]. So the one who claims knowledge of the future unseen contradicts the Qur'an, and denying the Qur'an is disbelief.

As for the present and the past, it is in reality a relative unseen (ghayb nisbi). It is unseen to me, but not unseen to the one who witnessed it. If an incident occurred in some city while I am not in that city, it is unseen to me, but it is not unseen to those who witnessed it. Thus, the future is absolute unseen, while the present and the past are relative unseen, which becomes apparent to the one who sees it and does not become apparent to the one who does not see it.

He said: (﴿ʿAllām al-ghuyub﴾: what is absent from His creation in the heavens and the earth. ﴿Say: The truth has come﴾), the author said: (Islam). There is no doubt that Islam is the religion of truth, and that it will prevail over all other religions, as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿It is He who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth, to make it prevail over all religion﴾ [al-Tawba 33]. Had the author generalized and said "the truth has come," meaning that everything the Messenger (ﷺ) reported and everything he brought of rulings is true, it would have been comprehensive.

(﴿And falsehood neither originates nor restores﴾ [Saba 49], i.e., it has left no trace.) This sentence, "mā yubdi'u al-bāṭil wa mā yuʿīd" (falsehood neither originates nor restores), or "mā yubdi'u fulān wa mā yuʿīd," is one of the Arabic idioms, a metaphor (kināya) for the destruction of that thing and its non-existence. Whoever does not originate, meaning does not bring a thing into being from the start, and does not restore what he did first, is non-existent in reality; he has no movement or activity. He is like one who is destroyed. The meaning is: falsehood does not originate anything that manifests from the beginning, and does not restore anything that manifests again. So it is destroyed, with no trace, neither at the beginning nor in restoration. Since the truth has come, and falsehood neither originates nor restores, its meaning is that dominion will belong to whom? It will belong to the truth, to what the Prophet (ﷺ) brought, even if they deny him.

If falsehood concerns reports, it is lying; if it concerns rulings, it is injustice and oppression. Everything that contradicts the command of Allah is injustice and oppression, and even if its people claim that they are just in it, they are liars. So we say that man-made laws that oppose the Shari'ah of Allah are falsehood, and we say they are oppression and injustice. As for what agrees with the Shari'ah, even if it is called a law or a system, it is Shari'ah. That is, if someone drafts specific articles on a ruling that are taken from the Book and the Sunnah, we do not say these are man-made laws or man-made systems; rather we say they are Shari'ah rulings, but arranged into articles, just as the jurists (may Allah have mercy on them) arranged jurisprudence into chapters. The difference lies in the manner of presentation, but otherwise it is truth.

As for codifying the Shari'ah in the sense of introducing rulings that contradict its rulings, this is disbelief: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, they are the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ma'ida 44]. But codifying it in the sense of organizing it and making it into specific articles is not objectionable, on condition that the ruling is not binding by these articles. For obliging judges or rulers, for example, to judge by these articles means they are obliged to judge by what they believe to be other than the truth, because people differ in their ijtihad. For example, a committee may consider the ruling in a matter to be such-and-such, while the judge considers the ruling to be otherwise. So placing them as explanatory, clarifying or indicative materials is without doubt not objectionable, but placing them as binding is not permissible, because people differ in their ijtihad.

(﴿Say: If I go astray﴾ from the truth, ﴿then I only go astray to my own detriment﴾, i.e., the sin of my error falls upon me, ﴿and if I am guided, it is by what my Lord reveals to me﴾ of the Qur'an and wisdom, ﴿indeed He is Hearing﴾ of the supplication, ﴿Near﴾ [Saba 50]).

﴿Say: If I go astray﴾: this is a matter of condescending to the opponent (tanazzul ma'a al-khasm), since it is well known that the Messenger (ﷺ) was the most rightly guided of people. This is like the statement of the believing man from the family of Pharaoh, who said: ﴿Will you kill a man because he says: My Lord is Allah, and he has come to you with clear proofs from your Lord? And if he is a liar, then upon him is his lie; and if he is truthful, some of what he threatens you with will strike you﴾ [Ghafir 28], although that believer believed that he was truthful. But this is a matter of condescending to the opponent in order to compel him to accept the truth.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Say: If I go astray, I only go astray to my own detriment﴾. It is known that a person does not wish to persist in misguiding himself. Likewise the Prophet (ﷺ), if he went astray, his straying would not be only (...) but upon him and upon those who follow him. This is why the straying of a scholar or the slip of a scholar is among the greatest things that corrupt people; the slip of a scholar is not minor, because he is a model and a community. ﴿If I go astray, I only go astray to my own detriment﴾, and there is nothing of that upon you. ﴿And if I am guided﴾: he did not say "then that is from myself," but attributed it to what the revelation sent down from Allah brought. This is why he said: ﴿then it is by what my Lord reveals to me﴾. The "bi" here is causal, and "mā" is either a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyya) or a relative pronoun (mawṣūla). If it is a relative pronoun, its returning pronoun is omitted, the sense being: "by what my Lord reveals to me," and if it is a verbal-noun particle, it needs no returning pronoun.

His saying ﴿what my Lord reveals to me﴾: revelation (wahy) linguistically is informing with concealment and speed. This is the linguistic meaning: informing with concealment and speed, whether that informing is by whispering, by a sign of the eye, or by a sign of the hand. From it is His saying: ﴿So he came out to his people from the sanctuary and signaled to them to glorify [Allah] morning and evening﴾ [Maryam 11]. It was not speech, because Allah said to him: ﴿Your sign is that you will not speak to the people for three days except by gestures﴾ [Ali 'Imran 41]. So "awḥā ilayhim" means "signaled to them." Thus wahy linguistically is informing with concealment and speed; so they said. In the Shari'ah, however, it is Allah, glorified and exalted, informing one of His creatures with a law that he is commanded to convey or not commanded to convey. If he is commanded to convey it, he is a messenger; if he is not commanded, he is a prophet.

His saying ﴿what my Lord reveals to me﴾: the idafa (attribution) here is a particular attribution. "My Lord": although Allah is the Lord of him and of others, the attribution here is a particular one, conveying what? It conveys care and kindness, because among the greatest blessings of Allah upon the servant is that revelation of the message be sent to him, so that he attains the highest rank among the children of Adam.

Likewise, among the blessing of Allah upon the servant is that He inspires him to acquire this message through learning; this is why scholars are the heirs of the prophets. So it is among the greatest blessings. This is why He said: ﴿by what my Lord reveals to me﴾, attributing lordship to Himself, because this particular lordship entails care, support, mercy and kindness.

﴿Indeed He is Hearing, Near﴾: "Indeed He is Hearing": the author said: (of the supplication). The correct view is that the verse here is general: He hears everything, not only supplication. He hears what I say to you, He hears what you say to me, and He hears my supplication too, in the sense of responding.

It has already passed with us that the hearing attributed to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is of two kinds:
Hearing in the sense of perceiving what is heard, and hearing in the sense of responding to what is heard.

Hearing in the sense of perceiving what is heard is sometimes meant as a warning (tahdid), sometimes meant as support (ta'yid), and sometimes meant to show comprehensiveness (bayan al-ihata), that is, Allah's encompassing of everything heard. These are three things.

Sometimes it is meant as a warning, like what? 
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes. And sometimes it is meant as support; an example?
* Student: His saying, Exalted, about Musa and Harun: ﴿Indeed I am with you both; I hear and I see﴾ [Ta-Ha 46].
* Shaykh: His saying about Musa and Harun: ﴿Indeed I am with you both; I hear and I see﴾ [Ta-Ha 46].

And sometimes it is meant to show comprehensiveness?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: ﴿Concerning her husband and complaining to Allah, and Allah hears your dialogue﴾ [al-Mujadila 1].

As for hearing in the sense of responding, it is like His saying: ﴿Indeed my Lord is the Hearer of supplication﴾ [Ibrahim 39], and the worshipper's saying: "Allah hears the one who praises Him."

As for His saying ﴿Near﴾: "qarib" is either an active participle or an attributive adjective (sifa mushabbaha), and the hidden pronoun in it returns to whom? It returns to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Every verb or attribute whose pronoun returns to Allah means the Essence of Allah. Pay attention to this rule mentioned by Ibn al-Qayyim in Mukhtasar al-Sawa'iq: every act or attribute that bears a pronoun returning to Allah means the Essence of Allah. But you must keep in mind the exaltation of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, above what does not befit Him, so the nearness here is the nearness of His mercy, or the nearness of His knowledge, or the nearness of His hearing or seeing, or the nearness of His Essence. Which one?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, not (...). He is near, that is, in His Essence. This is why Ibn al-Qayyim explicitly stated that He is near in His Essence. But you must know that along with His nearness in His Essence, He is established upon His Throne, so much so that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed the One you call upon is nearer to one of you than the neck of his mount" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6610), Muslim (2704/44), the wording from al-Nasa'i (7633), from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari]. He said this while they were riding their mounts. Yet, with all this, we must exalt Allah above what does not befit Him, so that we do not imagine that He is with us in place. This is impossible; rather He is near in His Essence while being exalted.

Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyya mentioned this in al-'Aqida al-Wasitiyya, saying: "He is above in His nearness, near in His loftiness."

Do not think that combining nearness and loftiness above the heavens is contradictory. Why? First: because Allah Himself combined them for Himself, and indicated both in the Book of Allah, and the Book of Allah cannot indicate contradiction: ﴿And if it had been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much discrepancy﴾ [al-Nisa' 82].

Second: Allah, glorified and exalted, is not like anything. That is, even if it were supposed that nearness and loftiness are contradictory with respect to creatures, that does not necessarily apply to the Creator. Why? Because "there is nothing like unto Him." This is why we say: Allah, Exalted, descends to the lowest heaven every night while He is nonetheless established upon His Throne. Do not say: this is impossible. We say: this is impossible for whom? For the created. As for the Creator, we must believe what He has informed us of His attributes, namely His istiwa' upon His Throne and His descent to the lowest heaven, and we say that this is possible with respect to the Creator.

The third aspect by which we combine nearness and loftiness: a thing may be high and yet near even to creatures, such as the moon. The moon is high, yet near, as if it were with you, in the place where you are, and its light reaches the earth while it is in the sky. I think two verses on this meaning passed with us in rhetoric:

"Near to the hands of the needy, yet far from every equal in generosity and rivalry,
Like the full moon, which rises high, yet its light is near to the travelers at night."

The point is that when Allah attributes something to Himself, whether an act or an attribute, it is not permissible for us to deviate from it by converting that attributed thing into something else; for if we do so, the people of interpretation (ta'wil) among the Mu'tazila and Ash'ari will argue against us, saying: "How do you interpret this verse, for example, while you reject our interpretation in other verses or other texts?" If you say to them: "This is prevented by reason," they say: "We also hold that the apparent meanings of verses or hadiths are prevented by reason. But if you keep the texts as they are, on their apparent indication, while exalting Allah above what does not befit Him, you will be safe in your religion, and safe before Allah, Mighty and Majestic, when He asks you on the Day of Resurrection: how did you handle My speech, and how did you take it out of its apparent meaning?" And you will also be safe from the objection of the people of interpretation.

It has already passed with us in the Summary of al-Hamawiyya that the philosophers who deny the resurrection, and indeed deny everything, argued against the Mu'tazila and the people of negation (ta'til), saying: "How do you permit interpretation in the verses and hadiths about the Attributes, but not permit interpretation in the texts about the resurrection? If you interpret in this, interpret in that; otherwise your contradiction is evident." We have already mentioned the answer of the Mu'tazila to the philosophers. What did they say to them?

They said: "We have known by necessary consistency that the Messengers came with affirming the resurrection, and we have known that the doubt that prevents it is corrupt; therefore it is obligatory to affirm it." O brothers, this argument is among the most important matters for the student of knowledge in the science of tawhid. We mentioned that this argument with which the Mu'tazila repelled the objection of the philosophers was used by the People of the Sunna against the Mu'tazila, saying: "We have known by necessity that the Messenger came with affirming the Attributes of Allah, and we have known the corruption of the doubt that prevents it; therefore it is obligatory to affirm them." Applying the principle consistently in this and that is what brings safety. But to be contradictory, interpreting in one matter and keeping the texts on their apparent meaning in another, is a delusion and a weakness of method.

So the point is: "near" here, we do not say: near in His knowledge, or near in His mercy, or near in His hearing, or the like, thereby restricting it to something, because if you say: near in His mercy, or His hearing, or His seeing, or His knowledge, or the like, you have restricted it. But if you say: near in His Essence, it includes everything that this Essence entails of attributes, so it is more comprehensive.

Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyya explicitly stated, in explaining the hadith of the Descent, that He, glorified and exalted, is near in Himself, and his student Ibn al-Qayyim said: He is near in His Essence. Yet, along with that, we must know with certainty that He is near while He is in the heaven upon His Throne, and there is no contradiction in this. You have learned the answer to what seems contradictory, and that the answer is from how many aspects? From three aspects. And Allah knows best.

* * *

(...) He did not ask anyone for a reward for conveying the message and warning the people, because He said: ﴿Say: Whatever reward I have asked of you, it is yours﴾ [Saba 47].

* Among the benefits also: condescension toward the opponent, or on the assumption that I had asked, ﴿then it is yours﴾.

* Another of its benefits: the prohibition of taking a wage for conveying religious knowledge. Its basis is that it contradicts the guidance of the Prophet (ﷺ); this is one aspect. Another aspect is that conveying the Shari'ah is obligatory upon a person, and what is obligatory is not permissible to take a wage for.

If you ask: is it permissible to take payment for teaching the Qur'an?

The answer: the scholars differed on this in two opinions, because the apparent meanings of the texts differ. Some of them said it is permissible, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The most deserving of what you take a wage for is the Book of Allah" [reported by al-Bukhari (5737) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas]. Also, this man does not take a wage for reciting the Qur'an; if he took a wage for reciting the Qur'an, we would say that is forbidden. Rather he takes a wage for teaching, for the effort and for settling this man. Therefore, if the matter were obligatory upon him, meaning if it were obligatory for him to teach this man, then taking a wage for it would be forbidden.

The third aspect: the Prophet ﷺ made it his dowry in marriage, saying: "I have married her to you for what you know of the Qur'an" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2310) and Muslim (1425/76) from the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd al-Sa'idi]. The dowry in marriage is a payment, as in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿So for what you have enjoyed from them, give them their payments﴾ [An-Nisa' 24]. Since the Prophet ﷺ made it a dowry in marriage, this shows that it is permissible to take compensation for teaching it.

Also, the Prophet ﷺ permitted taking a herd of sheep from the group who recited over the chief of a tribe who had been stung, and they took a herd of sheep from him, and the Prophet ﷺ approved of that [al-Bukhari (5737) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas]. They were not paid for reciting the Qur'an, but because they treated that stung man. This is the correct view: it is permissible to take a wage for teaching the Qur'an. However, if teaching the Qur'an is obligatory, as in the early period of Islam, then taking a wage for it is forbidden.

Would it be permissible, on the view that taking a wage for it is forbidden, to take a stipend from the public treasury (bayt al-mal) for the teacher of the Qur'an?
The answer: Yes, because this is not a wage. For this reason, it is permissible for the muezzin and the imam to take from the public treasury what helps them in their adhan and their leading of prayer.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the sincerity of the Prophet ﷺ in his proclamation and his call, as shown in His words: ﴿My reward is only from Allah﴾ [Saba' 47]. It is clear that he seeks reward from whom? From Allah. This is sincerity.

* Also among its benefits: the loftiness and high aspiration of the Messenger ﷺ, in that he chose the greater reward over the lesser, as shown in His words: ﴿My reward is only from Allah﴾.

* Also among its benefits: threatening the opponent with what the names and attributes of Allah require, as shown in His words: ﴿And He is Witness over all things﴾ [Saba' 47]. In this there is a threat to them: meaning, He will witness your denial and his proclamation.

* Also among its benefits: citing Allah's affirmation of a person's truthfulness in what he says. From where is this derived? From citing Allah the Exalted's affirmation of a person's words as true, as shown in His words: ﴿And He is Witness over all things﴾. This is supported by the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿But Allah bears witness to what He has sent down to you; He sent it down with His knowledge, and the angels bear witness﴾ [An-Nisa' 166]. The scholars said: Allah the Exalted's testimony to His Messenger, that what he brought is the truth, includes both verbal testimony and testimony by action, which is His affirmation of what he called people to and of permitting their wealth, their blood, and their families if they do not respond to him.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: Indeed, my Lord casts the truth, Knower of the unseen﴾ [Saba' 47].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the excellence of the Messenger ﷺ, through attributing lordship (rububiyyah) to him: the Lordship of Allah toward him, ﴿Say: Indeed, my Lord﴾. Is this lordship specific or general? Specific.

* Also among its benefits: the demonstration of the strength of Allah the Exalted, in that He hurls the truth against falsehood with force. Indeed, He says: ﴿Indeed, my Lord casts the truth﴾, meaning He hurls it with strength and vehemence against falsehood.

* Also among its benefits: the comprehensiveness of Allah's knowledge of what is witnessed and what is unseen. What is unseen is shown by His words: ﴿Knower of the unseen﴾, and what is witnessed is included a fortiori. That is, if He knows the unseen, then what is witnessed is all the more known.

* Also among them: the affirmation that what the Prophet ﷺ brought is true, as shown in His words: ﴿casts the truth﴾.

* Also among them: a threat to these deniers that their falsehood will be overcome. By what means? By the way of the true Islam, so their falsehood is overcome. This is supported by His words: ﴿Say: The truth has come, and falsehood can neither originate nor restore﴾ [Saba' 49]. ﴿The truth has come﴾: the truth is what (...). Falsehood is everything that opposes the truth.

﴿Say: If I go astray, I only go astray against myself; and if I am guided, it is by what my Lord reveals to me. Indeed, He is Hearing, Near﴾ [Saba' 50]. In this there is a challenge to these deniers of the Messenger ﷺ: that if he were astray, the effect of his error would show upon himself, and Allah would destroy him and not allow him to continue. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And if he had fabricated some sayings against Us, We would have seized him by the right hand, then We would have cut from him the aorta; and none of you could have held Us off from him﴾ [Al-Haqqah 44–47]. So if he were astray in what he brought, his error would fall upon himself, and his affair would be made clear.

Perhaps you have heard what Allah the Exalted revealed about the deniers who claimed prophethood and whom Allah destroyed, such as Musaylimah al-Kadhdhab and al-Aswad al-'Ansi and others. Allah the Exalted has made the misguidance and lying of all of them manifest. I once recounted to you what is related about the signs of Musaylimah; do you remember it? They say: Musaylimah claimed to be a messenger, and a well among his people's wells dried up, and only a little water remained. They came to him complaining of this matter. He wanted to imitate the Messenger ﷺ, so he took some water, put it in his mouth, then spat it back into the water, and waited for the water to surge until it reached the edge of the well. But the water in it dried up. Is this a sign or not? It is a sign of his lying. And a bald boy was brought to him, bald meaning he had only a little hair on him. They came to him so he would wipe his head, so that thick hair would appear. When he wiped his head, the hair that was there fell out. This was a sign of his lying.

So Allah the Exalted, in His wisdom, never allows a liar to be empowered, whoever he may be. Even a liar after the Messenger ﷺ, if he lies about what he calls people to, and he calls people to the truth for show and reputation, Allah the Exalted must make his affair manifest to people, certainly.

And whatever a person's disposition may be, even if he thinks it hidden from people, it will become known:

Here He says: ﴿Say: If I go astray, I only go astray against myself﴾ [Saba' 50], meaning: my affair and my error will become clear.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: acknowledging to Allah the Exalted the favour He has bestowed. As shown in His words: ﴿and if I am guided, it is by what my Lord reveals to me﴾ [Saba' 50].

* Also among them: that a person should attribute error to himself, and attribute correctness to whom? To Allah the Exalted, because (...). When we are correct, should we say: "by what our Lord reveals to us," or "by what our Lord revealed to His Prophet"? The latter is correct. So when we are correct, it is obligatory to attribute the blessing to its Giver, the Exalted, who is Allah the Exalted, and not to boast and consider it from our own selves. As for error, it is upon ourselves, because we are its cause.

* Also in it: the affirmation that the Prophet ﷺ is a messenger, as shown in His words: ﴿by what my Lord reveals to me﴾.

* Among its benefits: that reflection upon revelation, the Qur'an and the Sunnah, is a cause of guidance. Because the "bi" (by) in His words ﴿by what my Lord reveals to me﴾ is causal, and if that is a cause of guidance, then it is part of reason and insight that we reflect upon Allah's revelation and His law, and that we not seek correctness from anything other than them. We should not seek correctness from what so-and-so said and so-and-so said, but from what Allah and His Messenger said. For this reason Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Knowledge is what Allah said, what His Messenger said,
And what the Companions said; they are the people of true knowing.
Setting yourself against them in opposition out of folly
Between the Messenger and the opinion of so-and-so is not knowledge.

And he said in another place:

Knowledge is knowing guidance through its proof,
That is not the same as imitation; the two are not equal.

So the point is that guidance has a cause, which is reflection upon what Allah the Exalted revealed to His Prophet ﷺ.

* Among the benefits of the verse: the affirmation of causes, as shown in His words: ﴿by what my Lord reveals to me﴾, and that they are effective by Allah's permission, not effective in themselves. In this is a refutation of the Ash'aris, who say that causes do not act by themselves. They even say that when paper burns in fire, it was not burned by the fire, but burned at the fire, not by it. And when a glass bottle is struck by a stone and breaks, they say it was not broken by the stone, but broke at it. Look at the intellects! Why? They say: because if you affirm that the cause has an intrinsic effect, you have associated a partner with the Mighty Allah (shirk), since nothing acts by itself except Allah the Exalted. So if you affirm that the pebble breaks the glass, the pebble itself breaks the glass, and this is shirk with Allah. This means you have made this thing affect something. Do you understand?

A man was brought meat, and he began to cut it with a knife. Do we say it was cut by the knife? It was cut at the knife, not by it. See how the intellects reach this state. Now, the pebble is placed by the glass, placed gently on top of it: will it break? Now suppose the stone approaches the glass with approach and does not touch it, but rubs around it...
